Title: `exclude-newer-package` silently ignored by `uv pip compile` when combined with global `exclude-newer`
Text:
`exclude-newer-package` silently ignored by `uv pip compile` when combined with global `exclude-newer`

### Summary

First of all, thank you for contributing this amazing tool to the community. 

The [documentation](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/reference/settings/#exclude-newer-package) mentions that a global `exclude-newer` setting can be overwritten by using package specific `exclude-newer-package` settings. 

> Set a package to false to exempt it from the global [exclude-newer](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/reference/settings/#exclude-newer) constraint entirely.

This does not seem to work with `uv pip compile`

```sh
# create minimal requirements file with frequently updated package
printf "boto3" > req.in

# create config file 1 - global exclude-newer
printf 'exclude-newer = "7 days"\n' > config1.toml

# create config file 2 - global exclude-newer and then per-package overwrite
printf 'exclude-newer = "7 days"\nexclude-newer-package = { "boto3" = false }\n' > config2.toml

# compile environment
uv pip compile req.in 
# boto3==1.43.2

uv pip compile req.in --config-file config1.toml
# boto3==1.42.96

uv pip compile req.in --config-file config2.toml
# would have expected boto3==1.43.2, found boto3==1.42.96
```

I am not sure if I am misunderstanding how `--exclude-newer-package` works or in which context it works, but I expected the package level overwrite to work in the `config2.toml` examples

---

This behavior is consistent when using the CLI flags instead of a config file - although it seems the `uv pip compile` documentation does not explicitly mention the per-package-reset of global `exclude-newer` AFAICT. 

```sh
echo "boto3" > req.in

uv pip compile req.in --no-config -U
uv pip compile req.in --no-config -U  --exclude-newer "7 days"
uv pip compile req.in --no-config -U  --exclude-newer "7 days" --exclude-newer-package "boto3=false"
```

### Platform

Darwin 25.3.0 arm64

### Version

uv 0.11.8 (0e961dd9a 2026-04-27 aarch64-apple-darwin)

### Python version

Python 3.12.11

Title: `[tool.uv.build-backend.data]` files are not installed in editable mode
Text:
`[tool.uv.build-backend.data]` files are not installed in editable mode

### Summary

Files declared in `[tool.uv.build-backend.data]` are correctly packaged into the wheel by `uv build`, and a non-editable `uv pip install <wheel>` correctly copies them to the right destination (e.g., the `purelib` slot lands at site-packages root, `scripts` at the venv's `bin/`).

But an editable install (`uv pip install -e .`) silently skips them: no data files land, no warning. The dropped files are gone in editable mode whether they're `.pth` files, binaries, configs, etc.

```toml
# pyproject.toml
[build-system]
build-backend = "uv_build"
requires = ["uv_build>=0.11,<0.12"]

[project]
name = "mypkg"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.12"

[tool.uv.build-backend.data]
purelib = "data"
```

Layout:

```tree
uv-bug/
├── pyproject.toml
├── data/
│   └── mypkg-startup.pth
└── src/
    └── mypkg/
        └── __init__.py
```

Commands

```bash
mkdir uv-bug && cd uv-bug && uv venv
mkdir -p src/mypkg data && touch src/mypkg/__init__.py
echo 'import sys; print("[pth] fired", file=sys.stderr)' > data/mypkg-startup.pth
# Save the `pyproject.toml` block shown above as `uv-bug/pyproject.toml`.
export VIRTUAL_ENV="$PWD/.venv"  # so `uv pip install` targets this venv

# editable install: silent
# .pth never lands at site-packages root, doesn't fire
uv pip install -e .
.venv/bin/python -c ''

# non-editable install: .pth lands at site-packages root, fires on every startup
uv build --wheel
uv pip install --force-reinstall dist/*.whl
.venv/bin/python -c ''   # → "[pth] fired"
```

`<name>-<version>.data/` is the canonical way to ship arbitrary files alongside a Python package. With editable installs silently dropping them, development of any such project has a gap from production behavior in and editable dev setup.

### Additional context

[PEP 660](https://peps.python.org/pep-0660/) states that editable installs should match the regular-install behavior:

> When a project is installed in editable mode, users expect the installation to behave identically as a regular installation.

So `uv pip install -e .` silently dropping a `[tool.uv.build-backend.data]` can also be considered a divergence there.

For reference, Hatchling does not have this issue, one can use `tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel.force-include`.

```toml
# pyproject.toml
[build-system]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"
requires = ["hatchling"]

[project]
name = "mypkg"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.12"

[tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel]
packages = ["src/mypkg"]

[tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel.force-include]
"data/mypkg-startup.pth" = "mypkg-startup.pth"
```

`uv pip install -e .` against this `pyproject.toml` lands `mypkg-startup.pth` at site-packages root, and a fresh `.venv/bin/python -c ''` fires it, matching my desired behavior.

I think it's worth extending `uv_build`'s editable hook to ship `[tool.uv.build-backend.data]` entries the same way hatchling's `force-include` does. Or at least emitting a warning when a data file is silently skipped in editable mode.

### Platform

Darwin 25.3.0 arm64

### Version

uv 0.11.8 (Homebrew 2026-04-27 aarch64-apple-darwin)

### Python version

Python 3.12.8
Reply: While I agree that we should handle data files in editables, I recommend against including custom startup `.pth` files, they create hard to debug problems and aren't well supported by tooling such as type checkers and linters.

Text:

> To create a new project that uses the uv build backend, use uv init:

> ```

> ```
> uv init [OPTIONS] [PATH]
> ```
> ...
> ```
> [--app](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/reference/cli/#uv-init--app), --application
> ```
> Create a project for an application.
> This is the default behavior if --lib is not requested.
> ...
> By default, an application is not intended to be built and distributed as a Python package. The --package option can be used to create an application that is distributable, e.g., if you want to distribute a command-line interface via PyPI.

Using uv 0.11.8 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu)

Title: Unable to use system-installed PyGObject (GTK) in uv venv, causing matplotlib to fall back to non-interactive backend
Text:
Unable to use system-installed PyGObject (GTK) in uv venv, causing matplotlib to fall back to non-interactive backend

### Summary

When using a virtual environment created by `uv venv` (without `--system-site-packages`), Python cannot import the `gi` module even though the necessary system package (`python-gobject`) is fully installed via the system package manager (Arch Linux, `pacman`). This causes matplotlib to fall back to the non-interactive `Agg` backend, preventing any plot windows from appearing.

The core issue is that standard virtual environments isolate from system site‑packages. While this is correct for pure Python packages, it breaks commonly used GUI libraries (GTK, Qt, Tk) that are often installed at the system level.

Current workarounds (`--system-site-packages`, manually compiling `PyGObject` in every project, `.pth` files) are fragile, non‑portable, or destroy environment isolation. A native `uv` mechanism to handle system‑level GUI dependencies would greatly improve the user experience for the many developers and scientists who rely on interactive plotting on Linux.

Desired solutions could include:
- A way to automatically detect and expose system packages required for common GUI backends.
- A built‑in hook or plugin system (similar to `virtualenvwrapper`'s `postmkvirtualenv`) allowing users to run custom steps after venv creation.
- A command‑line flag to include specific system packages (more granular than `--system-site-packages`).
- Official documentation or a recipe that solves the “matplotlib + GTK/Qt on Linux” problem once and for all.

### Example

## Current behavior (broken)

$ pacman -Q python-gobject
python-gobject 3.56.2-1

$ uv venv
$ source .venv/bin/activate
$ uv pip install matplotlib

$ python -c "import gi"
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 1, in <module>
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'gi'

$ python -c "import matplotlib; print(matplotlib.get_backend())"
agg

## Desired behavior

After a hypothetical `uv` command like `uv venv --with-system-gui` (or an equivalent hook), the same setup would work out of the box:

$ uv venv --with-system-gui   # or similar mechanism
$ source .venv/bin/activate
$ uv pip install matplotlib

$ python -c "import gi; print('gi loaded successfully')"
gi loaded successfully

$ python -c "import matplotlib; print(matplotlib.get_backend())"
GTK3Agg   # or any interactive backend

This would allow interactive matplotlib plots to appear immediately, without additional manual steps.

Title: 0.11.9 release missing GitHub Artifact Attestations
Text:
0.11.9 release missing GitHub Artifact Attestations

## Disclaimer
This summary was created by AI. I validated that the findings were correct.
## Summary
The `0.11.9` release artifacts are missing GitHub Artifact Attestations (SLSA provenance). This causes tools that verify attestations before installing (e.g., [mise](https://github.com/jdx/mise)) to fail when attempting to install `uv@0.11.9`.
The [release notes](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/releases/tag/0.11.9) mention:
> Note due to a timeout publishing to crates.io, the GitHub portion of this release was published manually by a maintainer using the artifacts built in CI.

This manual publish appears to have skipped the attestation generation step.
## Reproduction
### Verify 0.11.9 (fails)
```bash
$ gh release download 0.11.9 --repo astral-sh/uv --pattern "uv-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz" --dir /tmp/uv-test
$ gh attestation verify /tmp/uv-test/uv-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz --repo astral-sh/uv
Error: HTTP 404: Not Found (https://api.github.com/repos/astral-sh/uv/attestations/sha256:ac3e5051edbf30613b0f90d1c18d4807fea6b246f37490799fee0c1284a658b2?per_page=30&predicate_type=https://slsa.dev/provenance/v1)
```
### Verify 0.11.8 (succeeds)
```bash
$ gh release download 0.11.8 --repo astral-sh/uv --pattern "uv-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz" --dir /tmp/uv-test-8
$ gh attestation verify /tmp/uv-test-8/uv-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz --repo astral-sh/uv
# (exits 0, no output — verification successful)
```
## Impact
Tools that rely on GitHub Artifact Attestations for supply-chain verification cannot install `uv@0.11.9`. For example, [mise](https://github.com/jdx/mise) (which uses the `aqua` backend to install `uv`) fails with:
```
mise ERROR Failed to install aqua:astral-sh/uv@latest: GitHub artifact attestations verification failed:
Verification failed: Workflow verification failed: expected 'astral-sh/uv/.github/workflows/release.yml',
found certificate: None, provenance: None
```
This breaks CI pipelines that use `mise` to install `uv` without pinning to a specific version (i.e., using `uv@latest`).
## Expected behavior
All release artifacts should have GitHub Artifact Attestations attached, as documented in the release notes' "Verifying GitHub Artifact Attestations" section.
## Suggested fix
Either:
1. Re-publish the attestations for the existing 0.11.9 artifacts (if possible), or
2. Document this as a known limitation of the 0.11.9 release and recommend pinning to 0.11.8 until 0.11.10 is released through the standard CI pipeline.
Reply:
We're planning to make a new release soon that will have attestations, in the meantime feel free to pin to 0.11.8 if lack of these causes issues. 

> https://releases.astral.sh/github/uv/releases/download/0.11.9/uv-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz 404-s for me as well

This is covered by https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/19282 and should be resolved.

Title: Regression in 0.11.9: `Failed to deserialize cache entry: invalid ID` for IDs written by older uv versions
Text:
Regression in 0.11.9: `Failed to deserialize cache entry: invalid ID` for IDs written by older uv versions

> ⚠️ **Note:** This issue was investigated and drafted with AI assistance (GitHub Copilot). The reproducer below has been executed and the failure was confirmed locally.

### Summary

Since 0.11.9 (PR #19201, "Remove our dependency on nanoid"), uv fails with `invalid ID: "<id>" (must be 16 ID characters in the alphabet)` when it encounters cache entries that were written by an older uv version. Older uv used `nanoid` with a 21-character token; the new `uv-fastid` deserializer strictly requires exactly 16 characters, so any pre-existing 21-character ID on disk now causes a hard failure instead of a cache miss.

The cache bucket version was intentionally not bumped in #19201, so existing caches on shared/CI workers are effectively poisoned after upgrading to 0.11.9 / 0.11.10.

### Reproduction

Self-contained shell reproducer (only requires `python3` + network for pip):

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Reproducer for uv 0.11.9/0.11.10 regression:
#   "Failed to deserialize cache entry: invalid ID ... (must be 16 ID characters in the alphabet)"
set -euo pipefail

WORK="$(mktemp -d)"
echo "Workdir: $WORK"
cd "$WORK"

export UV_CACHE_DIR="$WORK/uv-cache"
mkdir -p "$UV_CACHE_DIR"

mkdir -p pkg/src/dummy_pkg
cat > pkg/pyproject.toml <<'EOF'
[build-system]
requires = ["setuptools>=42"]
build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"

[project]
name = "dummy-pkg"
version = "0.0.1"
EOF
: > pkg/src/dummy_pkg/__init__.py

python3 -m venv pkgbuild-venv
./pkgbuild-venv/bin/pip install -q build
./pkgbuild-venv/bin/python -m build --sdist --outdir dist pkg >/dev/null
SDIST="$(ls "$WORK"/dist/*.tar.gz)"

install_uv() {
    python3 -m venv "$2"
    "$2/bin/pip" install -q "uv==$1"
}

echo "=== Step 1: prime cache with uv 0.11.8 ==="
install_uv 0.11.8 "$WORK/uv-old"
python3 -m venv "$WORK/target-venv"
"$WORK/uv-old/bin/uv" pip install \
    --python "$WORK/target-venv/bin/python" \
    --reinstall --no-deps "$SDIST"

echo "=== Step 2: inspect IDs in the cache ==="
find "$UV_CACHE_DIR" -maxdepth 4 -type d -name 'archive-*' -print -exec sh -c '
    ls "$1" | head -n 5 | while read -r name; do
        printf "  %s (len=%d)\n" "$name" "${#name}"
    done
' _ {} \;

echo "=== Step 3: rerun with uv 0.11.10 against the SAME cache ==="
install_uv 0.11.10 "$WORK/uv-new"
"$WORK/uv-new/bin/uv" pip install \
    --python "$WORK/target-venv/bin/python" \
    --reinstall --no-deps "$SDIST"
```

### Observed output

```
=== Step 2: inspect IDs in the cache ===
/tmp/tmp.SA4yr9SC6n/uv-cache/archive-v0
  SzRiWVFFInsNaf0g33NFd (len=21)
  UKJkCZ3IOEXWTD5T0Le59 (len=21)

=== Step 3: rerun with uv 0.11.10 against the SAME cache ===
uv 0.11.10 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu)
Using Python 3.14.4 environment at: target-venv
  × Failed to build `dummy-pkg @
  │ file:///tmp/tmp.SA4yr9SC6n/dist/dummy_pkg-0.0.1.tar.gz`
  ├─▶ Failed to deserialize cache entry
  ╰─▶ invalid ID: "HM0NxJml5hc7UjbfTWT1r" (must be 16 ID characters in the
      alphabet)
```

The failing ID is exactly 21 characters — the old `nanoid` length. Note also that during the priming step uv 0.11.10 already prints `WARNING: Cache entry deserialization failed, entry ignored` for some entries, suggesting there is already a graceful-degrade path elsewhere in the codebase that the failing call site does not use.

### Expected behavior

Unrecognized/legacy ID formats should be treated as a cache miss (or be ignored / migrated), not aborted with a hard error — consistent with the discussion on #19201 where bumping the bucket was considered acceptable specifically to avoid this class of failure.

### Original CI failure (real-world trigger)

```
× Failed to build `voraus-release-test @ file:///.../voraus_release_test-2.25.1.dev8+g5bd0c2738.tar.gz`
├─▶ Failed to deserialize cache entry
╰─▶ invalid ID: "gtl3Kss14gljY4ur63X_i" (must be 16 ID characters in the alphabet)
```

Triggered via `tox-uv ~=1.29.0` (which pulls `uv<1,>=0.9.1`) on a long-lived Jenkins agent whose cache was previously populated by uv ≤ 0.11.8.

### Platform

Linux (Debian-based Jenkins build agent and reproduced locally on Linux x86_64), Python 3.11 / 3.14.

### Version

```
Broken:    uv 0.11.9, uv 0.11.10
Last good: uv 0.11.8
```
Reply: Thanks for the report. We'll look into this.

Title: Installation fails if a direct dependency pins a prerelease package
Text:
Installation fails if a direct dependency pins a prerelease package

### Summary

Installing a non-prerelease package that pins a prerelease package fails. It suggests to use `--prerelease=allow`, but this is bad UX IMO, as there is only one correct way to do things here. Arguably worse, it means people will silently not get the latest version when installing.

We just released `max==26.3.0` which depends on `mojo-compiler==1.0.0b1`. Trying to install `max==26.3.0` gives this:

```sh
~/Documents/modular/scratch$ uv pip install max==26.3.0
  × No solution found when resolving dependencies:
  ╰─▶ Because there is no version of mojo-compiler==1.0.0b1 and max-core==26.3.0 depends on mojo-compiler==1.0.0b1, we can conclude that max-core==26.3.0 cannot be used.
      And because max==26.3.0 depends on max-core==26.3.0 and you require max==26.3.0, we can conclude that your requirements are unsatisfiable.

      hint: `mojo-compiler` was requested with a pre-release marker (e.g., mojo-compiler==1.0.0b1), but pre-releases weren't enabled (try: `--prerelease=allow`)
```

My understanding is that the resolver completely ignores prelease packages unless one of two things happens:
1. The package is specifically requested
2. `--prerelease=allow` is set.

However in this case, there is no way to install `max==26.3.0` without prerelease packages. I believe in this case (at least) we shouldn't need `--prerelease=allow`. I've also seen another case like this:
```sh
~/Documents/modular/scratch$ uv pip install sglang==0.5.10
  × No solution found when resolving dependencies:
  ╰─▶ Because only flash-attn-4<4.0.0b4 is available and sglang==0.5.10 depends on flash-attn-4>=4.0.0b4, we can conclude that sglang==0.5.10 cannot be used.
      And because you require sglang==0.5.10, we can conclude that your requirements are unsatisfiable.

      hint: `flash-attn-4` was requested with a pre-release marker (e.g., flash-attn-4>=4.0.0b4), but pre-releases weren't enabled (try: `--prerelease=allow`)
```

Perhaps if the requirements are unsatisfiable without prereleases, we could allow them (or at least the bare minimum necessary to resolve).

Admittedly, I think the `--prerelease=allow` flag has caused more headaches for me than problems it's solved, though I am working with largely pre-release packages so there's a bias there. If it were up to me I would flip the default, though I understand the intentions behind it.

Title: `uv python install` publishes managed Python before finalization, allowing `uv python find` to race and observe incomplete installs
Text:
`uv python install` publishes managed Python before finalization, allowing `uv python find` to race and observe incomplete installs

### Summary

`uv python install` appears to make a managed Python installation discoverable before all finalization steps have completed. A concurrent `uv python find` can therefore observe and query a partially finalized managed interpreter.

I checked this against `main` at commit `6c963dd3cb0ea4a39cebcef686dfc1329714532a` and the problem appears to be present already starting with ancient uv 0.2.22.

### Why this matters

This can allow `uv python find` to cache interpreter metadata from a pre-finalization state. In particular, `uv python install` finalizes the installation after publication with steps such as:

- `ensure_sysconfig_patched()`
- `ensure_build_file()`
- `ensure_minor_version_link()`
- `ensure_externally_managed()`

If `uv python find` probes the interpreter before `ensure_sysconfig_patched()` completes, uv may cache interpreter metadata derived from unpatched sysconfig data. That stale cache can survive after `uv python install` completes, because the interpreter executable timestamp may not change when sysconfig files are patched.

### Current code path

The install directory is published here, by renaming the extracted Python into the final managed install path:

https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/blob/6c963dd3cb0ea4a39cebcef686dfc1329714532a/crates/uv-python/src/downloads.rs#L1389-L1398

`uv python install` only performs finalization afterward:

https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/blob/6c963dd3cb0ea4a39cebcef686dfc1329714532a/crates/uv/src/commands/python/install.rs#L674-L678

The minor-version link is created even later:

https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/blob/6c963dd3cb0ea4a39cebcef686dfc1329714532a/crates/uv/src/commands/python/install.rs#L724-L733

`uv python install` does take the managed-install lock:

https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/blob/6c963dd3cb0ea4a39cebcef686dfc1329714532a/crates/uv/src/commands/python/install.rs#L326-L329

However, managed Python discovery does not appear to participate in that lock. `uv python find` discovers managed installs by reading the managed install root:

https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/blob/6c963dd3cb0ea4a39cebcef686dfc1329714532a/crates/uv-python/src/discovery.rs#L365-L373

`find_all()` reads directories directly and treats non-dot directories as managed installations:

https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/blob/6c963dd3cb0ea4a39cebcef686dfc1329714532a/crates/uv-python/src/managed.rs#L201-L243

So the race window is:

1. `uv python install` downloads/extracts Python under `.temp`.
2. It renames the extracted Python into the final managed installation directory.
3. Before finalization completes, another process runs `uv python find`.
4. `uv python find` sees the final directory and may query/cache the interpreter.
5. `uv python install` later completes finalization.

### Expected behavior

A managed Python installation should not be discoverable by `uv python find` until it is complete, or discovery should coordinate with the install lock so it cannot observe an installation while finalization is in progress.

### Actual behavior

The final managed install directory is published before finalization completes, and `uv python find` can discover it without waiting for the install lock.

### Possible fixes

Two possible approaches:

- Finalize the installation while it is still in a temporary/non-discoverable location, then atomically rename it into the managed install root only after finalization completes.
- Have managed Python discovery coordinate with the managed-install lock before enumerating installations.

The first option seems preferable because it preserves a simple invariant: anything visible in the managed install root is complete.

Title: Smarter fork reuse and/or prefetching across forks
Text:
Smarter fork reuse and/or prefetching across forks

In theory, subsequent forks after the first fork should be extremely fast, most of the metadata should be already loaded and most of the versions should come from preferences. In practice, it seems we spend a notable overhead in each fork for airflow.

Benchmark: `uv lock --exclude-newer 2026-03-18` on airflow 7fa400745ac7aebc7cc4ec21d3a047e9fb258310 on linux, with a walltime of 770ms:

* Pre-fork all marker environments (`requires-python` is `>=3.10,!=3.14`): 7ms
  * Pre-fork `python_full_version >= '3.12'`: 3ms
    * Pre-fork `python_full_version >= '3.13'`: 23ms
      * Pre-fork `python_full_version >= '3.14'`: 29ms
        * Fork `python_full_version >= '3.14' and sys_platform == 'win32'`: 161ms
        * Fork `python_full_version >= '3.14' and sys_platform == 'emscripten'`: 25ms
        * Fork `python_full_version >= '3.14' and sys_platform != 'emscripten' and sys_platform != 'win32'`: 26ms
      * Fork `python_full_version == '3.13.*'`: 18ms
    * Fork `python_full_version == '3.12.*'`: 25ms
  * Pre-fork `python_full_version < '3.12'`: 7ms
    * Fork `python_full_version == '3.11.*'`: 23ms
  * Fork `python_full_version < '3.11'`: 122ms

These forks do have slightly different sets of packages, mostly packages that are only included under certain markers, while the few differences in the versions of packages don't justify their runtime.

Text:
`uv pip compile` ignores `required-environments`

### Summary

`uv pip compile` seems to ignore `required-environments`, which differs in behavior from `uv lock`

Let's use `hdbscan` as our test subject. It does not publish Linux ARM wheels for Python 3.12. If we have this  `pyproject.toml`, where we add Python 3.12 Linux ARM to `required-environments` and use `no-build = true`:

```pyproject.toml
[project]
name = "test"
version = "0.0.1"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = ["hdbscan==0.8.42"]

[tool.uv]
no-build = true
required-environments = [
  "python_version == '3.12' and sys_platform == 'linux' and platform_machine == 'aarch64'",
]
```

- `uv pip compile` + `required-environments` runs without an error (unexpected)

  ```shell
    × No solution found when resolving dependencies for split (markers: python_full_version == '3.12.*' and platform_machine == 'aarch64' and sys_platform == 'linux'):
    ╰─▶ Because hdbscan==0.8.42 has no `python_full_version == '3.12.*' and platform_machine == 'aarch64' and sys_platform == 'linux'`-compatible wheels and your project depends on

        hint: The resolution failed for an environment that is not the current one, consider limiting the environments with `tool.uv.environments`.
  ```

If we instead use `environments`
```pyproject.toml
[project]
name = "test"
version = "0.0.1"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
```

Windows console launchers run base Python in stdlib venv --symlinks

## Summary

On Windows, if `uv pip install --python` installs `pip` into a stdlib virtual environment created with `python -m venv --symlinks`, the package is installed into the correct target environment and the generated launcher payload contains the correct target shebang. However, direct execution of the uv-generated `.exe` launcher starts the base Python interpreter instead of the virtual environment interpreter.

This does not reproduce in a normal non-symlink stdlib `venv`. The original pip/distlib launcher also works before uv replaces it.

Although the minimal reproduction uses `pip.exe`, this does not appear to be inherently pip-specific. It looks like a uv-generated Python console-entrypoint launcher issue in symlink venvs. `pip.exe` is used in the reproduction because it is already present in a fresh venv, easy to replace with `uv pip install --python`, and easy to verify with `--version`.

This looks related in theme to #1766, but the repro here is different: the console script `.exe` is not itself symlinked. Instead, the venv's `Scripts\python.exe` is a symlink to the base Python executable.

## Environment

```text
OS: Windows
Shell: PowerShell 7.4.14
Base Python: C:\Python310\python.exe
uv: uv 0.11.13 (4512a3931 2026-05-10 x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
```

## Reproduction

Run from an elevated PowerShell or with Windows Developer Mode enabled so that `venv --symlinks` actually creates symlinks:

```powershell
$uv = "C:\path\to\uv.exe"
$root = Join-Path $env:TEMP "uv_plain_symlink_repro"
Remove-Item $root -Recurse -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

C:\Python310\python.exe -m venv --symlinks $root
Set-Location $root
.\Scripts\Activate.ps1

Get-Item .\Scripts\python.exe | Format-List FullName,Length,Mode,Attributes,LinkType,Target
python -m pip --version
pip --version
Get-Item .\Scripts\pip.exe | Select-Object FullName,Length
Get-Content .\Lib\site-packages\pip-*.dist-info\INSTALLER

& $uv --version
& $uv pip install --python .\Scripts\python.exe pip==24.3.1

python -m pip --version
pip --version
.\Scripts\pip.exe --version
python .\Scripts\pip.exe --version
Get-Item .\Scripts\pip.exe | Select-Object FullName,Length
Get-Content .\Lib\site-packages\pip-24.3.1.dist-info\INSTALLER

$p = (Get-Command pip).Source
$raw = [Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetString([IO.File]::ReadAllBytes($p))
[regex]::Matches($raw, '#![^\r\n]+') | ForEach-Object Value
```

## Observed behavior

Before uv replaces `pip`, the symlink venv is healthy:

```text
Scripts\python.exe -> C:\Python310\python.exe
python -m pip --version -> pip 23.0.1 from ...\uv_plain_symlink_repro\lib\site-packages\pip (python 3.10)
pip --version           -> pip 23.0.1 from ...\uv_plain_symlink_repro\lib\site-packages\pip (python 3.10)
Scripts\pip.exe length  -> 108437
INSTALLER               -> pip
```

After uv installs `pip==24.3.1`:

```text
uv 0.11.13 (4512a3931 2026-05-10 x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
uv pip install --python .\Scripts\python.exe pip==24.3.1
Using Python 3.10.11 environment at: .
 - pip==23.0.1
 + pip==24.3.1

python -m pip --version       -> pip 24.3.1 from ...\uv_plain_symlink_repro\lib\site-packages\pip (python 3.10)
pip --version                 -> pip 24.3.1 from C:\Python310\lib\site-packages\pip (python 3.10)
.\Scripts\pip.exe --version   -> pip 24.3.1 from C:\Python310\lib\site-packages\pip (python 3.10)
python .\Scripts\pip.exe ...  -> pip 24.3.1 from ...\uv_plain_symlink_repro\lib\site-packages\pip (python 3.10)
Scripts\pip.exe length        -> 46080
INSTALLER                     -> uv
launcher shebang              -> #!TEMP_DIR\uv_plain_symlink_repro\Scripts\python.exe
```

## Expected behavior

All of these should resolve to the virtual environment:

```powershell
python -m pip --version
pip --version
.\Scripts\pip.exe --version
python .\Scripts\pip.exe --version
```

## Notes

The uv-generated launcher payload appears to point at the venv interpreter. Running the launcher as a Python script works:

```powershell
python .\Scripts\pip.exe --version
```

The failing path is direct native launcher execution:

```powershell
.\Scripts\pip.exe --version
```

That suggests the uv Windows launcher stub may be resolving or canonicalizing the symlinked interpreter to the base executable and then running outside the venv context.

## Negative control

A normal stdlib venv without `--symlinks` does not reproduce. After:

```powershell
uv pip install --python TARGET_DIR\Scripts\python.exe pip==24.3.1
```

direct execution of:

```powershell
TARGET_DIR\Scripts\pip.exe --version
```

stays in the target environment.

* Optionally include the index/source that reported the quarantine status

Title: uv add does not fullfill older package dependencies with name changed package
Text: uv add does not fullfill older package dependencies with name changed package ### Summary Unsure if I understand the issue correctly, please mind this assessment might be wrong: uv fails on `markupsafe` as index does not contain older version hints for `markupsafe` and `cpython 3.12` However, looking at the index directly on https://download.pytorch.org/whl/nightly/rocm7.2 shows versions for `Markupsafe` with `cpython 3.12` do exist starting with version `3.0.2` but `markupsafe` transitioned in a name change from `3.0.2` to `3.0.3` (all lowercase now). ### Platform Linux 6.17.0-23-generic x86_64 GNU/Linux ### Version uv 0.11.13 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu) ### Python version Python 3.12.3
Reply:
Hmm, I don't think that's a bug in uv: you're explicitly asking for `markupsafe==3.0.3` on Python 3.12, but the index you've specified doesn't have a wheel for that Python version. Per that link, the only wheel builds for `markupsafe==3.0.3` are for Python 3.14:

```
markupsafe-3.0.3-cp314-cp314-macosx_11_0_arm64.whl
markupsafe-3.0.3-cp314-cp314-manylinux2014_aarch64.manylinux_2_17_aarch64.manylinux_2_28_aarch64.whl
markupsafe-3.0.3-cp314-cp314-manylinux2014_x86_64.manylinux_2_17_x86_64.manylinux_2_28_x86_64.whl
markupsafe-3.0.3-cp314-cp314-win_amd64.whl
markupsafe-3.0.3-cp314-cp314t-macosx_11_0_arm64.whl
markupsafe-3.0.3-cp314-cp314t-manylinux2014_aarch64.manylinux_2_17_aarch64.manylinux_2_28_aarch64.whl
markupsafe-3.0.3-cp314-cp314t-manylinux2014_x86_64.manylinux_2_17_x86_64.manylinux_2_28_x86_64.whl
markupsafe-3.0.3-cp314-cp314t-win_amd64.whl
```

The case distinction (`markupsafe` vs. `Markupsafe`) is a red herring, uv knows how to properly equivocate between the two. 

In your case, I think you either need to:

- Loosen your bound (looks like there's a `markupsafe` build for 3.12 for other versions)
- Choose a different index (one that provides that version + CPython version variant?)
- Bump your Python version to 3.14

Which one of those is most correct depends on your use case.

Title: Docs for workspaces are missing a monorepo publish management guide
Text:
Docs for workspaces are missing a monorepo publish management guide

### Question

The current workspace documentation explains how to set up workspaces and internal dependencies, but there is no dedicated section on **how to manage publishing for monorepo projects**. This causes real-world friction in several common scenarios.

**Problems we encountered**

1. **Renaming packages when PyPI names are taken**  
   If a package name is already claimed on PyPI, you need to change `[project] name` in `pyproject.toml`. But uv then expects the source directory to follow the new name (e.g. `src/new_name`). This forces a cascade of renames across the monorepo — directories, module imports, internal dependency declarations — which is painful and error-prone.  
   It would be helpful if uv could **decouple the published name from the on-disk module layout**, or at least document a clear, supported pattern for this.

2. **Publishing only to GitHub (no PyPI) breaks non-uv users**  
   If you publish packages only to GitHub Releases (e.g. because PyPI names are unavailable), `pipx`, `pip`, and other tools cannot resolve inter-package dependencies. While `[tool.uv.sources]` allows pointing to Git subdirectories, those entries are uv-specific and are ignored by other tools. There is no guidance on how to make such a setup work for users outside the uv ecosystem.

3. **No reference example for CI/CD publishing of workspace members**  
   The docs show how to build and publish a single package, but there is no walkthrough for a monorepo where multiple packages must be published in order (respecting internal dependency order), using semantic versioning and trusted publishing. Many modern projects need this pattern.

**What would help**

- A guide on **“Publishing from a monorepo”** covering:
  - How to handle name conflicts when publishing to PyPI
  - How to configure a package so the published name differs from the source directory (or how to rename safely)
  - How to set up a GitHub Actions workflow for publishing workspace members in dependency order
  - How to approach GitHub-only publishing and its ecosystem compatibility limits

The documentation already has excellent workspace and publishing pages; connecting them with a practical monorepo publishing guide would fill this gap nicely.

### Platform

`Linux devhost 6.12.63+deb13-amd64 #1 SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Debian 6.12.63-1 (2025-12-30) x86_64 GNU/Linux`

### Version

`uv 0.10.11`

Title: --python <path> ignored for embedded/oxidized Python: venv substituted to managed intermediary (potential regression in 0.10.0)
Text:
--python <path> ignored for embedded/oxidized Python: venv substituted to managed intermediary (potential regression in 0.10.0)

### Question

I acknowledge this is an unusual setup. 

pypr8 is a custom Rust binary that embeds CPython 3.12 via PyO3, so we can compile Rust modules directly into the interpreter and expose them as built-in Python modules (via append_to_inittab!) rather than as separate dynamic extensions. 

The interpreter links its stdlib against a python-build-standalone distribution that currently lives under uv's managed-Python directory 

From every Python-level signal (sys.version, sys.executable, sys._base_executable) it presents as a normal CPython 3.12.13; it just has extra batteries linked in. 

We use uv venv --python bin/pypr8 to make this interpreter the base of the project's venv, and it worked transparently from 0.4.30 through 0.9.30.

When `uv venv --python <path>` is given an explicit path to a Python interpreter whose `sys.base_prefix` resolves to a uv-managed Python install directory, uv 0.10.0+ silently substitutes the venv's base interpreter to the managed minor-version intermediary directory. The log still claims the requested binary is being used. There appears to be no escape hatch.

1. Is the `--python <path>` → managed-intermediary substitution intentional when an explicit path is provided?
2. If yes, can an opt-out flag be added (e.g. `--no-transparent-upgrade` or honoring `python-preference = only-system` for this code path)?
3. If no, is this a regression worth fixing — the explicit path should win over the transparent-upgrade indirection.

## More Details

Bisect confirms this is a regression in **0.10.0** — last working version is **0.9.30**.

## Environment

- uv 0.11.14 (also reproduced on 0.10.0 .. 0.11.13)
- macOS, aarch64
- Custom binary `bin/pypr8`: a Rust executable embedding CPython 3.12.13 via PyO3, linked against the stdlib at `~/.local/share/uv/python/cpython-3.12.13-macos-aarch64-none/`.

```console
$ bin/pypr8 -c "import sys; print(sys.executable, sys._base_executable, sys.base_prefix, sep='\n')"
/path/to/repo/bin/pypr8
/path/to/repo/bin/pypr8
/Users/me/.local/share/uv/python/cpython-3.12.13-macos-aarch64-none
```

## Reproduction

```console
$ uv venv .venv --python /path/to/repo/bin/pypr8
Using CPython 3.12.13 interpreter at: /path/to/repo/bin/pypr8
Creating virtual environment at: .venv

$ readlink .venv/bin/python
/Users/me/.local/share/uv/python/cpython-3.12-macos-aarch64-none/bin/python3.12
```

Two things to note:

- The log line `Using CPython 3.12.13 interpreter at: /path/to/repo/bin/pypr8` is misleading — that path is **not** what ends up in the venv.
- `cpython-3.12-macos-aarch64-none` has no patch version — that's uv's *minor-version intermediary*, not the requested binary.

Expected: `.venv/bin/python` resolves to `bin/pypr8` (the explicitly requested binary). This is what 0.9.30 and earlier do.

## Bisect

| uv version       | `.venv/bin/python` target                                                  | Result |
| ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------ |
| 0.4.30 – 0.9.30  | `.../rust/target/release/pypr8`                                            | pass   |
| 0.10.0 – 0.11.14 | `~/.local/share/uv/python/cpython-3.12-macos-aarch64-none/bin/python3.12` | fail   |

The change appears to be [#17766](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/17766) (stabilizing transparent patch upgrades via minor-version intermediary directories), which structurally requires the venv's base to be the uv-managed intermediary.

## Workarounds attempted (none work)

- `--python-preference only-system` — still substituted
- `--no-managed-python` — still substituted
- `--no-python-downloads` — still substituted
- Passing the absolute binary path — still substituted (the log even confirms uv recognized the path)

## Impact

The explicit `--python <path>` argument is silently overridden when the target interpreter's `sys.base_prefix` falls inside `~/.local/share/uv/python/`. This makes uv unusable for projects that build a custom interpreter (PyO3 / `python-build-standalone`-linked binary) and need it to be the actual base of the venv — the venv ends up pointing at a different binary than the one requested, with no way to opt out.


### Platform

_No response_

### Version

_No response_
Reply: Hi @andyswift, thanks for opening an issue. That's an interesting setup! We'll triage and get back to you.

Title: Warn or deny project overrides that weaken user/system dependency cooldown policy
Text:
Warn or deny project overrides that weaken user/system dependency cooldown policy

**backstory**

I finally set a minimum release age (`exclude-newer`) in my global uv config (bc of the recent worm https://socket.dev/blog/tanstack-npm-packages-compromised-mini-shai-hulud-supply-chain-attack)

I excluded some personal packages from this cooldown, bc I do need the latest versions of those.

but now I discovered my user-configured exclusions were leaking into the `uv.lock`s of the projects I was working on: https://x.com/dasfacc/status/2055037715687645696

I work on the Pydantic AI repo, and this got me thinking that we should have a static check that prevents contributors from accidentally leaking _their_ exclusions into our `uv.lock`, and more importantly, have CI flag exclusions: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai/pull/5446

**realization**

then I learned that project config takes precedence over user/system config, and package-specific cooldown overrides can weaken a user’s global cooldown policy, which made me think we should have tools to prevent that kind of behavior, given our new security climate.

that’s why I’m opening this issue. I had codex provide examples and snippets so we can discuss possibilities, if you agree with the proposal.

thank you for your time and your work!

David

---

For example, a user might configure:

```toml
exclude-newer = "7 days"
```

But a project can add an override such as:

```toml
[tool.uv]
exclude-newer-package = { some-package = false }
```

or otherwise use a newer/more permissive cutoff for a package. That may be legitimate for private packages, security fixes, or operational exceptions, but it can also bypass the user's intended minimum release age policy.

It would be useful to have a user/system-level setting that controls what happens when project-level or lockfile-level cooldown settings weaken the user's configured policy.

### Example


```toml
# ~/.config/uv/uv.toml
exclude-newer = "7 days"

dependency-cooldown-override-policy = "deny" # allow | warn | deny

[[dependency-cooldown-override-allow]]
projects = ["~/work/pydantic-ai/**"]
repositories = ["https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai"]
packages = ["pydantic-harness"]
override-types = ["disable", "relax"]

[[dependency-cooldown-override-allow]]
projects = ["~/work/experiments/**"]
packages = [":all:"]
override-types = ["relax"]
```

The exact names are not important, but possible names include:

- `dependency-cooldown-override-policy`
- `exclude-newer-override-policy`
- `release-age-override-policy`
- `warn-on-exclude-newer-override`

The important behavior is:

- `allow`: current behavior
- `warn`: continue, but warn when a project weakens the user/system cooldown policy
- `deny`: fail unless the override matches an allow rule

An override would be considered weakening if it allows versions that the user/system cooldown would otherwise exclude, for example:

- disabling the cooldown for a package with `exclude-newer-package = { name = false }`
- using a shorter relative cooldown for a package
- using a newer absolute cutoff for a package
- possibly applying a more permissive per-index cooldown, if relevant

Allow rules probably need to match both where the override is coming from and what package it applies to. A project-only allowlist is too broad: I may trust a specific repository to override cooldowns for `pydantic-harness`, but not to bypass the policy for arbitrary packages.

The `repositories` field would be optional convenience. A path matcher is probably the clearest local security boundary, while repository matching could use normalized VCS remote URLs to allow any worktree of a trusted repository.

The exact schema is illustrative. If this followed existing uv conventions, `packages` might use package names plus an all-packages sentinel like `:all:` rather than shell-style `*`.

Title: `uv sync` does not properly recover from an environment with faulty packages (opencv-contrib-python package problem)
Text:
`uv sync` does not properly recover from an environment with faulty packages (opencv-contrib-python package problem)

### Summary

I encountered an issue with the opencv-python and opencv-contrib-python packages. When having both installed and then removing the former, `uv sync` does not properly synchronize the environment.

To reproduce the problem:
```
uv init
uv add opencv-python opencv-contrib-python
uv sync
uv run python -c "import cv2; print(cv2.__version__)"
# 4.13.0
uv remove opencv-python
uv sync
uv run python -c "import cv2; print(cv2.__version__)"
# AttributeError: module 'cv2' has no attribute '__version__'
```

To fix this problem, one can either remove the `.venv` folder and then run `uv sync` again or run
```
uv pip uninstall opencv-python opencv-contrib-python
uv sync
uv run python -c "import cv2; print(cv2.__version__)"
# 4.13.0
```

This problem is specific to the OpenCV package because `opencv-python` and `opencv-contrib-python` should [not be installed at the same time](https://github.com/opencv/opencv-python#installation-and-usage). The workaround for uv is from [here](https://github.com/invoke-ai/InvokeAI/issues/8103).

Having both packages installed is of course wrong and should not be done in the first place. However, the problem was originally discovered in a project which had both packages installed and then we found out that this should not be done so we removed `opencv-python`. The main problem I want to report here is that in this case it is not enough to run `uv sync` but I think it should have been. Especially since this leaves other `.venv`'s in a broken state which cannot easily be fixed if the problem is not known.

Title: Git credentials in workspace member `[tool.uv.sources]` not applied under `uv sync --frozen`
Text:
Git credentials in workspace member `[tool.uv.sources]` not applied under `uv sync --frozen`

### Summary

When `uv sync --frozen` is run against a workspace, credentials embedded in
`[tool.uv.sources]` entries that live in **workspace-member** `pyproject.toml`
files are silently dropped. The same entries work correctly under `uv lock`
and `uv sync` (without `--frozen`). For private git deps this manifests as
`fatal: could not read Username for 'https://github.com': terminal prompts disabled`.

### Minimal reproducible example

```
repo/
├── pyproject.toml              # workspace root; declares members; no [tool.uv.sources]
├── uv.lock
└── nested/
    └── pyproject.toml          # [tool.uv.sources]
                                # example = { git = "https://user:password@github.com/organization/repository", tag = "v1" }
```

Root `pyproject.toml`:

```toml
[project]
name = "root"
version = "0"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = ["example"]

[tool.uv.workspace]
members = ["nested"]
```

`nested/pyproject.toml`:

```toml
[project]
name = "nested"
version = "0"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = ["example"]

[tool.uv.sources]
example = { git = "https://user:password@github.com/organization/repository", tag = "v1" }
```

Steps:

1. `uv lock` from the repo root — succeeds; lockfile correctly records
   `git+https://github.com/organization/repository@<commit>` with no credentials (per
   the redaction behavior introduced in #5803).
2. `uv sync --frozen` from the repo root — **fails**:

   ```
   × Failed to download and build `example @ git+https://github.com/organization/repository@<commit>`
   ├─▶ Git operation failed
   ├─▶ failed to clone into: /root/.cache/uv/git-v0/db/...
   ├─▶ failed to fetch commit `<commit>`
   ╰─▶ process didn't exit successfully:
       `/usr/bin/git fetch --force --update-head-ok 'https://github.com/organization/repository' ...`
       (exit status: 128)
       --- stderr
       fatal: could not read Username for 'https://github.com': terminal prompts disabled
   ```

Workaround: move the credentialed `[tool.uv.sources]` entry into the
workspace-root `pyproject.toml`, or configure git directly via
`git config --global url.<auth>.insteadOf <bare>` / `GIT_ASKPASS` / `.netrc`.

### Root cause

Under `--frozen`, project discovery is intentionally scoped to the root only:

https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/blob/a4d9e42197d606474f085cff93caa200666512df/crates/uv/src/commands/project/sync.rs#L101-L110

`store_credentials_from_target` then iterates `target.sources()`, which walks
`workspace.sources()` plus each loaded member's `[tool.uv.sources]`:

https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/blob/a4d9e42197d606474f085cff93caa200666512df/crates/uv/src/commands/project/install_target.rs#L150-L174

With `MemberDiscovery::None`, members aren't loaded, so member-level
`[tool.uv.sources]` are invisible to `store_credentials_from_target`, and
`GIT_STORE` never gets the credentials. `GitSource::fetch` then runs against
the bare URL:

https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/blob/a4d9e42197d606474f085cff93caa200666512df/crates/uv-git/src/source.rs#L69-L75

### Expected behavior

`uv sync --frozen` should respect credentials defined in any workspace
member's `[tool.uv.sources]`, consistently with `uv lock` and `uv sync`
without `--frozen`. The lockfile already records workspace membership, so
credentials can be collected from each member's `pyproject.toml` on disk
without doing full member discovery / validation.

### Related

- #5803 — Redact registry credentials in lockfile (established that creds in
  `pyproject.toml` must be re-applied at install time; this issue is a
  follow-up where re-application is incomplete for workspaces under
  `--frozen`).
- #8529 — Provide a way to provide Git authentication for `tool.uv.sources`
  (broader umbrella; this issue is the concrete `--frozen` subset).

uv 0.11.14 (3fdfdc7d4 2026-05-12 aarch64-apple-darwin)

Python 3.14.2

Title: Support a `--fix` type flag for `audit` to allow automatic fixing of vulnerabilities according to semantic versioning
Text:
Support a `--fix` type flag for `audit` to allow automatic fixing of vulnerabilities according to semantic versioning

### Summary

I propose a `--fix` flag (or command) that would automatically fix vulnerabilities caught by the new `audit` command.

Where I currently work, I wrote a script that uses a combination of the [uv-secure](https://github.com/owenlamont/uv-secure) tool's JSON output alongside `jq` and `uv lock --upgrade-package` to achieve this, however it is finnicky and doesn't work perfectly.

The `audit` roadmap (#18506) calls out a specific `--fix` flag for this, but there's no issue assigned so I thought I'd throw my hat in.

I'm willing to help contribute to the implementation of this ticket, as my current project could really do with having this process automated. However, I understand that this would fall under a "new feature" bucket and would need a decision/design from the UV team, so I'd like to open this issue for discussion first.

@woodruffw it looks like you're the one who's most likely to have strong opinions one way or another about how this is implemented, would you be willing to discuss here? I've suggested a potential UX in the example section.

### Example

Running

```
uv audit --fix
```

would by default fix any vulnerabilities that only require a patch-level update to satisfy.

If possible, it would be nice to also include flags akin to NPM's `--force` flag, that would control which vulnerabilities would be automatically fixed. Although I'd suggest having `--only-patch` (the default), `--only-minor`, and `--all` or something along those lines
Reply:
Hi @crispyricepc, yep we're tracking this with the roadmap. An additional child issue is no problem, though.

As you've observed, the problem here is determining _what_ to fix when the user passes `--fix`. There are a couple of reasonable options here, each with downsides:

- We could perform lockfile-only fixes where a patch (or minor?) compatible fix is available. For example, if `1.2.3` is vulnerable but `1.2.4` or `1.3.0` is not, we could upgrade to either of those (with maybe a preference for the patch?). The downsides to this are that (1) `--fix` won't perform _all_ fixes, and (2) Python packaging is only semver by loose convention, so there's no guarantee that a patch/minor upgrade is actually compatible.
- We could perform _all_ fixes where an upgrade is available. For example, we could upgrade to `2.0.0` if `1.2.3` is vulnerable. The downside to this is breakage risk.
- We could do neither of the above, and instead _only_ fix ranges in the `pyproject.toml` (and then re-lock for the user). This has the advantage of letting us express fixed ranges directly in project metadata (which is probably what the user actually wants), but there's no _a priori_ guarantee that a compatible resolution for the new constraints can be found.

Of these, I _think_ I find the last one most appealing. I think we could also potentially make this configurable with the kinds of flags (and/or config) you've mentioned, but I think we probably shouldn't do that for an MVP implementation (because we'd need to figure out how best to communicate it to users in terms of not everything being semver).

If you're interested in working on that, I'd be happy to workshop the idea further. And please push back on any of the above too if you have better ideas; I haven't fully begun to think about an approach here yet 🙂 

(For context, I helped build `pip-audit`'s fix mode, but the implementation there doesn't have any constraint/soundness concerns. I probably would not repeat that design!)

Title: Windows console-script launcher silently falls back to system Python when venv path contains non-ASCII characters
Text:
Windows console-script launcher silently falls back to system Python when venv path contains non-ASCII characters

## Summary

On Windows, `uv`-built console-script launchers (`.exe` files in `.venv\Scripts\`) silently invoke the **system** Python instead of the venv Python when the venv path contains non-ASCII characters (Cyrillic / CJK / accented Latin). The result: editable installs appear broken — `ModuleNotFoundError` for the project's own package even immediately after `uv sync` succeeds.

## Environment

- uv version: **0.11.14** (also confirmed at 0.9.9 client-side; same launcher build path)
- Platform: Windows 10/11, system locale Russian (CP1251 default), CPython 3.12.3
- Reproduction venv path contains Cyrillic: `C:\Users\Виктор\Documents\Наука\...\.venv`

## Reproduction

1. Create a minimal project at a path with non-ASCII characters:

   ```powershell
   cd 'C:\Users\<Cyrillic-or-CJK-name>\projects'
   mkdir mmt-repro
   cd mmt-repro
   ```

2. `pyproject.toml`:

   ```toml
   [build-system]
   requires = ["uv_build>=0.11.3,<0.12"]
   build-backend = "uv_build"

   [project]
   name = "mmt-repro"
   version = "0.1.0"
   requires-python = ">=3.12,<3.13"

   [project.scripts]
   mmt-repro = "mmt_repro.cli:main"

   [tool.uv.build-backend]
   module-root = ""
   ```

3. Package:

   ```powershell
   mkdir mmt_repro
   ni mmt_repro\__init__.py
   Set-Content mmt_repro\cli.py 'def main(): print("hello")'
   ```

4. Install and run:

   ```powershell
   uv sync
   uv run mmt-repro
   ```

## Expected

Prints `hello`.

## Actual

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<frozen runpy>", line 198, in _run_module_as_main
  File "<frozen runpy>", line 88, in _run_code
  File "C:\Users\<Cyrillic>\projects\mmt-repro\.venv\Scripts\mmt-repro.exe\__main__.py", line 4, in <module>
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'mmt_repro'
```

## Diagnosis

Extracting the embedded `__main__.py` from the launcher `.exe` (which is `<launcher_bytes> + <zip_archive>`) shows the shebang:

```python
#!C:\Users\Виктор\Documents\...\.venv\Scripts\python.exe
# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
import sys
from mmt_repro.cli import main
...
```

The shebang is **correctly encoded as UTF-8** in the file (hex-verified: Cyrillic chars are `d0 92 d0 b8 ...`, valid UTF-8). However, the Windows launcher prefix appears to read the shebang using the system codepage (CP1251 / CP866 / CP1252 depending on locale), not UTF-8. The mis-decoded path doesn't resolve to a real `python.exe`, so the launcher silently falls back to whatever `python.exe` is on `PATH` — which on a typical user install is the system CPython, **not** the venv interpreter. That fallback Python doesn't see the venv's `pyvenv.cfg` and doesn't process the editable `.pth`, so the project's own package is unimportable.

Confirming the fallback by injecting the project root into `PYTHONPATH`:

```powershell
$env:PYTHONPATH = (Get-Location).Path
.\.venv\Scripts\mmt-repro.exe
# prints "hello" — the launcher DID invoke A Python; it just wasn't the venv's
```

`uv run python -m mmt_repro` works correctly (no launcher, no shebang). Only the `.exe` shim is affected.

## Suggested fixes

1. Generate the Windows launcher binary so it reads the embedded shebang as UTF-8 explicitly (the Python launcher source in `distlib`/`simple-launcher` family supports this — needs the launcher to call `MultiByteToWideChar` with `CP_UTF8` rather than `CP_ACP`).
2. Or: embed the venv Python path in a more launcher-friendly way (e.g. a `.pyvenv-ref` sidecar file alongside the `.exe`, or use the Python launcher (`py.exe`) with a `-3.12` style version arg instead of an absolute path).
3. As a documentation workaround, advise users with non-ASCII venv paths to use `uv run python -m <module>` form, which bypasses the launcher.

## Related

This affects any uv-built project with non-ASCII paths anywhere in the venv path (commonly: `C:\Users\<localized-name>\...` on non-English Windows installs). Several downstream projects have shipped workarounds in their docs; centralizing the fix in uv's launcher generation would unblock everyone.
Reply:
Please read our AI policy at https://github.com/astral-sh/.github/blob/main/AI_POLICY.md and use your own words to communicate.

I'm not able to reproduce this based on the information above. I tried these:

- Created a venv at a path containing Cyrillic, CJK, and `é` (`кириллица-漢字-é`).
- Installed the local `test\links\simple_launcher-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl`.
- Ran the generated `Scripts\simple_launcher.exe`.
- Put a fake `python.exe` first on `PATH` and reran the launcher.

In all cases, the launcher executed the venv interpreter and did not fall back to `python.exe` on `PATH`.

Title: Maturin 1.13.2 changes wheel contents on macOS
Text:
Maturin 1.13.2 changes wheel contents on macOS

See #19465

Using Codex to diagnose

> Maturin 1.13.2 changed how bindings = "bin" wheels are laid out when external shared-library dependencies are detected. The new behavior, introduced by [maturin#3147](https://github.com/PyO3/maturin/pull/3147), moves the real executable into {dist}.scripts/ under platlib and leaves a small Python launcher in .data/scripts/, so the executable can live at a predictable relative path to bundled shared libraries. uv’s macOS arm64 uv_build wheel hits this path because Maturin detects a dependency on Homebrew’s liblzma.5.dylib, so the wheel now contains both uv_build-*.data/scripts/uv-build and uv_build.scripts/uv-build. uv’s wheel-content checker still expects the pre-1.13.2 layout, which is why the release-binary CI job fails.
>
> The subtle part is that Maturin applies this relocation based on detecting external libraries, even in macOS warn mode where those libraries are not actually copied into the wheel. That means uv gets the new shim-based layout without a corresponding bundled .dylibs/ directory, which is consistent with Maturin’s current implementation but arguably broader than necessary. So there are two follow-up questions: uv needs to update its expected wheel contents for Maturin 1.13.2+, and it may be worth asking upstream whether the shim relocation should happen only when repair/bundling is actually performed rather than whenever external libraries are merely detected.

Title: Does `uv tool install` read `[[tool.uv]]` section of target `pyproject.toml`
Text:
Does `uv tool install` read `[[tool.uv]]` section of target `pyproject.toml`

### Question

I have a package with dependencies from a private index which is defined in the `[[tool.uv]]` section of the `pyproject.toml`:

```toml
dependencies = [
    "my-dependency", 
]

[tool.uv]
keyring-provider = "subprocess"

[tool.uv.sources]
my-dependency = { index = "my-index" }

[[tool.uv.index]]
name = "my-index"
url = "...."
explicit = true
```

When installing that package from a local path with `uv tool install .` or from the github repo `uv tool install "my-package @ git+ssh://git@github.com/xyz"` the `my-dependency` package is installed without issues. I didn't expect this to work because I didn't pass the private index with `--index` to the tool command. 

The [Configuration files](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/configuration-files/) docs say *"For `tool` commands... local configuration files will be ignored"* which matches @zanieb's comment [here](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/16021#issuecomment-3334132268). Therefore, I would have expected the `[[tool.uv]]` section of the `pyproject.toml` to be ignored in which case the `my-dependency` package should not have been found.

If I try to install `my-package` with `pip install "my-package @ git+ssh://git@github.com/xyz"` I get the expected error that no package `my-dependency` was found.

Can anyone explain this behavior?



### Platform

Ubuntu 24.04 x86_64

### Version

uv 0.11.15
Reply: For Git and local paths, yes; for packages installed from a registry, no.

Title: Define extra per `--package` with `uv sync`
Text:
Define extra per `--package` with `uv sync`

### Summary

When using `uv sync --package=A --package=B` and you want to install an extra of only one package, it is not possible AFAIK.

`uv sync --package=A --package=B --extra=E` installs the extra E of both packages. 

`uv sync --package=A[E] --package=B` is not accepted by the parser:
> invalid value 'A[E]' for '--package <PACKAGE>': Not a valid package or extra name: "A[E]". Names must start and end with a letter or digit and may only contain -, _, ., and alphanumeric characters.

I would suggest accepting `uv sync --package=A[E] --package=B` if that is possible.

### Example

`uv sync --package=A[E] --package=B` to install the extra E only of package A

Title: `uv lock` pins single-platform wheel when upstream's release is mid-upload, then breaks at `uv sync` with misleading `only has wheels with the following Python ABI tag` warning
Text:
`uv lock` pins single-platform wheel when upstream's release is mid-upload, then breaks at `uv sync` with misleading `only has wheels with the following Python ABI tag` warning

NOTE: I found the workaround for this issue with a claude.ai session and I have generated parts of this issue's text with claude.

---

## Summary

`uv lock` resolved `greenlet 3.5.1` at a moment when only one of its ten wheels had reached PyPI (the macOS freethreaded build). The remaining wheels -- linux x86_64, musllinux, win_amd64, win_arm64, etc. -- landed within five minutes. The lock file is frozen on that partial snapshot.

`uv sync` on a Linux CPython 3.15 host then fails with:

```
hint: You're using CPython 3.15 (`cp315`), but `greenlet` (v3.5.1) only has
wheels with the following Python ABI tag: `cp315t`
```

even though `cp315-cp315-manylinux_2_24_x86_64.manylinux_2_28_x86_64` wheel has been released in the meantime.

## Reproduction

1. Trigger `uv lock` (fresh checkout, `uv sync`, `uv add foo`) while an upstream dependency's release is mid-upload -- only some platform wheels published, others still being pushed by per-platform CI runners.
2. `uv` locks the wheels currently visible on PyPI's JSON index.
3. The remaining wheels land within seconds/minutes.
4. The lock file contains a single-platform wheel pin for a multi-platform package.
5. `uv sync` on any excluded platform fails with the ABI-tag hint above.

### Concrete data — `greenlet 3.5.1`

PyPI upload times (via `curl https://pypi.org/pypi/greenlet/json | jq`):

| Upload time (UTC)   | Filename                                                             |
|:--------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 2026-05-20 13:10:19 | `greenlet-3.5.1-cp315-cp315t-macosx_11_0_universal2.whl`             |
| 2026-05-20 13:12:07 | `greenlet-3.5.1-cp315-cp315-macosx_11_0_universal2.whl`              |
| 2026-05-20 13:13:15 | `greenlet-3.5.1-cp315-cp315-win_amd64.whl`                           |
| 2026-05-20 13:13:37 | `greenlet-3.5.1-cp315-cp315t-win_arm64.whl`                          |
| 2026-05-20 13:13:59 | `greenlet-3.5.1-cp315-cp315t-win_amd64.whl`                          |
| 2026-05-20 13:14:32 | `greenlet-3.5.1-cp315-cp315-manylinux_2_24_x86_64.…2_28_x86_64.whl`  |
| 2026-05-20 13:14:35 | `greenlet-3.5.1-cp315-cp315t-manylinux_2_24_x86_64.…2_28_x86_64.whl` |
| 2026-05-20 13:14:42 | `greenlet-3.5.1-cp315-cp315-musllinux_1_2_x86_64.whl`                |
| 2026-05-20 13:14:43 | `greenlet-3.5.1-cp315-cp315t-musllinux_1_2_x86_64.whl`               |
| 2026-05-20 13:15:37 | `greenlet-3.5.1-cp315-cp315-win_arm64.whl`                           |

`uv lock` ran between 13:10 and 13:12 and captured only the first wheel.

### Resulting lock entry

```toml
[[package]]
name = "greenlet"
version = "3.5.1"
source = { registry = "https://pypi.org/simple" }
wheels = [
    { url = "https://files.pythonhosted.org/packages/.../greenlet-3.5.1-cp315-cp315t-macosx_11_0_universal2.whl", ... },
]
```

One wheel. macOS-only. Freethreaded-only.

## Actual behaviour

`uv lock` silently produces a lock file that works on exactly one platform/ABI combination. The failure surfaces later, on a different machine, as a confusing ABI-tag error during `uv sync`.

## Expected behaviour

`uv lock` warns when a freshly-resolved version's wheel set is much smaller than the previous release's wheel set for the same package — e.g. `greenlet 3.5.0` ships ~60 wheels, `3.5.1` ships 1. That delta is a near-certain signal of an in-progress upload, detectable from the index alone without any user configuration, and the warning can recommend `--upgrade-package <name>` after the release settles.

`uv` should also maybe recommend defining an expected environment and error if no such wheel is found during a lock / upgrade.

## My Current Workaround

Quickfix:

```sh
uv lock --upgrade-package greenlet
```

Yet may happen again in future upgrades / locks.

I furthermore realized I could declare the platforms the project must support, so `uv lock` refuses to produce a lock missing a compatible wheel for any declared environment:

```toml
[tool.uv]
required-environments = [
  "sys_platform == 'linux' and platform_machine == 'x86_64'",
]
```

This may be something that `uv` should require / recommend to the user to define for their project to guarantee that it only upgrades to proper channels.

## Affected package:

- `greenlet 3.5.1`, pulled in transitively via `playwright 1.60.0`

## Related issue

- [#14885  `uv` attempts to install the newer version if one has been released while `uv` is running](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/14885)

### Platform

 Linux x86_64 (WSL2 Debian Trixie)

### Version

uv 0.11.15 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu)

### Python version

Python 3.15.0b1
Reply:
The fix for this is https://peps.python.org/pep-0694/

Unfortunately, there's not a great way for us to tell when this is happening in a generalizable form.

This behavior is intentional - I think it's the path of least surprise. `project.name` essentially is the identifier of the project for packaging purposes, and various tools and systems use a normalized version. I think normalizing at the point of generating the pyproject.toml is preferable

Title: Document malware check behavior
Text:
Document malware check behavior

The public docs should document https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/18781 (particularly after we remove it from preview).

Some key things we should document:

* We use OSV for malware reports, and users can configure their own API-compatible OSV service if they're hosting one.
* OSV in turn uses https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages for `MAL` advisories. `MAL` advisories are not propagated directly by PyPI, and are produced on timelines that aren't related directly to quarantine actions on PyPI.
* Malware checks are performed on locked resolutions, since installing from a lockfile doesn't re-access the index. For resolution itself, the equivalent behavior is controlled by PyPI's own quarantining abilities.

Title: Sync ZIP extraction overwrites conflicting duplicate entries
Text:
Sync ZIP extraction overwrites conflicting duplicate entries

## Summary

The seekable ZIP extractor writes entries with truncating file creation, so a ZIP or wheel with duplicate output paths can overwrite an earlier extracted file. The streaming extractor already handles this case with exclusive creation and rejects duplicate entries when their contents differ, so wheel installation behavior diverges depending on whether the sync or streaming path is used.

## Reproduction

1. Build a wheel or ZIP with two entries that resolve to the same enclosed path, such as `package/__init__.py`, but contain different bytes.
2. Install it through a local wheel path or a no-hash wheel download path.
3. The sync extractor succeeds and the extracted contents come from one duplicate entry.
4. Install the same wheel through a hash-required path, such as `--require-hashes`.
5. The streaming extractor rejects it with `ZIP file contains multiple entries with different contents`.

## Expected behavior

Sync extraction should match streaming extraction: allow duplicate file entries only when their contents match, and reject conflicting duplicates before anything can overwrite an extracted file.

## Impact

This makes extracted wheel contents depend on the extraction path and on duplicate entry ordering/concurrency. It also leaves the no-hash local and downloaded wheel paths less strict than the hashed streaming path.
Reply: @fallintoplace Are you able to reproduce this on recent versions of uv? We no longer use the sync ZIP extractor at all; it's been removed entirely.

Title: `uv cache prune` can delete directories outside `UV_CACHE_DIR` if a symlink is present in a cache bucket
Text:
`uv cache prune` can delete directories outside `UV_CACHE_DIR` if a symlink is present in a cache bucket

### Summary

`uv cache prune` resolves cache entries with `canonicalize()` before deleting them. If a symlink is present under a cache bucket, prune deletes the symlink target instead of the symlink itself, which means it can remove directories outside `UV_CACHE_DIR`.

This is distinct from the earlier symlink-mode issues like #12003 and #13270: even if pruning symlinked installs is unsupported, `uv cache prune` still should not escape the configured cache root.

### Repro

```bash
tmp_cache=$(mktemp -d)
victim_root=$(mktemp -d)
mkdir -p "$tmp_cache/environments-v2" "$victim_root/victim-dir"
printf 'payload' > "$victim_root/victim-dir/payload.txt"
ln -s "$victim_root/victim-dir" "$tmp_cache/environments-v2/escape"

UV_CACHE_DIR="$tmp_cache" uv cache prune -v

if [ -e "$victim_root/victim-dir" ]; then
  echo exists
else
  echo deleted
fi
```

### Actual behavior

The target directory outside the cache root is removed:

```text
Pruning cache at: /tmp/...
Removed 1 file (7B)
deleted
```

### Expected behavior

`uv cache prune` should never delete anything outside `UV_CACHE_DIR`. In this case it should either:

- remove the symlink itself, or
- ignore/reject unexpected symlink entries in cache buckets

but it should not follow the symlink and delete the resolved target.

### Likely cause

In `crates/uv-cache/src/lib.rs`, the prune path canonicalizes entries before passing them to `rm_rf`:

```rust
let path = fs_err::canonicalize(entry.path())?;
summary += rm_rf(path)?;
```

`rm_rf` itself uses `symlink_metadata`, so it behaves safely if it receives the original entry path. The unsafe part is resolving the path first.

The environment-path variant appears to have been introduced in #5286 (`479725920`), and the archive cleanup code still has the same pattern on current `main`.

### Platform

macOS (Homebrew `uv 0.11.14`)

### Version

Reproduced with:

- `uv 0.11.14 (Homebrew 2026-05-12 aarch64-apple-darwin)`
- current `main` still contains the same `canonicalize(...) -> rm_rf(...)` pattern in `crates/uv-cache/src/lib.rs`

### Additional context

Related history:

- #12003
- #13270
- #11694
Reply: Why would symlinks be present in the cache in the first place?

Title: `uv run` ignores active venv and `.python-version`, recreates venv with system Python
Text:
`uv run` ignores active venv and `.python-version`, recreates venv with system Python

## Description

When a virtual environment is created with `uv venv --python 3.12` and activated, `uv run` ignores the active venv and recreates it using the system Python (3.13), even when both `.python-version` and `pyproject.toml` `requires-python` are pinned to `>=3.12`.

## Environment

- uv version: `0.11.14`
- OS: Ubuntu (WSL2 on Windows 11)
- System Python: `3.13.5` at `/usr/bin/python3`
- Pinned Python: `3.12.12` (uv-managed)

## Steps to Reproduce

```bash
uv init cuda-project
cd cuda-project

# Pin python version
uv python pin 3.12
sed -i 's/requires-python = ">=3.13"/requires-python = ">=3.12"/' pyproject.toml

# Create venv explicitly with 3.12
rm -rf .venv
uv venv --python $(uv python find 3.12)

# Activate venv
source .venv/bin/activate

# Confirm python is 3.12
python --version  # shows Python 3.12.12 ✅

# Run via uv run
uv run python --version
```

## Expected Behavior

`uv run` should use the active venv (Python 3.12.12).

## Actual Behavior

`uv run` ignores the active venv, prints:

```
Using CPython 3.13.5 interpreter at: /usr/bin/python3
Removed virtual environment at: .venv
Creating virtual environment at: .venv
```

...and recreates the venv with system Python 3.13.

## Additional Notes

- `which python` correctly shows `.venv/bin/python` while venv is active
- `uv pip install` also ignores the active venv and targets `/usr` (system Python)
- The only workaround was using `python -m ensurepip` then `python -m pip install` directly
- `uv add ... --python 3.12` creates the venv with 3.12 correctly but `uv run` destroys it immediately after

## Workaround

```bash
uv venv --python 3.12
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m ensurepip --upgrade
python -m pip install 
python script.py  # use python directly, not uv run
```
Reply: Please include verbose logs.

```
[tool.uv]
default-groups = ["cpu"]
conflicts = [
    [{ group = "cpu" }, { group = "gpu" }],
]
```

which is "ok" for the common case for CPU machines, but this means on GPU machines you have to remember to do `--no-group cpu --group gpu` for every `uv` command (or to use `--no-sync` everywhere), which is extremely error-prone.

Note that all our GPU machines use the same version of CUDA, so we only need cpu vs gpu granularity.

Is there any way to automatically set the default groups on a per-machine basis instead of having to do it everytime when we invoke `uv`?

Naively, I could see a couple different ways of doing this:

* Allow a `UV_GROUP` environment variable (xref https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/11958): this way, we could just drop the right group into a `.env` file or something once per machine and not worry about it beyond that 
* Expand the automatic backend-selection to support other packages beyond PyTorch (xref https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/15461), which might let us just eliminate the need for 2 separate groups.
   * Perhaps there is some way to make this extensible by the user rather than having to make `uv` hard-code this? That way, we could manage this on our side instead of having to ask y'all for special support for each package.

_No response_

### Version

uv 0.11.16 (x86_64-unknown-linux-musl)

Title: Prerelease resolution behavior differs from Poetry — transitive prereleases bleed into unrelated packages
Text:
Prerelease resolution behavior differs from Poetry — transitive prereleases bleed into unrelated packages

### Question

### Background

I'm migrating a project from Poetry to uv. My project depends on a package (`roku`) whose latest version requires a **beta version of `pydantic-settings`**. In Poetry, this worked exactly as expected — I got the latest `roku` and the latest stable version of every other dependency.

### The problem

In uv, I have two options, both unsatisfying:

1. **Without `prerelease = "allow"`** — uv resolves an older version of `roku` (one that doesn't require the pydantic-settings beta), ignoring the latest release entirely.
2. **With `prerelease = "allow"`** — uv correctly picks the latest `roku`, but now also pulls in beta versions of unrelated packages (e.g. `httpx 1.0.0b0` instead of the latest stable `0.28.1`).

Neither option replicates Poetry's behavior.

### How Poetry handles this

Poetry's resolver is context-aware about prereleases. When a package in the dependency graph *requires* a prerelease, Poetry allows that prerelease only within the transitive chain that needs it. It doesn't treat "a beta exists somewhere in my graph" as a global signal to prefer betas for all packages. The result is intuitive: you get the best version of what you asked for, and stable everywhere else.

### What I'd expect from uv

A way to say: *"allow prereleases where the resolution actually requires them, without globally preferring prereleases for unrelated packages."*

### Question

Is there a planned or existing mechanism in uv to scope prerelease allowance to specific dependency chains — similar to how Poetry handles this — without requiring the user to manually enumerate all transitive prereleases?

### Platform

_No response_

### Version

0.11.16
Reply:
There aren't plans to address this today, as it would require significant changes to the underlying core resolver library.

It'd be nice to explore it in the future though.

In the meantime, yeah the solution is to opt-in by adding a pre-release specifier to a constraint on pydantic-settings.
