Title: Enterprise CA `UnsupportedCriticalExtension` TLS Failure
Text:
Enterprise CA `UnsupportedCriticalExtension` TLS Failure ## Summary Behind corporate SSL inspection we see `uv` fail HTTPS requests with: ``` invalid peer certificate: Other(OtherError(UnsupportedCriticalExtension)) ``` The failing certificate is an **inspection intermediate** with a **critical** `X509v3 Certificate Policies` extension (`Policy: X509v3 Any Policy`). The same chain is accepted by OpenSSL, curl, Git, and browsers. > [!IMPORTANT] > rustls/webpki rejects the critical `Certificate Policies` extension in the intermediate certificate during handshake validation, before trust-anchor differences matter. >This means neither `--system-certs` nor `UV_SYSTEM_CERTS` avoids the failure: those flags only change which trust anchors are loaded, not how certificates in the handshake are checked. This post documents a local reproduction using unmodified official `uv` binaries (rustls/webpki via reqwest). ## Environment - OS: Fedora Linux (linux x64) - uv: `0.11.19 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu)` from Astral install - OpenSSL: 3.5.5 - curl: 8.18.0 ## Background Enterprise inspection chains are typically: ```mermaid graph LR root["Root CA\n(trusted)"] int["Inspection Intermediate\n⚠️ certificatePolicies = critical, anyPolicy"] leaf["Leaf / server cert"] root --> int --> leaf ``` Only the **intermediate** carries the critical `anyPolicy` extension in our observed failures. Root and leaf certificates are otherwise normal. `uv` uses **rustls/webpki** for HTTPS by default ([`tls_backend_rustls()`](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/blob/main/crates/uv-client/src/base_client.rs)). When `SSL_CERT_FILE` is set, it **replaces** the bundled Mozilla roots (it does not supplement them). ## Prerequisites - `openssl`, `curl`, `bash` - Official `uv` from [docs.astral.sh/uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/) - A working directory (everything below uses `~/uv-tls-repro` as an example) ## Quick reproduction ```bash mkdir -p ~/uv-tls-repro && cd ~/uv-tls-repro # Save the two scripts from the collapsible sections below as: # ~/uv-tls-repro/generate-certs.sh # ~/uv-tls-repro/manual-repro-uv.sh chmod +x generate-certs.sh manual-repro-uv.sh ./manual-repro-uv.sh ``` `manual-repro-uv.sh` generates `~/uv-tls-repro/certs/` if needed, starts a local TLS server, runs curl (expect OK), then runs `uv pip install idna --dry-run` with `SSL_CERT_FILE` pointing at the test root (expect TLS failure). ## Working directory layout After setup you should have: ``` ~/uv-tls-repro/ generate-certs.sh manual-repro-uv.sh certs/ # created by generate-certs.sh root.pem root.key intermediate.pem intermediate.key leaf.pem leaf.key ``` ## Scripts
generate-certs.sh — root → intermediate (critical policies) → leaf ```bash #!/usr/bin/env bash # Generate a 3-tier chain: root -> intermediate (critical policies) -> leaf. # # Usage: ./generate-certs.sh [output-dir] # Default output: ./certs/ next to this script. set -euo pipefail SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)" OUT_DIR="${1:-${TLS_REPRO_CERT_DIR:-$SCRIPT_DIR/certs}}" mkdir -p "$OUT_DIR" cd "$OUT_DIR" echo "Generating TLS critical-policy fixtures in: $OUT_DIR" cat > root.cnf <<'EOF' [ req ] distinguished_name = dn x509_extensions = v3_ca prompt = no [ dn ] CN = Test Enterprise Root CA O = Example Corp [ v3_ca ] basicConstraints = critical,CA:TRUE keyUsage = critical,keyCertSign,cRLSign subjectKeyIdentifier = hash authorityKeyIdentifier = keyid:always,issuer EOF openssl req \ -new \ -newkey rsa:2048 \ -nodes \ -keyout root.key \ -x509 \ -days 3650 \ -out root.pem \ -config root.cnf cat > intermediate.cnf <<'EOF' [ req ] distinguished_name = dn prompt = no [ dn ] CN = Test Enterprise Inspection Intermediate O = Example Corp [ v3_int ] basicConstraints = critical,CA:TRUE,pathlen:0 keyUsage = critical,keyCertSign,cRLSign subjectKeyIdentifier = hash authorityKeyIdentifier = keyid:always,issuer certificatePolicies = critical,anyPolicy EOF openssl req \ -new \ -newkey rsa:2048 \ -nodes \ -keyout intermediate.key \ -out intermediate.csr \ -config intermediate.cnf openssl x509 \ -req \ -in intermediate.csr \ -CA root.pem \ -CAkey root.key \ -CAcreateserial \ -days 365 \ -out intermediate.pem \ -extfile intermediate.cnf \ -extensions v3_int cat > leaf.cnf <<'EOF' [ req ] distinguished_name = dn req_extensions = v3_req prompt = no [ dn ] CN = test.example [ v3_req ] basicConstraints = critical,CA:FALSE keyUsage = critical,digitalSignature,keyEncipherment extendedKeyUsage = serverAuth subjectAltName = DNS:test.example,DNS:localhost,IP:127.0.0.1 EOF openssl req \ -new \ -newkey rsa:2048 \ -nodes \ -keyout leaf.key \ -out leaf.csr \ -config leaf.cnf openssl x509 \ -req \ -in leaf.csr \ -CA intermediate.pem \ -CAkey intermediate.key \ -CAcreateserial \ -days 30 \ -out leaf.pem \ -extfile leaf.cnf \ -extensions v3_req echo "" echo "=== intermediate: critical Certificate Policies ===" openssl x509 -in intermediate.pem -text -noout | grep -A4 -i "Certificate Policies" echo "" echo "=== openssl verify ===" openssl verify -CAfile root.pem -untrusted intermediate.pem leaf.pem rm -f root.cnf intermediate.cnf leaf.cnf intermediate.csr leaf.csr *.srl echo "Fixtures ready in $OUT_DIR" ```
manual-repro-uv.sh — curl OK; uv default failure ```bash #!/usr/bin/env bash # Usage: ./manual-repro-uv.sh [certs-dir] [uv-binary] # Default certs-dir: ./certs next to this script. set -euo pipefail SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)" CERT_DIR="${1:-${TLS_REPRO_CERT_DIR:-$SCRIPT_DIR/certs}}" UV_BIN="${2:-uv}" PORT="${TLS_REPRO_PORT:-8443}" INDEX_URL="https://127.0.0.1:${PORT}/simple" CACHE_DIR="$(mktemp -d)" SERVER_PID="" cleanup() { if [[ -n "$SERVER_PID" ]] && kill -0 "$SERVER_PID" 2>/dev/null; t
Reply:
Please refer to our [AI policy](https://github.com/astral-sh/.github/blob/main/AI_POLICY.md). This issue appears to have been mostly written by an LLM, it meanders and contradicts itself. Please replace the description with a concise summary in your own words.

It would be helpful to know where this certificate originated from, which software/product/etc.

Based on what we've been able to gleam from what you've written, this does not necessarily appear to be a uv bug. The certificate marks its certificate-policies extension as critical, this technically contravenes guidance of some recent specifications, and more broadly even if webpki does accept critical certificate-policy extensions, rejecting critical extensions that it does not support is a standard safety measure for such a library. I've marked this as external for now.

It sounds like OpenSSL works for this, which to some extent implies it supports the extension whereas webpki does not, and it sounds like `--native-tls` works as a work-around for this environment?

Title: `uv init` package-by-default feedback thread
Text:
`uv init` package-by-default feedback thread

We're changing the default layout when creating a project with `uv init`. In the future, projects will have a build backend by default, and store the source code in a directory. This layout supports some additional features that the flat layout doesn't support.

So we go from this:

```
.
├── main.py
├── pyproject.toml
└── README.md
```

to this:

```
.
├── pyproject.toml
├── README.md
└── src
    └── foo
        └── __init__.py
```

Packaged projects can do a number of things that the unpackaged, flat layout without build backend can't do: The project can be imported from anywhere (`import foo`), it can be distributed (`uv publish`), it can be installed as dependency (`uv add path/to/foo_project` or `uv pip install -e path/to/foo_project`) and it can have entrypoints (`uv run foo` or just `foo` with an active venv). 

A packaged layout is also [required for most testing frameworks](https://hynek.me/articles/testing-packaging/):

```
.
├── pyproject.toml
├── README.md
├── src
│   └── foo
│       └── __init__.py
└── tests
    └── test_foo.py
```

You can try the new behavior with `uv init --preview-features package-by-default`, which makes the behavior of `uv init --package` the default. To go back to the old behavior, you can always use `uv init --no-package`.

There are still many projects for which the flat, unpackaged layout is the right choice, and this layout won't go away. Instead, we're changing the default to include a build backend and the nested directory layout a build backend requires, and making the non-packaged layout the option.

A preview of the updated documentation is available in https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/19026.

This thread is for feedback and questions on this change ahead of stabilization.

Title: Regression in workspace source override between uv 0.11.19 and 0.11.20
Text:
Regression in workspace source override between uv 0.11.19 and 0.11.20

### Summary

# Bug Description

I found a small regression between 0.11.19 and 0.11.20+ involving workspace members that also support standalone installation, causing a `Workspace members must be declared as workspace sources` error. My best guess is that this regression is related to https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/18311, but I haven't confirmed.

Using `override-dependencies` explicitly does not resolve the error. The problem looks related to https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/18232 and its associated PR https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/18954 but I don't know for sure.

.

│   ├── apps
│   │   └── app
│   │       └── pyproject.toml
│   ├── lib
│   │   └── pyproject.toml
│   └── pyproject.toml

requires-python = ">=3.11"
dependencies = [
    "app",
    "lib",
]

[tool.uv]
package = false

[tool.uv.workspace]
members = [
    "packages/app",
    "packages/lib",
]

[tool.uv.sources]
app = { workspace = true }
lib = { workspace = true }

`packages/pyproject.toml`:

    "app",

[tool.uv.sources]
app = { path = "app", editable = true }

Title: Support project-local task aliases in pyproject.toml
Text:
Support project-local task aliases in pyproject.toml

### Summary

Add support for defining project-local task aliases in `pyproject.toml` that can be executed through `uv run`.

### Example

Instead of repeatedly running:

```bash
uv run uvicorn app.main:app --reload --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000
```

Allow users to define:

```toml
[tool.uv.tasks]
dev = "uvicorn app.main:app --reload --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000"
test = "pytest"
lint = "ruff check ."
format = "ruff format ."
```

And then execute:

```bash
uv run dev
uv run test
uv run lint
uv run format
```

### Motivation

Many projects have common development commands that are long and frequently used.

Benefits:

* Reduces repetition of long commands.
* Improves onboarding by keeping common workflows in `pyproject.toml`.
* Makes project commands self-documenting.
* Avoids introducing an additional task runner dependency for simple projects.

### Existing Alternatives

Current options include:

* Running the full command with `uv run`.
* Makefiles.
* Justfiles.
* Taskipy.
* Poe the Poet.

These work well, but a lightweight built-in solution could improve the developer experience for smaller projects.

Title: Regression in 0.11.22: `uv venv` writes truncated `version_info` to `pyvenv.cfg`, breaking pre-commit health check
Text:
Regression in 0.11.22: `uv venv` writes truncated `version_info` to `pyvenv.cfg`, breaking pre-commit health check

### Summary
`uv 0.11.22` writes a truncated `version_info` into `pyvenv.cfg` (missing the `.final.0` release-level suffix that `venv` / `virtualenv` produce). When pre-commit creates its hook environments via `pre-commit-uv` (i.e. `uv venv`), pre-commit's post-install health check compares the recorded version against the interpreter's full version string, finds a mismatch, and rejects the environment — aborting the run before any hook executes. This is a regression: `uv 0.11.21` worked. Looks like a re-introduction of #1689 ("We now match `venv` when reporting the Python version").

### Regression (bisected via CI)
Identical project, runner image, reusable workflow (same commit), `pre-commit-uv 4.2.1`, and managed `cpython-3.13.14`. The only variable that changed is the uv version (CI resolves uv to latest each run):

- 2026-06-18, uv **0.11.21** -> pre-commit passes (all hooks green)
- 2026-06-19, uv **0.11.22** -> pre-commit fails at the health check

### Observed failure (uv 0.11.22)
Step: `uv tool run --with pre-commit-uv pre-commit run --show-diff-on-failure --color=always --all-files`, `UV_MANAGED_PYTHON=1`, ubuntu-22.04.

```
[INFO] Installing environment for https://github.com/pre-commit/pre-commit-hooks.
[INFO] Once installed this environment will be reused.
[INFO] This may take a few minutes...
[INFO] Using pre-commit with uv 0.11.22 via pre-commit-uv 4.2.1
An unexpected error has occurred: AssertionError: BUG: expected environment for python to be healthy immediately after install, please open an issue describing your environment

more info:

virtualenv python version did not match created version:
- actual version: 3.13.14
- expected version: 3.13

Check the log at /home/runner/.cache/pre-commit/pre-commit.log
Error: Process completed with exit code 3.
```

`actual version` is the real interpreter (`3.13.14`); `expected version` is what was recorded in `pyvenv.cfg`.

### Minimal reproduction
`uv venv` writes a truncated `version_info` compared to `virtualenv`:

```
$ uvx virtualenv /tmp/vetest && grep version_info /tmp/vetest/pyvenv.cfg
version_info = 3.13.0.final.0

$ uv venv /tmp/uvtest --python 3.13.0 && grep version_info /tmp/uvtest/pyvenv.cfg
Using CPython 3.13.0 interpreter at: ~/.pyenv/versions/3.13.0/bin/python3.13
version_info = 3.13.0
```

### Expected vs actual
- Expected: `version_info` in `X.Y.Z.final.0` form (matching `venv` / `virtualenv`).
- Actual: truncated (`3.13.0` in the local repro; reported as `3.13` by pre-commit in CI). Either way it diverges from the format pre-commit expects, so the health check fails.

### Environment
- uv: 0.11.22 (regressed); 0.11.21 worked
- pre-commit-uv: 4.2.1
- OS: ubuntu-22.04 (CI), macOS arm64 (local repro)
- Related: #1689
Reply:
I'm slightly baffled here.

`uv venv --python 3.13.0 <path>` produces the same result for me on both 0.11.21 and 0.11.22. In fact I can't find any recent version that produces a different result. Tested on Ubuntu and macOS.

That is, it's missing `.final.0` in both cases. So I can reproduce the discrepancy, but not a regression?

Title: Version aware deny-list for resolution for some enterprise indices
Text:
Version aware deny-list for resolution for some enterprise indices

### Summary

Sometimes enterprise indices are actually just permissive proxies. For instance devs can install pretty much anything on it, just not bring it back through CI when they want to push the code on to main. There are some good and bad reasons for this, but nonetheless it is.

The effect is that things work in dev but not in CI.

I'd like a way for a project (maybe even at the machine level) to have a sort of deny-list that's enforced during resolution (add/lock/sync/run), so devs hit the same wall locally that CI enforces.



  - Version-aware, not just names
  - Silent drop: a banned version is just unavailable and the resolver picks an allowed
    one
  - Ability to source from a standalone file: instead of inlining the list in the pyproject.toml file I'd like a file in the workspace. the reason for this is the file would be always changing, and it's really for developer quality of live not necessarily "production" config

What I've found in existing features:
  - exclude-dependencies is a silent drop, but name/inline only.
  - Constraints files are file-sourced and version-aware, but they hard error instead of silently selecting only allowed versions

I had claude put together a rough api prototype of what I sort of had in mind in this draft pr #19931

Text:
Packages ignore `extra-build-dependencies` of local editable dependencies: is this expected?

### Question

Let's say I create `proj1`, with the pyproject.toml as follows:
```toml
[project]
name = "proj1"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Add your description here"
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
authors = []
dependencies = [
  "gdal==3.8.0",
  "rasterio>=1.5.0",
]

[project.scripts]
proj1 = "proj1:main"

[build-system]
requires = ["uv_build>=0.11.23,<0.12.0"]
build-backend = "uv_build"

[tool.uv]
extra-build-dependencies = { gdal = ["numpy"] }
```

It depends on GDAL which requires numpy in order to be able to used the module `gdal_array`. 

Now, I create `proj2` with the following pyproject.toml:
```toml
[project]
name = "proj2"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Add your description here"
readme = "README.md"
authors = []
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = [
    "geopandas>=1.1.3",
    "proj1",
]

[project.scripts]
proj2 = "proj2:main"

[build-system]
requires = ["uv_build>=0.11.23,<0.12.0"]
build-backend = "uv_build"

[tool.uv.sources]
proj1 = { path = "../proj1", editable = true }
```

`proj2`'s folder is parallel to `proj1`'s folder, and it depends on `proj1`. When I run `uv sync`, everything works, I can import all packages from `proj1`, and I can even run `uv run python -c "from osgeo import gdal"` just fine. But, running `uv run python -c "from osgeo import gdal_array"` fails.

However, if I add 
```toml
[tool.uv]
extra-build-dependencies = { gdal = ["numpy"] }
```
to `proj2`'s pyproject.toml, everything works as expected, `gdal_array` included.

I get that `extra-build-dependencies` is a local option for `proj1`, but is it ok for it to be ignored by `proj2`, which needs `numpy` in order to build `gdal`, a dependency `proj2` does not directly installs?

### Platform

Darwin 25.5.0 arm64

### Version

uv 0.11.23 (3cdf50e09 2026-06-19 aarch64-apple-darwin)
Reply:
Yeah, it's intentional that the settings are not loaded from dependencies. It's unfortunate it's repetitive, but it's also the kind of thing that ought to be declared properly in `gdal` so all of the dependent packages don't need to declare this.

While it'd be nice to load this particular setting from a child project, that'd be inconsistent with the way uv handles settings more generally.

I'd recommend using a workspace and declaring the setting there?

Title: Cross-building win->linux using explicit ``--python-platform=`` installs to wrong site-packages dir
Text:
Cross-building win->linux using explicit ``--python-platform=`` installs to wrong site-packages dir

### Summary

I'm cross-building a bundled python environment on a windows host using uv. This is then deployed via a tarball to a debian box. This allows us to bootstrap custom wrapper and authentication logic for our controlplane (including a private package index) using an internal handshake protocol. Put simply, bundled prebuilt environments get around the chicken-vs-egg problem for authenticating to the internal index.

Currently, when building on windows for a linux target, uv installs packages to the wrong site-packages directory, and also -- weirdly -- installs the wrong platform's scripts, despite (as far as I can tell) installing the correct wheels. Specifically:

* Packages are installed to ``/lib/site-packages`` instead of ``/lib/python3.14/site-packages``
* Entrypoints are installed to ``/Scripts`` instead of ``/bin``

As a workaround, we have logic on the host that checks if it's running on a windows machine and targeting unix, and if so, it does the equivalent of ``mv bundle-env/lib/site-packages/* bundle-env/lib/python3.14/site-packages/`` (we invoke all of our entrypoints directly via ``bundle-env/bin/python -m <entrypoint>``, so the scripts being for the wrong platform doesn't cause problems for us). This appears to work, though we're currently dealing with some other issues as well, so it's not 100% clear either way if things are actually fully running yet.

The expected behavior would of course be that uv installs the correct scripts for the target platform, and installs the packages in the correct location for the target as well.

## Further reference

### Build commands (on windows host)

All of this is scripted, so we're invoking via subprocesses. We first download and unzip a python-build-standalone distribution, then install into it using a pre-generated ``pylock.toml`` and ``uv pip sync``.

```python

                    # Note: the actual env is included under the python folder in

                    # toplevel dir!
                    '--prefix=python',
                    f'--python-platform={arch}-{platform}',
                    'pylock.toml',],
                cwd=tmpdir,
                # Note: we have our own handling
                check=False,
                stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
                stderr=subprocess.STDOUT,)
await anyio.run_process(
                [
                    'uv', 'pip', 'install',
                    f'--index={TTPYPI_URL}',
                    '--link-mode=copy',
                    # Note: the actual env is included under the python folder in
                    # the tmpdir; it **doesn't** get extracted directly to the
                    # toplevel dir!
                    '--prefix=python',
                    f'--python-platform={arch}-{platform}',
                    '--no-deps',
                    f'{normalize_name(spec.pkg.pkg_name)}=={spec.version}',],
                cwd=tmpdir,
                # Note: we have our own handling
                check=False,
                stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
                stderr=subprocess.STDOUT,)

Title: `uv tree --invert` silently discards leaf-loops
Text:
`uv tree --invert` silently discards leaf-loops

### Summary

If you have `A -> B <-> C` `uv tree` will do its best to print this out, showing A -> B -> C -> B(*)

If you then run this through `uv tree --invert` we will print nothing, because we will invert the graph, try to compute roots based on "nodes with 0 in-degree" and determine there are no such nodes.

This isn't as simple as cycles causing problems, as e.g. `A -> B <-> C -> D` prints fine because invert(D) has 0 in-degree and we're off to the races.

A more subtle in-between point is:

A -> B
A -> C
C <-> D

In this case I believe `uv tree --invert` will print only `B -> A`, as it finds that invert(B) has 0 in-degree and print all its children.

# Semantic Issue

The fundamental problem is the logical behaviour of `--invert` is "turn the leaves into roots, reverse the edges, and run as normal". This doesn't work for leaf-like cycles, as no member of the cycle is a leaf. We should either warn/complain this happens (meh) or perform some arbitrary tie break, declaring some member of the cycle to be the leaf.

`uv tree` (non-inverted) already sort of does this, as it has a way to go "oh yeah but we already saw this" and terminate the cycle:

```
root v0.1.0
└── package-a v0.1.0
    └── package-b v0.1.0
        └── package-a v0.1.0 (*)
package-b v0.1.0 (*)
package-a v0.1.0 (*)
(*) Package tree already displayed
```

I have a vague notion in mind that you can "just" run breadth-first search and then all the nodes for which you visit no children (because all them were already visited) are your leaves but I don't want to think too hard about it right now.


# Reproduction

Reproduction script here:

<details>
<summary>script demonstrating this failure mode</summary>

```sh
#!/bin/sh
set -eu

UV_BIN=${UV_BIN:-uv}
PROJECT_DIR=$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/uv-tree-invert-cycle.XXXXXX")
trap 'rm -rf "$PROJECT_DIR"' EXIT HUP INT TERM

# Create this dependency graph entirely from local workspace packages:
#
#     root -> package-a -> package-b
#                ^            |
#                +------------+
#
# The cycle is a leaf strongly-connected component: neither package in it has
# a dependency outside the cycle.
mkdir -p "$PROJECT_DIR/packages/package-a" "$PROJECT_DIR/packages/package-b"

cat >"$PROJECT_DIR/pyproject.toml" <<'EOF'
[project]
name = "root"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.11"
dependencies = ["package-a"]

[tool.uv.sources]
package-a = { workspace = true }

[tool.uv.workspace]
members = ["packages/*"]
EOF

cat >"$PROJECT_DIR/packages/package-a/pyproject.toml" <<'EOF'
[project]
name = "package-a"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.11"
dependencies = ["package-b"]

[tool.uv.sources]
package-b = { workspace = true }
EOF

cat >"$PROJECT_DIR/packages/package-b/pyproject.toml" <<'EOF'
[project]
name = "package-b"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.11"
dependencies = ["package-a"]

[tool.uv.sources]
package-a = { workspace = true }
EOF

cd "$PROJECT_DIR"

echo '$ uv --version'
"$UV_BIN" --version

echo
echo '$ uv lock'
"$UV_BIN" lock

echo
echo '$ uv tree --frozen'
"$UV_BIN" tree --frozen

echo
echo '$ uv tree --frozen --invert'
# The inverted graph has no node with in-degree zero, so uv chooses no roots.
# It then exits successfully without rendering any of the three packages.
set +e
"$UV_BIN" tree --frozen --invert >invert.stdout 2>invert.stderr
status=$?
set -e
cat invert.stdout
cat invert.stderr >&2

stdout_bytes=$(wc -c <invert.stdout | tr -d ' ')
echo "exit status: $status"
echo "stdout bytes: $stdout_bytes"

if [ "$status" -eq 0 ] && [ "$stdout_bytes" -eq 0 ]; then
    echo
    echo "BUG REPRODUCED: --invert succeeded but silently omitted the entire dependency graph."
    exit 0
fi

echo
echo "Bug was not reproduced (expected exit status 0 and empty stdout)." >&2
exit 1
```

</details>

Title: `uv tool`: give users a flexible way to install tools with modifications
Text:
`uv tool`: give users a flexible way to install tools with modifications

TL;DR: users want something like `pipx inject` for `uv tool install`, but that's not something we want to add: it violates our idioms around declarative packaging, is hard to guarantee sound resolutions for, etc.

It seems like most user requests for something like `uv tool inject` are really an [XY problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XY_problem): what users want is an easy way to install a tool with specific modifications, _without_ having to remember/save a long list of `--with` options. In other words, users don't want `uv tool inject` per se, they want a way to avoid `uv tool install ... --with abc --with def --with ghi ...`.

One way we could accomplish this is to have _something_ like a `pyproject.toml`, but geared specifically towards tool installation. One open question is how much information would need to go in that file (e.g. non-default indices, etc.).

See #14746 and #7312 (and probably others) for some more context.

Title: `uv audit`: Add support for `--vex` to  ignore vulnerabilities from a vex file
Text:
`uv audit`: Add support for `--vex` to  ignore vulnerabilities from a vex file

### Summary

Hi!

Currently, vulnerabilities can be ignored through inline arguments `--ignore` and `--ignore-until-fixed` in `uv audit`, but I think this can become (1) cumbersome and is not really (2) explicit in repositories, as these arguments, including their vulnerabilities, are often hidden inside scripts executing `uv audit`.

Most importantly: (3) No one knows **why** the vulnerabilities are ignored.

Therefore, I propose we add an optional argument `--vex`, denoting the path to a vex file.

---

Vex files contain a machine-readable format (mostly json) to mark whether a vulnerability can be exploited given some context. Most notably, such a context can be the _code_ of a repository. Each vulnerability listed needs an explanation (3) **why** it can (not) be exploited.

These files are often used in Enterprise settings with tools like Sonatype (see [SBOM VEX Workflow](https://help.sonatype.com/en/sbom-vex-workflow.html#sbom-vex-workflow)) to triage vulnerabilities, create waivers, and secure the supply chain for internal software.

Furthermore, other scanning tools like `trivy` already support a `--vex` flag (in that case OpenVEX).

I think VEX files are a (2) very durable and explicit way to handle (supply chain) vulnerabilities in projects, which would pair great with `uv audit` as it would allow a (1) central way to both declare vulnerabilities, and respect them when scanning.

Examples for vex formats, which could be supported, are:
- [OpenVEX](https://github.com/openvex/spec)
- [CycloneDX VEX](https://cyclonedx.org/use-cases/vulnerability-exploitability/)

---

If it is decided that this is an extension worth pursuing, then I would be happy to get to work.

### Example

Instead of a long collection of inline `--ignore` and `--ignore-until-fixed` arguments:

```bash
uv audit --ignore CVE-2024-14027 --ignore CVE-2026-3713 --ignore-until-fixed CVE-2026-29786 ...
```

The user could just provide `--vex` with the path to a vex file:

```bash
uv audit --vex openvex.json
```

or

```bash
uv audit --vex cyclonedx.vex.json
```

This would greatly enhance UX and make ignoring vulnerabilities more explicit.
Reply:
Hi @TimCares, thanks for opening an issue.

> Instead of a long collection of inline `--ignore` and `--ignore-until-fixed` arguments:

Is there a reason you'd pass these via the CLI at all, rather than using `uv.toml` or `pyproject.toml` to configure your ignores?

For example:

```toml
[tool.uv.audit]
ignore = ["PYSEC-2022-43017", "GHSA-5239-wwwm-4pmq"]
```

Docs here: https://docs.astral.sh/uv/reference/settings/#audit

I think that's what we'd generally recommend for anything other than one-off audits. In practice people tend to denote their reasons for ignoring vulns with TOML comments, although I think a potentially valuable improvement would be to allow each ID to be given a structured reason, e.g.:

```toml
[tool.uv.audit]
ignore = [
  {
	id = "PYSEC-...",
    reason = "The codebase is haunted",
  }
]
```

My first hunch is that we _probably_ don't want to support another file format here, particularly not if there's a lack of ecosystem industry/tooling consensus on _which_ format to support _and_ we have our own config already. But I'm curious if there's a gap with the current config that a new format would help with specifically.

Title: `uv build`: produce an error if the user tries to include their cache
Text:
`uv build`: produce an error if the user tries to include their cache

This is a partial revival of the underlying cause of https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/11213 -- if a user does something like `UV_CACHE_DIR=.uv-cache` and then does `uv build`, their backend may try and include all of `.uv-cache/`.

That in turn has three problems:

1. It's not at all related to dist construction and shouldn't be in dists at all;
2. It's liable to cause extremely weird downstream errors (like hardlink extraction problems or overlong paths, depending on the host);
3. It's _potentially_ a security/infoleak issue, if the cache contains anything sensitive.

The user's build backend is potentially entirely arbitrary, so I think what `uv build` needs to do is pre-check the project directory itself to see if the cache directory is enclosed under it. We should then produce a reasonable error (or maybe a warning for now?) if we detect that.

Title: `build`: warn on packaging a `py.typed` marker but missing the `Typing :: *` classifier
Text:
`build`: warn on packaging a `py.typed` marker but missing the `Typing :: *` classifier

### Summary

A typed project or partial stubs-only package will ship a `py.typed` marker as per https://typing.python.org/en/latest/spec/distributing.html#packaging-type-information

But it's easy to forget to also add the appropriate Trove Classifier for discoverability. I think the `uv-build` backend already outputs warnings in  some scenarios (for example: version numbers that don't match their canonical representation, deprecated classifiers, etc). It feels well within scope to warn about incorrect or missing classifiers.
In this case, having either `Typing :: Stubs Only` or `Typing :: Typed` should be enough to avoid the warning I'm suggesting.

A warning is non-blocker, and doesn't require packaging standard changes (as I'm not requesting something like automatic classifier insertion here)

Relates to https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/16426:
> Currently, a typed project, more specifically a 'library' project, should advertise that its typed in two ways:
>   * a `Typing :: Typed` trove classifier to aide in PyPI search
>   * a `py.typed` 'marker' file in the project to signal type checkers to use the library's type hints in downstream usage
>       (this is pretty basic and known, just putting it here for completeness sake)

Inversely, having the classifier in a package that doesn't ship a `py.typed` file OR ends in `-stubs` (the package module name, not the distribution) should also be a warning.

Title: uv add --no-index --find-links fails to resolve platform-specific dependencies that are not required on the current platform
Text: uv add --no-index --find-links fails to resolve platform-specific dependencies that are not required on the current platform ### Summary ## Summary `uv add` fails when resolving a package that contains platform-specific dependencies, even though those dependencies are not applicable to the current platform. In contrast, both `pip install` and `uv pip install` succeed using the exact same local wheel repository. This appears to be an issue in the dependency resolver used by `uv add` (lock generation), rather than package installation. ## Environment * OS: Linux x86_64 * Python: 3.12 * uv: 0.11.24 ## Steps to reproduce Create a clean project: ```bash mkdir opensandbox-env cd opensandbox-env uv init ``` Download all required wheels: ```bash mkdir ../python-wheels pip download \ --only-binary=:all: \ -d ../python-wheels \ opensandbox-server ``` Verify that the package can be installed: ```bash uv pip install \ --no-index \ --find-links ../python-wheels \ opensandbox-server ``` This succeeds. Now try: ```bash uv add \ opensandbox-server \ --no-index \ --find-links ../python-wheels ``` ## Actual behavior Dependency resolution fails with: ``` Because only pywin32{sys_platform == 'win32'}<304 is available and docker==7.1.0 depends on pywin32{sys_platform == 'win32'}>=304, we can conclude that docker==7.1.0 cannot be used. ``` The resolver trace also contains: ``` docker==7.1.0 depends on pywin32{sys_platform == 'win32'}>=304 no versions of pywin32{sys_platform == 'win32'}>=304 ``` ## Expected behavior Since the current platform is Linux, the dependency ``` pywin32 >=304 ; sys_platform == "win32" ``` should not participate in dependency resolution for the current environment. Both ```bash pip install opensandbox-server ``` and ```bash uv pip install \ --no-index \ --find-links ../python-wheels \ opensandbox-server ``` work correctly. I would expect `uv add` to either: 1. Ignore platform-specific dependencies that do not match the current environment when generating the lock file, or 2. At least not fail because a Windows-only dependency is unavailable in an offline Linux environment. ## Additional observations The local wheel directory does **not** contain any `pywin32` wheel, because `pip download` correctly skips Windows-only dependencies on Linux. The resolver message is also a little confusing: ``` Because only pywin32<304 is available... ``` However, the debug trace reports: ``` no versions of pywin32>=304 ``` which seems inconsistent. It may simply be an error-message formatting issue, but it made debugging more difficult. ## Notes This issue only affects `uv add`. The following commands all succeed: ```bash pip install opensandbox-server ``` ```bash uv pip install opensandbox-server ``` Only `uv add` fails while resolving dependencies for lock generation. ### Platform Rocky Linux 9.6 ### Version uv 0.11.24 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu) ### Python version Python 3.12.13
Reply:
I think this is broadly intentional. `uv add` does a [universal resolution](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/resolution/#universal-resolution), so it doesn't special-case the current platform in any way -- it solves in the same way regardless of what machine you're on. You can tell uv to (e.g.) ignore Windows with:

```toml
[tool.uv]
environments = ["sys_platform == 'linux'"]
```

Title: Warn when `pyproject.toml` uses TOML 1.1 syntax (e.g. multi-line inline tables) that Python's `tomllib` can't parse
Text:
Warn when `pyproject.toml` uses TOML 1.1 syntax (e.g. multi-line inline tables) that Python's `tomllib` can't parse

## Summary

`uv`'s TOML parser (`toml_edit`) accepts **multi-line inline tables** in `pyproject.toml`, which are a TOML **1.1** feature. The released TOML spec is **1.0.0**, and the Python standard library's `tomllib` (TOML 1.0) rejects them. As a result, `uv` happily reads a `pyproject.toml` that a `tomllib`-based build backend cannot — and for a `setuptools`-built package, `uv sync`/`uv build` then fails deep inside the build backend with an opaque error.

The failure surfaces far from its cause: resolution succeeds, then the editable build dies with a `tomllib.TOMLDecodeError` traceback that points into `setuptools`, not at the offending lines in the user's own `pyproject.toml`. "It Just Works" feels like a selling point of `uv`, so accepting config that predictably breaks the build is a UX defect.

I'd like `uv` to **warn (or lint) when `pyproject.toml` uses TOML 1.1 syntax that stdlib `tomllib` cannot parse** — multi-line inline tables being the obvious case — ideally pointing at the exact key/lines, since `uv` is well-positioned to know the file is likely to be re-parsed by a `tomllib`-based build backend.

## Example

A package built with the `setuptools` backend:

```toml
[build-system]
requires = ["setuptools"]
build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"

[project]
name = "demo"
version = "0"
requires-python = ">=3.11"

[tool.uv]
exclude-newer-package = {
  ruff = "3 days",
}
```

`uv` parses this fine and resolves, but `uv sync` then fails when it builds the package:

```
× Failed to build `demo @ file:///.../demo`
╰─▶ Call to `setuptools.build_meta.build_editable` failed (exit status: 1)
    ...
    tomllib.TOMLDecodeError: Invalid initial character for a key part (at line 11, column 26)
```

The same `[tool.uv]` block in a project **without** a `[build-system]` (a workspace/virtual root) causes no error, because nothing ever re-parses it with `tomllib` — which makes the inconsistency easy to hit by accident.

Notes:
- This is **not** Python-version dependent: `tomllib` rejects the multi-line inline table identically on 3.11 and 3.14.
- The workaround is simply to use valid TOML 1.0 (a `[tool.uv.exclude-newer-package]` table section). The request is purely for `uv` to surface the problem early instead of letting the build fail opaquely.
- Tested with `uv 0.11.25`.
Reply: Starting with the next breaking release, we will rewrite TOML 1.0 to TOML 1.1 when building the packages (https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/18741); supporting TOML 1.1 without rewriting is an intermediary state during which the rewriting is option (`--preview-features toml-backwards-compatibility`)

Title: Allow opt-in reuse of isolated build environments for native-build backends (scikit-build-core, meson-python)
Text:
Allow opt-in reuse of isolated build environments for native-build backends (scikit-build-core, meson-python)

### Summary

Currently, uv creates a fresh, disposable isolated venv (at a new temp path) for every PEP 517 build. For backends like setuptools, hatchling, flit, or pdm-backend this is right as there's no persistent native build state, so a clean env every time costs little and buys hermeticity.

This system becomes weak for build-systems such as  scikit-build-core and meson-python which  drive an underlying native build system (CMake/Ninja, Meson/Ninja) that maintains its own on-disk incremental-build cache (CMakeCache.txt, build.ninja, Meson's meson-info/build.ninja). That cache stores absolute paths (`Python_EXECUTABLE`, `pybind11_DIR`/nanobind's cmake dir, include paths, etc. which are resolved from the isolated build venv. Because that venv's path changes on every single build invocation, the native cache is effectively invalidated every time, even with tool.scikit-build.build-dir set to a persistent, project-local directory. In practice this means editable/iterative C-extension development under build isolation pays a near-full reconfigure+rebuild cost on every change, which is why users end up reaching for --no-build-isolation + manually preinstalled build deps just to get incremental builds back (see #17153, scikit-build/scikit-build-core#1115).

My proposed solution:
Add an opt-in setting, e.g. tool.uv.cached-build-isolation-package = ["mypkg"] (name TBD) that:

- Places that package's isolated build environment at a deterministic, content-addressed path under the uv cache dir (e.g. ~/.cache/uv/build-envs/<hash>), where the hash is derived from the resolved build-system.requires set + interpreter + platform (analogous to how ~/.cache/uv/builds/ already caches built wheels by sdist hash).
- Reuses that directory across invocations as long as the hash is unchanged; automatically creates a new one (and lets the old one age out) when build deps actually change.
- Is locked per-directory the same way the rest of the uv cache is, so concurrent builds (CI matrices, parallel uv sync) don't corrupt a shared env.
- Participates in uv cache prune / uv cache clean like everything else so no new GC mechanism needed.
- Changes only where the env lives on disk, not the isolation/resolution semantics: it's still a separate env from the project env, still rebuilt from scratch if the requirement hash changes, still subject to --no-cache/--refresh.

As far as I can tell this only matters for backends that shell out to a native build system with its own incremental cache. The reason this change is scoped to uv and not those downstream build tools is that those projects can persist their own build-dir, but they can't control where uv places the isolated venv whose paths get baked into that build-dir's cache. The instability is upstream of them, reusing that specific temp directory is inherently uv's call to make. 

### Example

Currently, when users make small edits when developing C extensions to their python package, the entire package must be recompiled as the native cache is invalidated on new venv creations. The new system would allow the build system and type checkers to have a dependable path to the build dependencies allowing the native cache to be reused, drastically improving development time and friction.
Reply:
> That cache stores absolute paths (`Python_EXECUTABLE`, `pybind11_DIR`/nanobind's cmake dir, include paths, etc. which are resolved from the isolated build venv.

Ideally, we instead change scikit-build-core and meson to remove those from their cache. There's a lot of prior discussion in https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/14269 https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/10214 https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/14383 https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/13998 https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/17153 and https://github.com/scikit-build/scikit-build-core/issues/1115 https://github.com/scikit-build/scikit-build-core/pull/420 https://github.com/mesonbuild/meson-python/issues/393, though the discussion seems to have stalled or closed (https://github.com/scikit-build/scikit-build-core/issues/1115#issuecomment-4872478776), have you raised the problem in the build tools themselves? The problem would exist with any build tool using isolated build environments, and the caching doesn't need to depend on the venv location.

Title: gui-scripts entry point doesn't persist when launched via `uv run` on Windows (works when trampoline exe invoked directly)
Text:
gui-scripts entry point doesn't persist when launched via `uv run` on Windows (works when trampoline exe invoked directly)

### Summary

On Windows, running a project's `gui-scripts` entry point via `uv run <name>` returns exit code 0 with no error output, but the GUI process does not persist — no window stays open and no process remains running afterward. Invoking the generated trampoline executable directly (`.venv\Scripts\<name>.exe`) works correctly and the window stays open as expected. Invoking the entry point function directly via `uv run python -c "from pkg.module import main; main()"` also works correctly.

This suggests `uv run <name>` resolves/launches the `gui-scripts` entry point differently from a direct invocation of the trampoline exe it generates, at least in terms of how the GUI-subsystem process's lifetime is tracked/waited on.

### Environment

- uv 0.11.26 (396ef7ce4 2026-06-30 x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
- Windows 11 Pro 10.0.26200
- Python 3.13 (uv-managed, via `.python-version`)
- PySide6-Essentials 6.11
- Reproduced both from VS Code's integrated PowerShell terminal and a plain PowerShell 7 window

### pyproject.toml (relevant part)

```toml
[project.gui-scripts]
apk-explorer = "apk_explorer.gui.main_window:main"
```

`main()` roughly does:

```python
def main(argv=None) -> int:
    app = QApplication([...])
    window = MainWindow()
    window.show()
    return app.exec()
```

### Repro steps

1. `uv sync`
2. `uv run apk-explorer`
   - Returns immediately with exit code 0, no output.
   - `Get-Process -Name apk-explorer` checked immediately after finds nothing — no window ever persists / stays visible.
3. Compare: `.\.venv\Scripts\apk-explorer.exe` (direct invocation of the generated trampoline)
   - Process starts and persists normally; window opens and stays open until closed by the user.
4. Compare: `uv run python -c "from apk_explorer.gui.main_window import main; main()"`
   - Also works correctly; window opens and stays open.

### Expected

`uv run apk-explorer` should behave the same as directly invoking `.venv\Scripts\apk-explorer.exe` — the GUI window should open and persist normally.

### Possibly related

- #2956 (GUI scripts open an unwanted terminal window) — different symptom (extra console window appears), but same general area (Windows gui-scripts trampoline handling); reportedly fixed by #4409.
- #9152 (`--gui-script` flag for `uv run <script.py>`) — suggests `uv run`'s default handling of GUI-subsystem processes needed dedicated flag support for ad-hoc scripts; possibly the same underlying gap also affects project `gui-scripts` entry points invoked via `uv run <name>`.

Happy to provide a minimal reproduction repository if useful.

Title: extra != '...' environment markers always evaluate to false
Text:
extra != '...' environment markers always evaluate to false

### Summary

If you do `uv init etest` and add to pyproject.toml
```toml
[project]
...
dependencies = [
  "requests; extra != 'h'"
]
optional-dependencies = {"h" = ["httpx"]}
```
uv seems to _never_ install requests, whether or not you specify the `h` extra. This happens both with `uv sync`/`uv sync --extra h`, as well as, if you `uv build` the project, `uv pip install`ing either the wheel or the sdist.

This seems possibly related to #17967, where a paid of `extra ==`/`extra !=` in `tool.uv.sources.*.marker` (not on the dependency itself) causes the entire dependency to be dropped.

My motivation here is that `onnxruntime` and `onnxruntime-gpu` are alternatives; they both provide the same files, and whichever one is installed last wins. I want to be able to write a pyproject.toml file with
```toml
[project]
...
dependencies = [
  "onnxruntime; extra != 'gpu'",
]

[project.optional-dependencies]
gpu = [
  "onnxruntime-gpu",
]
```
so that installing the project with no extras gets you `onnxruntime`, and installing the `[gpu]` extra gets you _only_ `onnxruntime-gpu`. However, if I do this, installing the project with no extras installs neither of them.

(Curiously, pip has the opposite bug: `extra != '...'` markers always evaluate to true. This is mentioned in passing in [a DPO thread from a few years ago](https://discuss.python.org/t/the-extra-environment-marker-and-its-operators/4976/15).)

### Platform

Ubuntu 24.04 x86_64

### Version

uv 0.11.24 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu)

### Python version

3.14
Reply: We should probably warn on `extra !=`, see https://github.com/pypa/pip/issues/14139#issuecomment-4881162728 for discussion on why the uv resolver doesn't support this.

Title: Allow `uv version --bump` to handle dynamic versions
Text:
Allow `uv version --bump` to handle dynamic versions

### Question

My releaase process uses GH actions to do the main work, when a new tag is created.

I would like to release by 

- `uv version --bump stable` (assuminig the project has a pre-relase version)
- ... create and push the tag
- GH action is triggered by the tag in and
  - checks whether the tag name matches the project version.
  - build, test, upload, ...
  - bump next pre-release `uv version --bump patch` + `uv version --bump dev`

Problem is, that `--bump` can only handle versions stored in in `pyproject.toml` 
directly
```toml
[project]
version = "0.1.0"
```

In order to have the version also available in `__init__.py`, I have to do something like this (which does not always work, depending on how the library is not installed):
```py
from importlib.metadata import PackageNotFoundError, version as dist_version
from pathlib import Path
import re

def _detect_version() -> str:
    """Resolve package version from installed metadata or local pyproject.toml."""
    try:
        return dist_version("myproject")
    except PackageNotFoundError:
        pass

    pyproject = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "pyproject.toml"
    try:
        text = pyproject.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        match = re.search(r"^version\s*=\s*['\"]([^'\"]+)['\"]", text, re.MULTILINE)
        if match:
            return match.group(1)
    except OSError:
        pass

    return "0.0.0"


__version__ = _detect_version()
```


I would prefer to have the authorative version in `__init__.py`:
```py
__version__ = "0.1.0"
```
and `pyproject.toml`:
```toml
dynamic = ["version"]
```

Does this make sense? 
The `uv version --bump` tool is really handy. Is it planned to make it vork for `__version__` as well?

If it makes sense to you, please consider it a feature request ;-)

### Platform

_No response_

### Version

uv 0.11.25 (Homebrew 2026-06-26 aarch64-apple-darwin)
Reply:
We suggest not storing versions in `__init__.py` and are unlikely to support this in `--bump`.

You should use `importlib.metadata` to fetch the version of a package https://docs.python.org/3/library/importlib.metadata.html#overview

Text:
Linehaul: include `rustc_version`

Our modeling of linehaul is aware of `rustc_version`, but we intentionally leave it empty because of performance concerns:

https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/blob/9adb63eba0f8b721491d56fcf75ae0d9fe4b5789/crates/uv-client/src/linehaul.rs#L148-L149

This is something we _may_ want to re-evaluate given uv's popularity: projects like PyCA Cryptography rely on `rustc_version` in the linehaul metrics to determine when they can safely bump their MSRV, but that signal doesn't capture uv's user base at the moment.

Some misc notes:

- On my local machine, `rustc --version` takes 2ms. However, it _could_ be significantly more in the worst case, e.g. if a user has some kind of corporate MDM or other monitoring software installed (or if their `rustc` is a shim, etc.)
- We could potentially foreclose on some of the performance risk here by doing an `mtime`-aware cache of `rustc --version`, i.e. read from a cached copy of the version until the `rustc` binary itself changes. This would be somewhat flimsy with shims, however.

Context: https://github.com/pypa/pip/pull/9987
Reply: Could projects such as cryptography use [konstin/puccinialin](https://github.com/konstin/puccinialin)to avoid the dependence on the system rust toolchain? Arguably the rustc version doesn't capture the signal they are looking for, as systems with rustup will respect `rust-toolchain.toml`, but those with only a distro toolchain won't.

Title: uv export --format=pylock.toml omits the required packages key when there are no dependencies
Text:
uv export --format=pylock.toml omits the required packages key when there are no dependencies

### Summary

When a project has no dependencies, `uv export --format=pylock.toml` produces a `pylock.toml` that lacks the top-level `packages` key entirely. PEP 751 marks `packages` as required, so even with zero dependencies the output should include `packages = []`.

**Reproduction**

```console
$ uv init test-export
$ cd test-export
$ uv export --no-emit-project --format=pylock.toml
Using CPython 3.14.2
Resolved 1 package in 0.37ms
# This file was autogenerated by uv via the following command:
#    uv export --no-emit-project --format=pylock.toml
lock-version = "1.0"
created-by = "uv"
requires-python = ">=3.11"
```

No `packages` key is emitted.

Passing this file to pip fails, since the key is required:

```console
$ pip3 wheel -r pylock.toml
WARNING: Using pylock.toml as a requirements source is an experimental feature. It may be removed/changed in a future release without prior warning.
ERROR: Invalid pylock file 'pylock.toml': Missing required value in 'packages'
```

**Expected**

According to the [PEP 751](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/pylock-toml/), packages is a required top-level key. uv export should always include it, emitting packages = [] when there are no dependencies, so that the generated file conforms to PEP 751.


**Version**

```console
$ uv --version
uv 0.11.26 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu)
```


### Platform

Ubuntu 24.04

### Version

uv 0.11.26 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu)

### Python version

CPython 3.14.2

Title: "Redundant" env markers removed in 0.11.25 break exported lockfile
Text:
"Redundant" env markers removed in 0.11.25 break exported lockfile

### Summary

The changes introduced in #19933 have broken lockfile exporting. With `uv <0.11.25`, everything was working fine. Our project doesn't have a `tool.uv.environments` configuration.

**Here's what happened:**

Our CI tests need to export the lockfile into the requirements.txt format by running `uv export --frozen --all-extras --group test --format requirements-txt`. The reasons for this are irrelevant.

One of our transitive dependencies is `backports-zstd` (via `urllib3[zstd]`), which backports the zstd module of the stdlib on older Python versions and which is incompatible on Python 3.14 and above:

```toml
[[package]]
name = "urllib3"
version = "2.7.0"
source = { registry = "https://pypi.org/simple" }
sdist = { url = "https://files.pythonhosted.org/packages/53/0c/06f8b233b8fd13b9e5ee11424ef85419ba0d8ba0b3138bf360be2ff56953/urllib3-2.7.0.tar.gz", hash = "sha256:231e0ec3b63ceb14667c67be60f2f2c40a518cb38b03af60abc813da26505f4c", size = 433602, upload-time = "2026-05-07T16:13:18.596Z" }
wheels = [
    { url = "https://files.pythonhosted.org/packages/7f/3e/5db95bcf282c52709639744ca2a8b149baccf648e39c8cc87553df9eae0c/urllib3-2.7.0-py3-none-any.whl", hash = "sha256:9fb4c81ebbb1ce9531cce37674bbc6f1360472bc18ca9a553ede278ef7276897", size = 131087, upload-time = "2026-05-07T16:13:17.151Z" },
]

[package.optional-dependencies]
brotli = [
    { name = "brotli", marker = "platform_python_implementation == 'CPython'" },
    { name = "brotlicffi", marker = "platform_python_implementation != 'CPython'" },
]
zstd = [
    { name = "backports-zstd", marker = "python_full_version < '3.14'" },
]
```

Exporting this results in the `python_full_version < '3.14'` marker to be included, so when running on Python 3.14, this dependency will be skipped, as expected.

```
$ uv export --frozen --all-extras --group test --format requirements-txt | grep backports-zstd
backports-zstd==1.5.0 ; python_full_version < '3.14' \
```

However, now with #19933 merged and included in `uv >=0.11.25`, when updating the lockfile (e.g. by adding a new dependency and running `uv lock --no-upgrade`), the "redundant" markers will be removed:

```toml
[[package]]
name = "urllib3"
version = "2.7.0"
source = { registry = "https://pypi.org/simple" }
sdist = { url = "https://files.pythonhosted.org/packages/53/0c/06f8b233b8fd13b9e5ee11424ef85419ba0d8ba0b3138bf360be2ff56953/urllib3-2.7.0.tar.gz", hash = "sha256:231e0ec3b63ceb14667c67be60f2f2c40a518cb38b03af60abc813da26505f4c", size = 433602, upload-time = "2026-05-07T16:13:18.596Z" }
wheels = [
    { url = "https://files.pythonhosted.org/packages/7f/3e/5db95bcf282c52709639744ca2a8b149baccf648e39c8cc87553df9eae0c/urllib3-2.7.0-py3-none-any.whl", hash = "sha256:9fb4c81ebbb1ce9531cce37674bbc6f1360472bc18ca9a553ede278ef7276897", size = 131087, upload-time = "2026-05-07T16:13:17.151Z" },
]

[package.optional-dependencies]
brotli = [
    { name = "brotli", marker = "platform_python_implementation == 'CPython'" },
    { name = "brotlicffi", marker = "platform_python_implementation != 'CPython'" },
]
zstd = [
    { name = "backports-zstd" },
]
```

This results in `backports-zstd` losing its env marker in the exported requirements.txt format, and an env based on Python 3.14 will attempt to install it, which will not work and result in a build error.

```
$ uv export --frozen --all-extras --group test --format requirements-txt | grep backports-zstd
backports-zstd==1.5.0 \
```

### Platform

any

### Version

0.11.26

### Python version

3.14.6
Reply: Thanks for the report. This seems unintentional, I believe we can reconstruct the full markers on export.

Title: uv incorrectly excludes pre-releases of the base release of a `<V.post` specifier
Text:
uv incorrectly excludes pre-releases of the base release of a `<V.post` specifier

### Summary

uv and packaging disagree on whether `0.12.a1` can satisfy `<0.12.post2`. packaging includes these as of 26.1 (pypa/packaging#1140).

The spec:

> The exclusive ordered comparison `<V` MUST NOT allow a pre-release of the specified version unless the specified version is itself a pre-release.

packaging reads "the specified version" of `<0.12.post2`  to be `0.12.post2` and therefore pre-releases of the specified version are of the form `0.12.post2.devN`.

<specifier>
Test Cases:
<details>
packaging >= 26.1:

```python
from packaging.specifiers import Specifier

assert Specifier("<0.12.0.post2").contains("0.12.0a1")
```

uv, fails on main:

```rust
#[test]
fn less_than_post_release_admits_base_prereleases() {
    let specifier: VersionSpecifier = "<0.12.0.post2".parse().unwrap();
    let range = Ranges::<Version>::from(specifier);
    assert!(range.contains(&"0.12.0a1".parse().unwrap()));
}
```
</details>
</summary>

In particular if you look at the property tests I add to packaging: https://github.com/pypa/packaging/pull/1144, uv's current behavior breaks the invariant:

> given versions v1 and v2 and v2 < v1 then if the specifier <V matches v1 it should also match v2.


References: pypa/packaging#1140, pypa/packaging#1144; #16868, #16881, #19778

### Platform

Any

0.11.28

Title: `uv export` does not output correct relative paths for workspace members
Text:
`uv export` does not output correct relative paths for workspace members

### Description

When a workspace contains two modules and there is a dependency between them, `uv export` does not resolve relative paths between their directories.
For example, when there are `lib` and `app` modules within a workspace and `app` depends on `lib`, running `uv export` in the `app` directory outputs `-e ./lib` instead of the expected `-e ../lib`.

(I think this behavior is unexpected, but is this intentional?)

### Reproducible procedures and its output

### Commands to reproduce

```bash
uv init --bare
uv init --lib lib
uv init app
cd app
uv add lib@../lib
cat pyproject.toml
uv export --format requirements.txt --no-emit-project --no-hashes
```

### `pyproject.toml` in the child package `app`

```toml
[project]
name = "app"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Add your description here"
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.13"
dependencies = [
    "lib",
]

[tool.uv.sources]
lib = { workspace = true }
```

### Resulting `requirements.txt`-format output

```
# This file was autogenerated by uv via the following command:
#    uv export --format requirements.txt --no-emit-project --no-hashes
-e ./lib
    # via app
```

### Notes

`sam build` runs commands as follows internally (which are executed from [`aws-lambda-builders`](https://github.com/aws/aws-lambda-builders), and fails with an error due to the issue above:

```bash
uv export --format requirements.txt --no-emit-project --no-hashes --no-default-groups --output-file /tmp/path/to/lock_requirements.txt --python 3.13
uv pip install -r /tmp/path/to/lock_requirements.txt --target /path/to/deps/dir --cache-dir
```
Reply: I think this is generally intended -- we export relative to the workspace root, regardless of where you are in the workspace.

Title: Feature: Named, shared environments independent of a project directory
Text:
Feature: Named, shared environments independent of a project directory

### Summary

#1495 (conda-like global environments) was closed as completed by #18214; its duplicates #12740 and #13457 are closed, and #12358 (open) covers only listing. `centralized-project-envs` (#18214, uv 0.11.28) relocates a project's `.venv` into the cache, still one environment per project and activated by path. The named and shared use cases from those threads remain unaddressed and untracked.

Use cases not covered by `centralized-project-envs`:

- One environment shared across many projects or scripts, so heavy dependencies (e.g. PyTorch, several GB) install once rather than per project (#13457, #12740).
- Several named environments for one project whose dependency sets can't coexist (my case).
- One named environment shared across checkouts of the same repo (worktrees, parallel branches), reused without rebuilding (my case).
- Named ad-hoc environments not tied to any project, created and removed from anywhere, as with `conda create -n <name>` (#13457).
- Activate, list, and remove environments by name, backed by a registry and shell integration (#1495 companion requests, #12740, #12358).

Cache linking does not make this redundant. uv links cached packages into each venv (reflink or hard link, by platform and filesystem), but:

- across drives or filesystems (a separate data drive, NFS/NAS, or any cross-drive case on Windows), it falls back to full copies (`Failed to hardlink files; falling back to full copy`) (my cache does not sit on the same drive as my code)
- it dedups only same version packages, so projects resolving independently to different versions keep distinct copies, and the cache retains every version;
- it never covers per-venv bytecode (`__pycache__`) or the venv tree. It dedups files, not environments: still one venv and one activation per project.

`UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT` can target an external env per directory, but offers no activation, listing, or removal by name. conda covers all of the above.

Without this, I stay on a conda + uv workflow and can't migrate to only uv.



### Example

Hypothetical command names to illustrate:.

```
uv venv --name app-stable --python 3.12
uv venv --name app-next --python 3.12
uv activate app-stable          # by name, from any directory
uv venv --list
uv venv --delete app-next
```

One env shared across checkouts:

```
cd ~/checkout-a && uv activate app-stable
cd ~/checkout-b && uv activate app-stable   # same env, no rebuild
```
Reply:
Thanks for writing this up. A couple small notes.

> Several named environments for one project whose dependency sets can't coexist (my case).

We are exploring this concept a bit as different "dependency universes" for a project.

> cross drives or filesystems (a separate data drive, NFS/NAS, or any cross-drive case on Windows), it falls back to full copies (Failed to hardlink files; falling back to full copy) (my cache does not sit on the same drive as my code)

Centralized storage does help with this, since we colocate the environment with the cache instead of your project.

Title: Migrating a databricks project to use uv
Text:
Migrating a databricks project to use uv

### Question

I know uv isn't fully supported in databricks yet (there is partial support with serverless computes but that's just for `uv pip install`). 

However, I kinda managed to migrate a legacy databricks project (think multiple messy requirements.txt with weird pins) to a proper pyproject.toml project with the help of uv. I basically cleaned the requirements.txt a bit, used `uv add -r requirements.txt` to create a `pyproject.toml` and `uv.lock` with proper dependencies.

The trouble starts when I want to use the new format in databricks. As I said before, databricks does not support uv (we are using databricks jobs which define `libraries: ...` to define what dependencies to use. For now, I found a way around this, I am basically exporting `uv.lock` to a much stricter `requirements.txt` with pinned versions. I am enforcing this with our CI process (pre-commit hooks to export, CI to validate by generating a new file and comparing). It works great, I can still use the `requirements.txt` in databricks, while ensuring I have proper versioning with uv. That is, until I run into the following issues:

2. Some dependency versions clash with the versions of the pre-installed libraries in the cluster (by default). This hasn't caused any issues per-se, but I have got a few warnings, and I am starting to wonder if we need to pin every dependency based on the databricks cluster.

My question is, is there any solution to this? Some better way to handle this mess? I wasn't going to ask this (I have seen the other open issues related to this topic), but I noticed the following tip in your documentation, so I thought no harm in asking:

> In general, we recommend against using both a uv.lock and a requirements.txt file. The uv.lock format is more powerful and includes features that cannot be expressed in requirements.txt. If you find yourself exporting a uv.lock file, consider opening an issue to discuss your use case.

Title: Workspace discovery cache is rebuilt after settings resolution
Text:
Workspace discovery cache is rebuilt after settings resolution

## Summary

A command can build the workspace discovery cache twice even when settings resolution leaves the cache root unchanged.

The early discovery performed while resolving settings populates a WorkspaceCache. run() then creates a new default WorkspaceCache before command dispatch, so the same large workspace is discovered again.

This appears to be a remaining in-process cache reuse opportunity after #12096 and the large-workspace startup work in #18311.

## Reproduction

I used an offline synthetic workspace with 1,500 members and measured a release build with two independent runs of 30 alternating baseline/candidate pairs.

Current main:

- workspace discovery builds: 2
- mean startup time: 185.775 ms
- median startup time: 184.607 ms

A small prototype reuses the early cache only when the provisional and resolved cache roots are equal:

- workspace discovery builds: 1
- mean startup time: 124.233 ms
- median startup time: 120.863 ms
- mean reduction: 33.13%
- faster in 59 of 60 paired samples

When uv.toml changes the cache root, the prototype creates a fresh cache and discovery remains 2 to 2.

## Proposed scope

- carry the early WorkspaceCache into command dispatch
- reuse it only when the resolved cache root matches
- retain existing invalidation behavior for workspace mutation paths
- add a focused regression test for matching and changed cache roots

The prototype passes the focused regression, uv-workspace tests, workspace integration tests, cargo check, clippy, fmt, and diff checks.

Would this small follow-up be welcome as a pull request?
Reply: That's a good find, thank you! I had Codex do it here: https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/20356

Title: Publishing package to Artifactory subfolder
Text:
Publishing package to Artifactory subfolder

### Question

Hello!
In my corporate infrastructure we are using Artifactory index to publish Python packages and each team has its own subfolder in the index to prevent collisions in package names. So I want to be able to deploy package directly to my team's own folder but it turned out to be not so obvious task.

Publishing directly to index URL:
`https://<ARTIFACTORY_BASE_URL>/artifactory/api/pypi/<INDEX_NAME>`
leads to an error that it is prohibited by policy. It's okay because Artifactory expects us to publish in a subfolder.

So we can try to add subfolder name in URL:
`https://<ARTIFACTORY_BASE_URL>/artifactory/api/pypi/<INDEX_NAME>/<SUBFOLDER_NAME>`
but then uv will report an 404 Not Found error. Indeed such endpoint doesn't exist in classic PyPI API.

Poetry 1.x was able to solve this problem by setting package name as `<SUBFOLDER_NAME>/<PACKAGE_NAME>`. But it is now not supported by PEP 508 as both Poetry 2.x and uv  use the standard [project] section.

There is one workaround from JFrog how-to (https://jfrog.com/help/r/artifactory-how-to-upload-a-pypi-package-to-artifactory-via-rest-api/artifactory-how-to-upload-a-pypi-package-to-artifactory-via-rest-api) that suggests using cURL to request Artifactory REST API instead of PyPI API. This works but I wonder if there is some solution to let it work with native uv publishing?

### Platform

_No response_

### Version

_No response_
Reply:
This sounds like a deficiency in Artifactory: based on that link they're not using PyPI's upload API for their "subfolder" concept:

> When attempting to upload specific PyPI packages to designated subfolders for permission control and organization, neither twine nor sdist support direct uploads to subfolders. This is because the PyPI API in Artifactory does not inherently allow subfolder creation. Instead, folder management is handled through the standard repository API.

(Their language makes it sound like a deficiency in twine and other uploading clients, but based on your description of the behavior you've seen with Poetry 1.x it sounds like they're doing something really hacky like treating a package named `foo/bar` as having a "subfolder".)

The correct solution here is for JFrog to support PyPI's upload API style on that endpoint (and [PEP 694](https://peps.python.org/pep-0694/) once it's finalized). If you have a support contact/representative at JFrog, can you contact them to ensure they're aware of this?

## Summary

`--extra` defined on the workspace root is rejected when targeting a member with `--package`. The only workaround is `--all-packages`, which installs dependencies from **all** workspace members — not just the targeted one.

**Reproduction:**

```sh
# Setup workspace
uv init --name root --no-readme
uv add requests click
uv add --optional extra-deps httpx

uv init worker --name worker --no-readme
uv add --package worker requests rich
```

**`--package` fails on root extras:**

```sh
uv sync --locked --package worker --extra extra-deps --no-install-workspace --dry-run
```

```
error: Extra `extra-deps` is not defined in the project's `optional-dependencies` table
```

**`--all-packages` works but pulls in all members' dependencies:**

```sh
uv sync --locked --all-packages --extra extra-deps --no-install-workspace --dry-run
```

```
Would install 14 packages
 + anyio==4.14.1
 + certifi==2026.6.17
 + charset-normalizer==3.4.7
 + click==8.4.2       # root-only dep — should not be installed
 + h11==0.16.0
 + httpcore==1.0.9
 + httpx==0.28.1      # extra dep — correct
 + idna==3.18
 + markdown-it-py==4.2.0
 + mdurl==0.1.2
 + pygments==2.20.0
 + requests==2.34.2
 + rich==15.0.0       # worker dep — correct
 + urllib3==2.7.0
```

`--no-install-workspace` skips the workspace *packages* but still installs their *dependencies*. Python 3.13.12

Title: `uv pip compile`/`uv pip sync` silently ignore the `--cert` flag instead of erroring
Text:
`uv pip compile`/`uv pip sync` silently ignore the `--cert` flag instead of erroring

### Summary

uv's `pip`-compatibility layer accepts pip's `--cert` flag on `uv pip compile` and `uv pip sync`, but silently ignores it — no warning, no error, no effect. This is inconsistent with every other unsupported/redundant compat flag (including the adjacent `--client-cert`, which correctly errors), and it's a silent footgun: a user migrating a `pip-compile --cert /corp/ca.pem` command reasonably believes their custom CA bundle is in effect when it is not.

### Reproduction

```console
$ echo "idna==3.6" > requirements.in
$ uv pip compile --cert /path/does-not-exist.pem requirements.in
# → proceeds normally; the (nonexistent!) cert path is never validated or used
```

Compare with the sibling flag, which does error:

```console
$ uv pip compile --client-cert /path/x.pem requirements.in
error: pip-compile's `--client-cert` is unsupported (uv doesn't support dedicated client certificates)
```

### Root cause

In `crates/uv-cli/src/compat.rs`, both `PipCompileCompatArgs` and `PipSyncCompatArgs` declare a `cert: Option<String>` field (so clap accepts `--cert`), but neither struct's `validate()` ever inspects `self.cert`. Every other field in those structs is handled with either a `warn_user!` or an `anyhow!` error.

### Expected behavior

Consistent with `--client-cert` and the module's documented contract ("return an error [when an argument] does not match uv's behavior"), `--cert` should error and point users at the supported mechanism — the `SSL_CERT_FILE` / `SSL_CERT_DIR` environment variables ([docs](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/authentication/certificates/)).

### Notes

This is scoped narrowly to the compat-layer no-op. It is _not_ a request for a first-class `--cert` flag or config key (that's #6715) and does not touch uv's global TLS behavior. I have a fix + integration tests ready and will open a PR.

### Platform / version

Reproduced on `main` (uv 0.11.28), macOS.

Title: `uv lock` is not idempotent for impossible cross-variable markers
Text:
`uv lock` is not idempotent for impossible cross-variable markers

### Summary

I'm working on marker logic and doing a comparison of different libraries, while doing a scan of uv, I found a couple of bugs.

When two dependencies each carry an impossible platform marker, uv drops only one of them per lock, and which one it keeps changes between runs. `uv lock` never converges and `uv lock --check` always fails.

pyproject.toml:

```toml
[project]
name = "demo"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.9"
dependencies = [
        "certifi ; os_name == 'nt' and sys_platform == 'linux'",
        "idna ; os_name == 'posix' and sys_platform == 'win32'",
]
```

Then:

```shell
$ uv lock
Using CPython 3.14.6
Resolved 2 packages in 181ms

$ uv lock
Using CPython 3.14.6
Resolved 2 packages in 296ms
Added certifi v2026.6.17
Removed idna v3.18

$ uv lock
Using CPython 3.14.6
Resolved 2 packages in 3ms
Removed certifi v2026.6.17
Added idna v3.18
```

`uv lock --check` always fails.

This is probably because `crates/uv-pep508/src/marker/algebra.rs` encodes known-impossible platform pairs in `exclusions()`. Its private conjunction writes results into the shared memo cache without applying the exclusion check, and the public `and()` reads that cache before reaching the exclusion check.

Title: feat(init/run): improve default project UX (src/ layout, default run targets, and lazy venv)
Text:
feat(init/run): improve default project UX (src/ layout, default run targets, and lazy venv)

### Summary

`uv` has dramatically improved the Python packaging and CLI experience. Drawing inspiration from modern toolchains like Cargo, we can make the out-of-the-box developer experience (DX) even more seamless with a few quality-of-life adjustments to `uv init` and `uv run`. 

The goal of these proposals is to reduce boilerplate, encourage best practices by default, and make newly initialized projects feel cohesive immediately.

### Proposed Improvements

#### 1. Support (or default to) a `src/` layout
The `src/` layout is widely recognized as a (Python) best practice because it prevents accidental imports of local code and ensures tests run against the installed package. 

* **Proposal:** Either make `src/` the default layout for `uv init`, or add a flag (e.g., `uv init --src`).
* **Expected Structure:**
  ```markdown
  my-project/
  ├── pyproject.toml
  ├── README.md
  └── src/
      └── my_project/
          └── __init__.py (or main.py)
```

#### 2. Allow `uv run` with no arguments (using standard entry points)
In Cargo, running `cargo run` just works because the entry point is defined in the manifest. In Python, we can put it in the `[project]` table.

* **Proposal:** If a user runs `uv run` without specifying a script or command, `uv` should look for a default entry point.
* **How it could work:** If `pyproject.toml` defines a Python file, or a script, `uv run` executes it:
```toml
  [project]
  main = "src/main"
```
  Running `uv run` would be equivalent to running `uv run src/main`.

#### 3. Initialize the virtual environment during `uv init`
Currently, `uv init` creates the project structure but doesn't bootstrap the virtual environment until the first run/add command, or unless `uv venv` is run.

* **Proposal:** Have `uv init` optionally or automatically trigger the creation of the `.venv` in the background (or provide a `--venv` flag) so the project is instantly IDE-ready (e.g., for VS Code or PyCharm interpreter detection).

### Discussion: Community / Ecosystem Health (Alternative Packages)

As a secondary idea: many developers (especially beginners) install legacy packages (like `pygame`) without realizing there are modern, active community forks (like `pygame-ce`). 

While this is outside the scope of project initialization, `uv` could eventually offer a way to suggest modern alternatives during `uv add` or via a new command like `uv doctor` / `uv deps upgrade`. 

*Example:*
```bash
(python) ➜  python git:(development) ✗ uv add pygame
Warning: 'pygame' is legacy. Did you mean to install 'pygame-ce'? (y/n)
```

### Mentions of existing behavior / Prior Art
* **Cargo (Rust):** `cargo init` creates a runnable project immediately; `cargo run` executes the binary target without further configuration.
* **Poetry / Hatch:** Both offer layout configurations, with Hatch defaulting to `src/` in many templates.
