Title: Yanked wheel is retained in `uv.lock` even when a non-yanked wheel exists for the same version
Text:
Yanked wheel is retained in `uv.lock` even when a non-yanked wheel exists for the same version

### Summary

When a release has multiple wheels and only some of them are yanked (PEP 592 
per-file yanking, as opposed to yanking an entire release), `uv lock`/`uv sync` 
correctly avoid *selecting* the yanked wheel as the installed distribution, but 
the yanked wheel's URL and hash are still written into `uv.lock`'s `wheels` 
array for that package version. This happens regardless of which of the two 
wheels is the one marked yanked.

### Environment

- Index server: devpi, using the development releases that add per-file yank
  support:
  - `devpi-server==7.0.0b13`
    https://m.devpi.net/fschulze/dev/devpi-server/7.0.0b13
    (wheel: https://m.devpi.net/fschulze/dev/+f/a37/190b5b98e8f58/devpi_server-7.0.0b13-py3-none-any.whl)
  - `devpi-client==7.4.0.dev0`
    https://m.devpi.net/fschulze/dev/devpi-client/7.4.0.dev0
    (wheel: https://m.devpi.net/fschulze/dev/+f/62f/ee02e649fc647/devpi_client-7.4.0.dev0-py3-none-any.whl)
- Test registry: `http://127.0.0.1:8888/root/test`
- Package under test: `numpy==2.1.3`, two wheels for cp312/x86_64:
  - `numpy-2.1.3-0008fix-cp312-cp312-manylinux_2_27_x86_64.whl`
  - `numpy-2.1.3-cp312-cp312-manylinux_2_17_x86_64.manylinux2014_x86_64.whl`

### Repro

1. Using the devpi-server/devpi-client releases above (the first devpi versions
   to support yanking a single file within a release rather than the whole
   release), yank one wheel of `numpy==2.1.3` and leave the other unyanked.

2. Confirm via the index's simple API (both HTML and PEP 691 JSON) that exactly
   one of the two wheels carries `data-yanked` / `"yanked": "<reason>"`, e.g.:

```json
   {"filename": "numpy-2.1.3-cp312-cp312-manylinux_2_17_x86_64.manylinux2014_x86_64.whl",
    "yanked": "broken release", ...},
   {"filename": "numpy-2.1.3-0008fix-cp312-cp312-manylinux_2_27_x86_64.whl", ...}
```

3. `uv lock` (or `uv sync`) with `numpy>=2.1.3` as a dependency, pointed at that
   index.

4. Inspect `uv.lock`: **both** wheel entries appear under `[[package]] name = "numpy"`,
   including the yanked one, with its full URL and sha256 hash.

5. Reverse which wheel is yanked (unyank the manylinux_2_17 build, yank the
   0008fix build instead) and repeat. Result is symmetric: whichever wheel is
   yanked, it is still present in the regenerated lockfile.

### Why per-file yanking matters here, even though PyPI/Warehouse doesn't need it

PyPI conventionally yanks entire releases at once, so most tooling has only
ever had to reason about "is this whole version yanked." Private indexes that
build their own wheels hit a case Warehouse doesn't: a build for a given
version can fail or turn out broken for one platform tag, and the fix isn't a
new build number, it's a rebuild against a *different* manylinux tag (e.g. the
CI image gets bumped from `manylinux_2_17` to `manylinux_2_27`, or a build
picks up a newer/older glibc baseline). The wheel filename's build tag exists
to disambiguate multiple builds of the *same* platform tag; it has no way to
express "this replaces that other, differently-tagged wheel." Since the
version number can't be bumped either (nothing about the package's code
changed), yanking the specific broken file is the only mechanism available to
mark it unusable while leaving the version itself, and any lockfiles that
already pin to it via other still-good wheels, installable. Deleting the file
outright would break anyone who already resolved against that version; per-file
yanking is exactly the tool PEP 592 exists to provide for this. This is a new
capability in devpi as of `devpi-server` 7.0.0b13 / `devpi-client` 7.4.0.dev0
(linked above), so it's plausible no PEP 592 consumer has exercised this
specific partial-yank scenario against uv before.

### Root cause (as far as I can tell from the source)

- `crates/uv-resolver/src/version_map.rs` correctly computes per-file
  `WheelCompatibility::Incompatible(IncompatibleWheel::Yanked(...))` for a
  yanked file when a version is only partially yanked (comment there explicitly
  acknowledges this PEP 592 edge case).
- However, `PrioritizedDist::built_dist()` in
  `crates/uv-distribution-types/src/prioritized_distribution.rs` only strips
  wheels from the list it hands back (which ultimately becomes `uv.lock`'s
  `wheels` array) via `WheelCompatibility::is_excluded()`:

```rust
  fn is_excluded(&self) -> bool {
      matches!(self, Self::Incompatible(IncompatibleWheel::ExcludeNewer(_)))
  }
```

  This matches `ExcludeNewer` but not `Yanked`, so a yanked-but-not-selected
  wheel survives into the lockfile's wheel list even though it's correctly
  excluded from being the *installed* (`best_wheel_index`) wheel.

### Why this must be fixed at lock time, not install time

I traced this further and confirmed the fix genuinely has to happen when
`uv.lock` is written, there's no later point in the flow where a stale/yanked
entry could still be filtered out:

- The `Wheel` struct persisted into `uv.lock`
  (`crates/uv-resolver/src/lock/mod.rs`) has **no `yanked` field at all**. Once
  a wheel's URL/hash is written into the lock, all information about its yank
  status is gone.
- `uv sync --frozen` reads the lockfile and installs from it directly, with
  zero network calls for metadata (per `LockMode::Frozen` in
  `crates/uv/src/commands/project/lock.rs`, "*don't attempt to lock the
  project*"). It cannot re-check yank status even in principle.
- Plain `uv sync` only re-resolves if the lockfile looks stale relative to
  `pyproject.toml`'s constraints; a file being yanked after the fact isn't one
  of the triggers uv checks for; per uv's own docs, "*uv will not consider
  lockfiles outdated when new versions of packages are released*", the same
  applies here.
- Even `uv sync --locked`, which does force a fresh resolution to validate
  the lock, only errors if the *result differs*. Because of this bug, a fresh
  resolution against the same index state produ
Reply: Thanks for the report! I don't know if I'd consider this a bug, given the guarantees we provide about the contents of `uv.lock` (none, AFAIK). But I agree it could be better :)

Title: `exclude-newer` behavior with pull-through PyPI caches missing upload timestamps & locking build backends
Text:
`exclude-newer` behavior with pull-through PyPI caches missing upload timestamps & locking build backends

### Question

Hi team,

First of all, thank you for developing `uv`—the performance and tooling experience have been fantastic.

We would appreciate some guidance on best practices regarding `--exclude-newer` when operating with an in-cluster pull-through cache, as well as preventing build-backend resolution during frozen CI pipelines.

### Context & CI Design
- **Pull-Through Cache:** We run an in-cluster pull-through PyPI cache ([`proxpi`](https://github.com/epiclabs-io/proxpi)) inside our Kubernetes runner environment.
- **CI Philosophy:** **No dependency resolution should happen in CI.** 
  - We maintain a strictly version-controlled `uv.lock`.
  - All CI jobs run with `UV_FROZEN: "1"` and `UV_EXCLUDE_NEWER: "P2D"` so runners only download and install pinned artifacts directly from the internal cache without performing solver operations or querying upstream PyPI.
- **Project Structure:** Standard PEP 621 / PEP 517 project using `hatchling` as the build backend (`[build-system] requires = ["hatchling"]`).

### The Problem
While application dependencies are completely frozen by `uv.lock`, building the project wheel in CI triggers PEP 517 build isolation. This introduces an unexpected dynamic resolution step for `build-system.requires` (`hatchling`).

Because `proxpi` is a lightweight caching proxy, its simple index responses do not forward or store release upload timestamps. As a result, `uv` emits warnings for every candidate version and then fails:

```text
warning: hatchling-1.32.0.tar.gz is missing an upload date, but user provided: 2026-09-01T18:02:59.443957116Z
warning: hatchling-1.32.0-py3-none-any.whl is missing an upload date, but user provided: 2026-09-01T18:02:59.443957116Z
...
warning: hatchling-0.8.0-py2.py3-none-any.whl is missing an upload date, but user provided: 2026-09-01T18:02:59.443957116Z
  × Failed to build `myproject @ file:///workspace/...`
  ├─▶ Failed to resolve requirements from `build-system.requires`
  ├─▶ No solution found when resolving: `hatchling`
  ╰─▶ Because there are no versions of hatchling and you require hatchling, we
      can conclude that your requirements are unsatisfiable.
hint: `hatchling` was filtered by `exclude-newer` to only include packages uploaded before 2026-09-01T18:02:59.576541647Z.
```

### Why this happens
1. `proxpi` lacks upload timestamps, so `uv` assigns the fallback cutoff date (`2026-09-01T...`) to all `hatchling` versions.
2. Under `exclude-newer` (which excludes releases uploaded at or after the cutoff), every candidate version is filtered out, causing the build to fail.

### Questions / Guidance Requested
1. **Fully Locking Build Backends:** Since our goal is **zero resolution in CI**, is there a recommended way to lock `build-system.requires` (e.g. `hatchling`) in `uv.lock` alongside application dependencies so that building the wheel is completely deterministic and requires no index resolution?
2. **Handling Simple Caches under `exclude-newer`:** When using lightweight caching proxies like `proxpi` that lack timestamp metadata, is there a recommended way to allow `uv` to accept cached packages without completely disabling `exclude-newer` globally maybe by not doing any rolution at all?

Thank you for your time and guidance!

### Platform

arm64

### Version

uv 0.12.9
Reply:
As you've discovered, `UV_FROZEN` doesn't (yet) freeze isolated build requirements. That's tracked in #5190.

One option today is to put build dependencies into a dependency group, add them to the lockfile, then in CI sync them explicitly and disable build isolation. This ticks off the no-resolution-in-CI requirement.

If you're OK with just build dependency pinning, after https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/21411 lands (hopefully very soon, I'm actively working on it) you'll be able to put exact pins and hashes in `build-constraint-dependencies`, enable `require-build-hashes = true`, and carry on using normal isolated builds. No dependency group shenanigans, but resolution still runs for the build dependencies, applying for example `exclude-newer`.

For the exclude-newer bit, uv always rejects files with unknown upload times - the error message prints the cutoff date, it's not evidence of assigning the cutoff date to `hatchling` versions. The optimal solution (in my admittedly privileged opinion 😄) is to add upload timestamp support to `proxpi`, but you could work around this locally by disabling `exclude-newer` for the proxy index [like so](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/indexes/#configuring-exclude-newer-for-an-index).

Title: Windows: uv pip install --overrides fails when requirements file path contains spaces
Text:
Windows: uv pip install --overrides fails when requirements file path contains spaces

### Summary

When `uv pip install --overrides` is given a requirements file whose path contains a space, uv appears to split the path at the space, despite the path being passed as a single quoted argument.

I noticed this bug when attempting to upgrade Unsloth Studio using their PowerShell installer script. My user name has a space (`Damon Lynch`), which was causing the installer to fail. I used ChatGPT to help me isolate the issue.  The minimal reproduction below is from me.

### Minimal Reproduction

```
$dir ="D:\uv test"
uv venv $dir
$override = Join-Path $dir "override.txt"
Set-Content -LiteralPath $override -Value "idna==3.10"
uv pip install ` --python "D:\uv test\Scripts\python.exe" ` --overrides "$override" ` --dry-run ` requests
error: File not found: `D:\uv`
```

Perhaps of interest is that the `--python` path does not need to contain a space to reproduce the problem. For example, with a Python executable at a space-free path:
```
uv pip install ` --python "D:\UVTEST~1\Scripts\python.exe" ` --overrides "$override" ` --dry-run ` requests
error: File not found: `D:\uv`
```

For comparison, the same installation works when the override file is located at a path containing no spaces, e.g. dir `uv-test`:
```
$dir ="D:\uv-test"
uv venv $dir
$override = Join-Path $dir "override.txt"
Set-Content -LiteralPath $override -Value "idna==3.10"
uv pip install ` --python "D:\uv-test\Scripts\python.exe" ` --overrides "$override" ` --dry-run ` requests
```

It seems to me that uv should treat the value passed to `--overrides` as a single path, regardless of spaces in that path, and successfully read the requirements file.


### Platform

Windows 11 x64

### Version

uv 0.12.9 (9f9286029 2026-09-01 x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)

### Python version

Python 3.14.7

Title: Command to verify uv.lock is legitimate
Text:
Command to verify uv.lock is legitimate

### Summary

Currently, there seems to be no way to verify that a uv.lock has not maliciously been tampered with. It would be nice if this can be automatically checked, because manually verifying lock file changes is error-prone and likely often neglected (even the github UI hides uv.lock diffs per default).

I would like to have a command (part of `uv sync`, `uv lock` or `uv audit`) that checks if the dependencies in uv.lock match the definitions in pyproject.toml. I think this would require fetching the metadata again from PyPi.

This is to prevent against this scenario:
- some creates a malicious PR: pyproject.toml looks good (only pytest is updated); uv.lock has legitimate updates + a single wheel url has been changed to point to the attacker-controlled domain pythonhcsted instead of pythonhosted
- maintainer looks at the PR:
- - either only verifies the pyproject.toml diff. Easy and short to verify
- - or even expands the uv.lock diff and needs a lot of luck to find the difference between `pythonhcsted` and `pythonhosted` (`c` vs `o`)

It seems that the only safe way to handle PRs that add lines to uv.lock files is to close them, because I have no way to tell if there is a security issue hidden inside. I'd like that to be different, and also I guess many maintainers are not aware of this.

This issue is not unique to uv. For instance, here is an article describing malicious package-lock.json changes in npm: https://snyk.io/blog/why-npm-lockfiles-can-be-a-security-blindspot-for-injecting-malicious-modules/

### Example

I lack the knowledge how exactly things work in the background, but from a high level point of view I want something like this:

```bash
uv lock --verify
# check that there are no unexpected dependencies in `uv.lock` that are neither declared in pyproject.toml nor are they transitive dependencies
# verify that uv.lock versions are within the version ranges of pyproject.toml
# verify that sdist and wheel urls point to the urls described by the index in pyproject.toml
```

This could also be considered as a flag in setup-uv, so open source repositories are more likely to use this in their workflows before installing dependencies.
Reply: Would `uv lock --check --refresh --no-build` work for this?

Title: uv check overrides ty exclusions for automatically selected workspace members
Text:
uv check overrides ty exclusions for automatically selected workspace members

### Summary

`uv check` reports type errors inside a workspace member even when that member is under a directory excluded by `[tool.ty.src].exclude`.

In our repository, `vendor/sglang/python` was listed in `[tool.uv.workspace].members`, while `[tool.ty.src].exclude` contained `vendor`. Running plain `uv check` still checked the vendored code and produced a large number of diagnostics. Running `uv check --no-project` respected the exclusion and stopped reporting diagnostics from that directory.

### Expected behavior

When running `uv check` without explicitly selecting a package, I expect the configured ty exclusions to remain effective, including for workspace members. Workspace membership controls dependency and project organization; it does not necessarily mean every member should be type-checked.

### Possible cause / design question

It appears uv passes workspace member directories as explicit paths to ty. Since ty gives explicit paths precedence over exclusions by default, paths generated internally by uv can override the user's exclusion configuration.

Could `uv check` honor ty exclusions for these automatically selected paths, or provide a way to enforce them (equivalent to ty's `--force-exclude`)? If the current behavior is intentional, documenting this interaction would help.

Related: #20233 (workspace package selection), #19791 (custom ty configuration).

### Environment

- uv 0.12.10 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu)
- ty 0.0.79, selected by uv
- Python 3.12
- Virtual workspace with a vendored package declared as a member
Reply: Thanks for reporting the issue! While we address this, I think a good workaround is to list `vendor/**` in the ty exclusions

Title: `uv sync` validates a `build-system.requires` wheel against the wrong platform's hash from `uv.lock`
Text:
`uv sync` validates a `build-system.requires` wheel against the wrong platform's hash from `uv.lock`

### Summary

When `uv sync --no-install-project` resolves `[build-system].requires` for an editable dependency, and that resolution needs a platform-specific wheel for a package that also appears in the project's own `uv.lock`, `uv` validates the downloaded wheel against the hash recorded in `uv.lock` for the other platform's wheel of the same package/version.
This fails with a **"Hash mismatch"** error, but there is no actual corruption: both the **"Expected"** and **"Computed"** hashes are genuinely correct but just belong to two different wheels of the same package/version.

This seems to be a regression in `uv 0.12.11`, which is still present in the latest version (i.e. `uv 0.12.13` as of the moment I am posting it).
Older versions like `0.12.10` work fine.

I am attaching a `.zip` file with slimmed-down version of the larger original project where I faced the issue.
It basically contains two packages, `main` and `my-dep`.  
The package `my-dep` requires `torch==2.13.0` in the `build-system`, while the package `main` depends on:
- `my-dep` installed as editable
- `torch==2.13.0`, for which two indices are configured so it resolved to the CPU-only package on `aarch64` platforms and to the CUDA package everywhere else.  
Everything is wrapped in a `Dockerfile` to make it easier to run/reproduce.
It runs fine in `linux/amd64` but in `linux/arm64` it fails.

[minimal-repro.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32107368/minimal-repro.zip)

To reproduce it, please run:
```sh
# this one works
docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64 .

# this one does NOT work
docker buildx build --platform linux/arm64 .
```

There is another `Dockerfile` using `uv 0.12.10` which works fine as mentioned above:
```sh
# works fine

# works fine

```

Title: Include license information in cyclonedx export
Text:
Include license information in cyclonedx export

### Summary

In my experience, I've typically needed to include license information for each component in an SBOM. This functionality currently does not exist in `uv export --format cyclonedx-1.5`. It appears that an optional license field already exists in the component struct used to generate the SBOM but it is always set to None.

I'm not too familiar with how the export receives package information but my quick skim didn't show any easily accessible means of obtaining the license from a given Package. The only struct I could find that contains such information is `Metadata23` and it wasn't clear to me how that could be made available to the export.

I'm also not sure how easy it is to acquire this information without having the package downloaded. Pypi exposes this through their API but I don't know if that sort of API is available through any index or just pypi. And direct url dependencies wouldn't provide such an API either, potentially forcing a wheel download just to obtain the necessary metadata. Still, that seems preferable to having to fully sync the project as would be required by a tool like cyclonedx-bom.

### Example

_No response_
Reply:
> I'm also not sure how easy it is to acquire this information without having the package downloaded. Pypi exposes this through their API but I don't know if that sort of API is available through any index or just pypi.

License metadata isn't part of the standard index API, so uv can't assume that it's present for arbitrary (non-PyPI) indices. The closest standard equivalent would be PEP 658 for sidecar metadata, but this is optional and not widely adopted by third-party indices.

(And unfortunately, even with detached metadata, projects are required to use Metadata 2.4 or higher to have the modern parseable license fields (`License-File` and `License-Expression`).)

TL;DR: this is sort of gummed up in various places, and would not be easy to expose directly in uv. We could _potentially_ expose it in a subset of cases (i.e. where we have local metadata, it's at least 2.4, and has well-formed license fields), but this would not generalize very cleanly, especially across third-party registries.

Title: A pure-Rust allocator for uv-performance-memory-allocator
Text:
A pure-Rust allocator for uv-performance-memory-allocator

### The value of integrating

`crates/uv-performance-memory-allocator` says its own purpose plainly: pull in mimalloc on Windows and tikv-jemallocator on most other platforms. So uv already treats the allocator as a performance decision worth a dedicated crate, and already carries two C allocators to make it — each needing a C toolchain on the platforms it covers.

rusty_alloc is not a different design being offered as an alternative: it is the mimalloc v2.4.5 algorithm rebuilt in safe Rust, implementing about 150 of mimalloc's roughly 157 `mi_*` entry points, with the C original kept in-tree purely as a differential oracle. So on the Windows arm this is the same algorithm, and it would let one entry replace both arms rather than adding a third.

That matters for what uv does. Resolution builds and discards a large graph of candidate versions, and installation unpacks and writes thousands of small files, with `rayon = "1.10.0"` spreading both across a pool — so allocations are routinely freed on a worker that did not make them. On exactly that path the rusty_alloc README measures **0.83x mimalloc's instructions** (`xthread` — every free performed by a non-owning thread). It has 9,261 downloads on crates.io and no build script.

Not asking you to change the default — this would sit behind an off-by-default feature in that same crate.

### How to integrate

```toml
[features]
rusty-alloc = ["dep:rusty_alloc-api"]   # opt in; the mimalloc/jemalloc arms stay as they are

[dependencies]
rusty_alloc-api = { version = "2.1", optional = true }
```

```rust
#[cfg(feature = "rusty-alloc")]
#[global_allocator]
static GLOBAL: rusty_alloc_api::RustyAlloc = rusty_alloc_api::RustyAlloc;
```

Nothing else changes: same resolver, same lockfile, same CLI. Because it is pure Rust it needs no per-platform toolchain, so one arm could eventually cover Windows, macOS and Linux alike — which is the part worth measuring even if the ratios come out level.

### Remade With Rust & MATA

We are rebuilding the C libraries Rust projects still depend on, in safe Rust — allocators, codecs, compression, parsers, identity and storage — so a build can drop its C pieces without losing performance. The org is at https://github.com/Remade-With-Rust. If this is not for you, please close the issue.

Title: ZIP extraction rejects DEFLATE-compressed empty directory with data descriptor
Text:
ZIP extraction rejects DEFLATE-compressed empty directory with data descriptor

# ZIP extraction rejects DEFLATE-compressed empty directory with data descriptor

uv 0.12.13 (0ebbd9274, macOS arm64) rejects a valid empty directory whose DEFLATE payload is two bytes and whose compressed size is recorded in a data descriptor.

## Actual result

```
Bad compressed size (got 00000000, expected 00000002) for file: META-INF
```

## Reproduction

Run the accompanying `reproduce.py` with Python 3 and uv installed. It creates two synthetic packages, serves them on loopback, and installs them into temporary targets with uv 0.12.13 and `--no-cache`. No proprietary code, credentials, or third-party SDK source is included.

Both archives have an empty `META-INF/` directory compressed with DEFLATE (compressed size 2, uncompressed size 0). Python `ZipFile.testzip()` passes for both. The streaming-written archive uses data descriptors and fails; the seekable-written archive has the same contents without descriptors and installs successfully. The script asserts both outcomes and cleans up its temporary artifacts.

The official archive also reproduces this:

```
uv pip install --no-cache --target /tmp/ibapi-repro 'ibapi @ https://interactivebrokers.github.io/downloads/twsapi_macunix.1050.01.zip#subdirectory=IBJts/source/pythonclient'
```

Observed archive SHA-256: `aa065722ca732a41aab202c7bb72932e179b86e7ec51cefa063eb1983fe9f597` (11,413,089 bytes).

## Source diagnosis

At uv main commit `c0df400a4cf4aad88f7f34bb2ac3ebb5a8f3839e`, `crates/uv-extract/src/stream.rs` lines 225–259 handle directory entries and set `ComputedEntry.compressed_size` to zero. Lines 434–443 compare that value with the data descriptor's compressed size. An empty DEFLATE stream has nonzero compressed length, so this comparison rejects the valid archive.

Suggested correction: consume the directory entry through the checked reader, measure actual compressed and uncompressed lengths, and validate the measured values against header/descriptor/central-directory facts. Preserve CRC checks, empty-directory enforcement, and malformed-descriptor rejection. Merely copying the descriptor's length into the computed value or disabling validation would mask corruption.

## Acceptance criteria

- The synthetic descriptor case and its no-descriptor control both install successfully.
- Nonempty directory payloads, invalid CRCs, inconsistent sizes, and malformed descriptors remain rejected.
- The unchanged official archive installs directly with validation enabled.
- A release containing the regression fix passes direct URL lock and clean locked installation before downstream vendoring is removed.

This report includes a tested reproduction and source diagnosis, not a compiled or validated Rust patch.

## Self-contained reproduction script

```python
"""Isolated uv regression: compressed empty directory with data descriptor."""
import functools
import http.server
import io
import json
import subprocess
import tempfile
import threading
import zipfile
from pathlib import Path


class StreamingBuffer(io.BytesIO):
    def seekable(self):
        return False

    def seek(self, *args):
        raise io.UnsupportedOperation("streaming output")


with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix="uv-directory-repro-") as root:
    root = Path(root)
    for name in ("descriptor", "no_descriptor"):
        buffer = StreamingBuffer() if name == "descriptor" else io.BytesIO()
        with zipfile.ZipFile(buffer, "w", compression=zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED) as archive:
            archive.writestr("META-INF/", b"")
            archive.writestr("pyproject.toml", '[build-system]\nrequires=["setuptools"]\nbuild-backend="setuptools.build_meta"\n[project]\nname="uv-directory-repro"\nversion="0.0.1"\n')
            archive.writestr("repro.py", "VALUE = 1\n")
        (root / f"{name}.zip").write_bytes(buffer.getvalue())
        with zipfile.ZipFile(io.BytesIO(buffer.getvalue())) as archive:
            assert archive.testzip() is None
            entry = archive.getinfo("META-INF/")
            print(json.dumps({"archive": name, "compressed_size": entry.compress_size, "uncompressed_size": entry.file_size, "data_descriptor": bool(entry.flag_bits & 8)}), flush=True)
    handler = functools.partial(http.server.SimpleHTTPRequestHandler, directory=str(root))
    server = http.server.ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), handler)
    threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()
    try:
        for name in ("descriptor", "no_descriptor"):
            result = subprocess.run(["uv", "tool", "run", "--from", "uv==0.12.13", "uv", "pip", "install", "--no-cache", "--target", str(root / name), f"http://127.0.0.1:{server.server_port}/{name}.zip"], text=True, capture_output=True, timeout=120)
            print(json.dumps({"archive": name, "returncode": result.returncode, "stderr": result.stderr}), flush=True)
            assert (result.returncode != 0) == (name == "descriptor"), result.stderr
    finally:
        server.shutdown()

Title: Best way to handle architecture dependent environments
Text:
Best way to handle architecture dependent environments

### Question

Hi,

I have a project dependent on libraries like torch and jax which needs to install different packages based on the accelerator they use. While this is not a problem in development, when I submit a job to a hybrid GPU cluster, the environment needs to have the correct package based on which hardware the code is running on (e.g. torch-cuda or torch-rocm). Therefore, I prepared the following `pyproject.toml` file and defined the `rocm` and `cuda` packages to be mutually exclusive:

```
[project]
name = "new-project"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "desc"
requires-python = ">=3.14"
dependencies = [
    "jaxtyping>=0.2",
    "scipy>=1.14",
    "numpy>=2.1",
    "jaxlib",
]

# hardware targets as extras
[project.optional-dependencies]
rocm = [
    "torch>=2.13.0,<2.14",
    "torchvision",
    "triton-rocm",
    "jax[rocm7-local]",
]
cuda = [
    "torch>=2.13.0,<2.14",
    "torchvision",
    "triton",
    "jax[cuda13]>=0.4",
]

# rocm and cuda are mutually exclusive
[tool.uv]
conflicts = [
    [
        { extra = "rocm" },
        { extra = "cuda" },
    ],
]

[[tool.uv.index]]
name = "pytorch-cuda"
url = "https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu132"
explicit = true

[[tool.uv.index]]
name = "pytorch-rocm"
url = "https://download.pytorch.org/whl/rocm7.2"
explicit = true

[tool.uv.sources]
torch = [
  { index = "pytorch-cuda", extra = "cuda" },
  { index = "pytorch-rocm", extra = "rocm" },
]
torchvision = [
  { index = "pytorch-cuda", extra = "cuda" },
  { index = "pytorch-rocm", extra = "rocm" },
]
triton-rocm = { index = "pytorch-rocm", extra = "rocm" }
```

And when submitting an sbatch file to the cluster I use:
```
if lspci | grep -qi "NVIDIA"; then module load CUDA; else module load rocm; fi
if nvidia-smi > /dev/null 2>&1; then
  uv sync --extra cuda
elif rocminfo > /dev/null 2>&1; then
  uv sync --extra rocm
else
  uv sync
fi

srun ...
```
so that the architecture the code is running on is detected and proper packages are installed before the run. However, this causes problems when I submit multiple jobs to the queue and some of them go to AMD GPUs and some go to NVIDIA GPUs as the `uv sync` command changes the files inside `.venv`.

So, I would like to know if there is a way to use multiple `.venv` environments in one project or having a virtual environment where some packages point to different files based on hardware the code is running on?

Kind regards,
Abdullah

### Platform

Linux 5.14.0-611.34.1.el9_7.x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux

### Version

uv 0.12.12 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu)
Reply:
How is the code shared between the different hardware environments?

If, for example, the home directory of the user running `uv sync` is unique per environment, while the project code is shared via some kind of file store, then the [`centralized-project-envs` preview feature](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/projects/layout/#centralized-project-environments) may help here.

Title: 0.12.14: `uv pip install --system` fails in official `python:*` Docker images — "Cannot install into symlinked directory: /usr/local/man"
Text:
0.12.14: `uv pip install --system` fails in official `python:*` Docker images — "Cannot install into symlinked directory: /usr/local/man"

## Summary

Since 0.12.14, installing any wheel that ships man pages in its `.data/data/` tree fails inside the official `python:*` Docker images, because `/usr/local/man` is a symlink to `share/man` in those images. 0.12.13 and earlier install fine.

The behaviour comes from #21569 ("Reject symlinked wheel installation destinations", labelled `internal`), which is not mentioned in the 0.12.14 changelog, so the failure appears out of nowhere for anyone tracking `ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:latest`.

## Reproduction

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.11-slim-bookworm
COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.12.14 /uv /bin/uv
RUN uv pip install --system clevercsv==0.8.4
```

```
error: Failed to install: clevercsv-0.8.4-cp311-cp311-manylinux2014_aarch64.manylinux_2_17_aarch64.manylinux_2_28_aarch64.whl (clevercsv==0.8.4)
  cause: The wheel is invalid: Cannot install into symlinked directory: /usr/local/man
```

Same Dockerfile with `uv:0.12.13`, `0.12.10`, `0.12.0`, `0.11.0`: succeeds.

Fails identically with `uv:0.12.14` on `python:3.11-bookworm` (non-slim), `python:3.13-bookworm`, `python:3.12-slim-bullseye` and `python:3.12-slim-trixie`.

```
$ docker run --rm python:3.11-slim-bookworm ls -l /usr/local/man
lrwxrwxrwx 1 root root 9 Aug 24 00:00 /usr/local/man -> share/man
```

The symlink is present in every official Debian-based `python` image variant, so this affects any `uv pip install --system` of a wheel that ships man pages (e.g. `clevercsv`).

The check in `crates/uv-install-wheel/src/wheel.rs` rejects any symlink found while walking the `.data/` destination tree, without considering whether the link target stays inside the same prefix.

## Expected

Either install the data files through the symlink when it resolves to a location inside the same prefix (`/usr/local/share/man` is still under `/usr/local`), or emit a warning and skip the man pages. Failing the whole install with "The wheel is invalid" is misleading: the wheel is fine, the destination layout is the distro's default.

At minimum, the change should be listed in the changelog as a breaking change with the workaround.

## Workaround

```dockerfile
RUN rm -f /usr/local/man && mkdir -p /usr/local/man
```

before the install step, or pin `ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.12.13`.

Possibly related: #21255 (console scripts failing when the venv contains a `lib -> usr/lib` symlink).

## Environment

- uv 0.12.14 (aarch64-unknown-linux-musl), from `ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.12.14`
- `python:3.11-slim-bookworm` (Python 3.11.16), Docker on macOS/arm64
- Command: `uv pip install --system clevercsv==0.8.4` (also reproduces with a project `uv pip install --system .` that depends on clevercsv)


### Platform

debian bookworm (docker conatainer) Linux 7.0.12-linuxkit aarch64 GNU/Linux

### Version

uv0.12.14

### Python version

Python 3.11
Reply: Sorry for the regression, this has been fixed in 0.12.15.

Title: `uv check` and `ty check` report different errors
Text:
`uv check` and `ty check` report different errors

### Summary

It appears to be related to `uv check` using the version of python in `.venv` and ignoring the `requires-python` field in the pyproject.toml whereas ty does?

As a minimal example, with `pyproject.toml`

```toml
[project]
name = "demo"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
```

and `demo.py` in the same directory (I know the code itself is questionable - it's minified from a bigger project)

```python
from types import UnionType
from typing import Union, get_origin, get_args, Any

def convert_type(typ: Any) -> type:
    root = get_origin(typ)
    args = get_args(typ)
    if args:
        new = tuple(convert_type(i) for i in args)
        if root == UnionType:
            root = Union
        return root[new] if root else typ
    return typ
```

Running `ty check` (and `uv run ty check`) gives `All checks passed`, whereas `uv check` gives 

```
error[not-subscriptable]: Cannot subscript object of type `<special-form 'typing.Union'>` with no `__class_getitem__` method
  --> demo.py:12:16
   |
12 |         return root[new] if root else typ
   |                ^^^^^^^^^

Found 1 diagnostic
```

If I change the version of python in the `pyproject.toml` to `3.14`, `ty check` starts reporting the error or if I use `uv check --python 3.12`, uv stops reporting it.

Passing `--ty-version` to `uv check` with the same version as ty, doesn't make a difference.

uv version 0.12.15
ty version 0.0.81

### Platform

Arch - Linux 6.18.51-1-lts x86_64 GNU/Linux

### Version

uv 0.12.15 (d35f1f270 2026-09-15 x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu)

### Python version

3.14.0
Reply:
Thanks for the report! This is intentional behavior, but something we've been debating internally quite a bit, so your feedback is very much appreciated.

Currently `uv check` will prefer the existing environment's python version and pass this preference over to ty. This is consistent with other uv commands like `uv run` (which will also use the existing env), but as you point out, it's inconsistent with `ty check` unfortunately.

I'd argue uv's behavior is more technically correct, especially in cases when you have dependencies that are gated by python version (e.g. `foo ; python_version == '3.12'` and `bar ; python_version > '3.12'`). At the same time, the type checker's responsibility is to ensure you're not using Python (typing) features that don't work with your declared `requires-python` versions, which is what informs ty's behavior. Arguably that's a more important safety net.

Even if we address this python-version-preference discrepancy, there are several others, for example:
- `uv check` by default will check multiple workspace members in some cases, while `ty check` will only check the current project
- `uv check` excludes PEP 723 scripts, unless explicitly requested; ty includes them (but doesn't prepare their environments)

So just fixing the python version issue will not make `uv check` be a drop-in replacement for `ty check` (and that's okay, just pointing it out).

Title: Intermittent SIGABRT on aarch64 (GCP Axion / AWS Graviton) during package downloads - AWS-LC RNDR no-retry
Text:
Intermittent SIGABRT on aarch64 (GCP Axion / AWS Graviton) during package downloads - AWS-LC RNDR no-retry

### Summary

# Summary

On aarch64 Linux, uv 0.11.8 occasionally dies with SIGABRT (exit 134), silently, during any cold-cache operation that downloads from the index (uv run/uv sync/uv pip install).

Warm cache never triggers it.

Output is just the usual progress lines, then a core dump — no error.

# Backtrace (rebuilt with debug info; shipped binaries are stripped):
```
abort() ← AWS-LC rand_bytes_core (rand.c) ← RAND_bytes ← aws_lc_rs::rand::fill
        ← rustls SessionId::random ← rustls ClientConnection::new ← tokio-rustls/reqwest connect
```

# Root cause

uv downloads over HTTPS.  rustls (default provider aws-lc-rs) calls RAND_bytes per handshake.

On aarch64 FEAT_RNG CPUs, AWS-LC uses the RNDR instruction with no retry (rndr-armv8.pl); a single transient RNDR failure aborts the process.

# Upstream

aws/aws-lc#3453 (also aws/aws-lc-rs).

# Environment

GCP Axion (n4a, Neoverse-N3), aarch64, Ubuntu 24.04; ~3–4% of downloads, clustered on some physical hosts; both the musl-static and glibc uv builds affected; also expected
on Graviton3/4.

# Workaround (no rebuild)

OPENSSL_armcap=~0x20000 in uv's environment → AWS-LC skips RNDR → 0 aborts across 380 builds (vs ~4–5%), AES/SHA acceleration retained.

# Ask

It's ultimately an AWS-LC bug, but uv is where it surfaces as a hard crash for arm64 cloud users. Could uv document the workaround, track the AWS-LC fix, and/or consider preferring
OS getrandom over RNDR on aarch64 (or a config knob)?

### Platform

Ubuntu 24.04 on GCP, n4a

### Version

0.11.8

### Python version

3.14.4
Reply:
I think you copy pasted the summary straight from an LLM, please don't do that.

As for resolving this, there's a workaround, it doesn't seem to have security impact, and there's a fixed version. We will just look into bumping this. It will happen eventually through renovate but we might do it early.

The things you suggest as resolutions are rather extreme/weird but I'll chalk it up to the LLM...

Title: uv upgrade cannot authenticate while uv sync --upgrade does
Text:
uv upgrade cannot authenticate while uv sync --upgrade does

### Summary

## Summary

`uv upgrade` cannot authenticate against a private index, while `uv sync --upgrade` and `uv lock --upgrade` can, given identical configuration and credentials. `uv upgrade` accepts none of the index or authentication options that the other resolving commands accept, and credentials supplied via `UV_EXTRA_INDEX_URL` appear not to be honoured.

## Reproduction

`pyproject.toml`, with a private index declared as explicit and a package pinned to it:

```toml
[project]
name = "repro"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.14"
dependencies = ["my-private-pkg"]

```

Then:

```bash
uv sync --upgrade   # succeeds, resolves and installs my-private-pkg
uv upgrade          # fails
```

Both commands re-resolve the project's dependencies, so both should authenticate against the private index the same way.

## Actual

`uv upgrade` fails to query the index and then reports the pinned package as absent:

Text:
UV_SYSTEM_CERTS=false can still fall through to UV_NATIVE_TLS=true without warning

#21788 suppresses the `UV_NATIVE_TLS` deprecation warning whenever `UV_SYSTEM_CERTS` is present, but effective-value resolution only consumes `Some(true)` for `UV_SYSTEM_CERTS` before falling through to `UV_NATIVE_TLS`.

That leaves this case:

```sh
UV_SYSTEM_CERTS=false UV_NATIVE_TLS=true uv ...
```

The warning is suppressed because `UV_SYSTEM_CERTS` is present, but deprecated `UV_NATIVE_TLS=true` still makes the effective `system_certs` value true.

This also differs from the intended behavior described on #21788: if `UV_SYSTEM_CERTS` is set, `UV_NATIVE_TLS` should be ignored entirely.

Expected: explicit `UV_SYSTEM_CERTS=false` wins and the deprecated variable is ignored. If the deprecated variable is still allowed to control the result, the warning should not be suppressed.

Title: Install order is non-deterministic when two distributions claim the same path
Text:
Install order is non-deterministic when two distributions claim the same path

When two wheels install the same path with different content, which one wins varies between runs, so the resulting environment is not byte-reproducible.

### Repro

```console
uv venv v
uv pip install --python v databricks-sdk==0.133.0 databricks-sql-connector==4.5.0 databricks-sqlalchemy==2.0.10
wc -c v/lib/python*/site-packages/databricks/__init__.py
```

All three ship `databricks/__init__.py` — the first two a 537-byte namespace declaration, the third an empty file. Repeat the install and the size flips between 537 and 0. In a 219-package environment I measured it flipping on roughly 1 build in 4, which changed the digest of an OCI layer built from the venv.

### Cause

Reading 0.12.15 (d35f1f2):

- `crates/uv-installer/src/preparer.rs:83,100` — the install list is collected through a `FuturesUnordered` and `try_collect`, so the `Vec<CachedDist>` is in download/unzip completion order.
- `crates/uv-installer/src/preparer.rs:96` — `sort_unstable_by_key` on size leaves equal and unknown sizes (`u64::MAX`) in arbitrary relative order.
- `crates/uv-installer/src/installer.rs:172` — that `Vec` is then installed with `par_iter`, and `install_wheel` writes files with no arbitration for a shared path.

`UV_CONCURRENT_INSTALLS=1` does not help: it sets the rayon thread count (`crates/uv/src/lib.rs:567` → `crates/uv-configuration/src/threading.rs:67`) but does not reorder the list, so one thread still walks a completion-ordered `Vec`.

### Suggestion

Make the install order deterministic — return prepared wheels in input order, or sort `wheels` before `par_iter`. That would not pick a "correct" winner for a genuine collision, but it would make the outcome stable across runs.

`InstallState::warn_package_conflicts` (`crates/uv-install-wheel/src/linker.rs:106`) already detects this shape, but it is behind the `DetectModuleConflicts` preview flag and compares file length rather than content.
Reply: This is a duplicate of https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/6568

Title: granular and user-friendly management of cached packages
Text:
granular and user-friendly management of cached packages

Using a symlink cache is the only way to prevent wastage of disk space for a machine with multiple projects.

Different projects may have different dependencies and when some are upgraded, the previous version is left behind unused in the cache. This is wasteful for disk space.

The current operations allowed for cache handling are mostly related to full-blown purge which would require a re-download of previously downloaded packages. These network transfers are wasteful.

It would be useful to have specific commands that allow the following:
- they list what packages+versions are in the cache
- allow purging individual package+version combinations
- less importantly: a way to exhamine how much disk space is being used by every cached package+version combination

thank you and keep up with the great work.
Reply:
Thanks for the feedback! A couple notes...

> Using a symlink cache is the only way to prevent wastage of disk space for a machine with multiple projects.

This is not true, we use reflinks and hardlinks by default.

> The current operations allowed for cache handling are mostly related to full-blown purge

We have `uv cache prune` for this purpose

Title: Provide a way to add/remove additional requirements after installation of tools
Text:
Provide a way to add/remove additional requirements after installation of tools

### Summary

#### Summary
Provide a straightforward way to modify (add, remove, or update) additional dependencies (`--with`) associated with an already installed tool without requiring users to manually reconstruct the original installation command.

---

#### Problem Statement
Currently, `uv tool install <package> --with <dep>` allows users to inject extra dependencies at install time, and `uv tool list --show-with` allows inspecting them. 

However, once a tool is installed, there is no direct, low-friction path to alter its set of extra dependencies. The current workaround requires reinstalling the main tool while manually reproducing all original options alongside the revised `--with` arguments. Even with `uv tool list --show-xxx`, reconstructing the exact original installation invocation is manual and error-prone.

---

#### Use Case: Plugin Management
A widespread pattern in the Python ecosystem involves CLI applications that rely on modular, third-party plugin packages (for example, `ocrmypdf`, `pytest`, or `flake8`). 

In these ecosystems:
1. **Plugins must reside in the same environment** as the primary executable to be discovered at runtime.
2. **Plugins are installed incrementally:** Users frequently discover, install, update, or remove plugins long after the core tool was first installed.
3. **Plugins vary in source:** They may come from PyPI, VCS repositories, or local `.whl` files.

Because plugins are developed independently, users need an easy way to treat an installed `uv tool` environment as a target for adding or removing auxiliary packages over time.

---

#### Additional Context
* **Real-world example:** `ocrmypdf` heavily relies on separate plugin packages installed into the same environment.
* Supporting post-install dependency management will make `uv tool` a much more versatile replacement for isolated CLI tools with rich plugin ecosystems.

### Example

#### Proposed Solutions / UX Suggestions

Introduce explicit management commands targeting an installed tool's environment:

```bash
# Add or update one or more dependencies/plugins to an existing tool environment
uv tool alter <tool> --add-with <package>
# or possibly, to update only if already existing,
uv tool alter <tool> --update-with <package>

# Remove a dependency/plugin from an existing tool environment
uv tool alter <tool> --remove-with <package>
```

Title: `install.sh` unresolved `$XDG_DATA_HOME/../bin` causes false "shadowed by other commands" warning and unnecessary rc-file edits
Text:
`install.sh` unresolved `$XDG_DATA_HOME/../bin` causes false "shadowed by other commands" warning and unnecessary rc-file edits

### Summary

When `XDG_DATA_HOME` is set, `install.sh` derives its install directory as the literal string `$XDG_DATA_HOME/../bin` and never resolves it. Because two later checks compare that string against a resolved path, they result in:

1. Spurious `WARN: The following commands are shadowed by other commands in your PATH: uv uvx` on every install, when nothing is shadowed.
2. The `PATH`-modification step concludes the install dir isn't on `PATH` when it is, and appends source lines to six shell config files that didn't need them.

The second one is self-reinforcing: the line it adds prepends the unnormalized path to `PATH`, which guarantees the warning fires on every subsequent run, including runs with an explicit `UV_INSTALL_DIR`.

## Environment

- `uv 0.12.17 (635500036 2026-09-18 aarch64-apple-darwin)`
- macOS 27.0 (build 26A428, Darwin 27.0.0, arm64)
- `XDG_DATA_HOME=$HOME/.local/share`
- `$HOME/.local/bin` already on `PATH`, added by my own shell config
- `zsh`, with `ZDOTDIR=$HOME/.config/zsh`
- No other uv on the system (no Homebrew formula, no cargo install, one binary total)

## Reproduction

```zsh
$ export XDG_DATA_HOME="$HOME/.local/share"
$ export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
$ curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

downloading uv 0.12.17 aarch64-apple-darwin
installing to /Users/me/.local/share/../bin
  uv
  uvx
everything's installed!
WARN: The following commands are shadowed by other commands in your PATH: uv uvx
```

`which -a uv` returns exactly one path. Nothing is shadowed.

The install also appended `. "$HOME/.local/share/../bin/env"` to `~/.profile`, `~/.bashrc`, `~/.bash_profile`, `~/.bash_login`, `~/.zshrc/`. `~/.zshenv`, and created `~/.config/fish/conf.d/uv.env.fish` and `~/.config/fish/`  on a machine with no fish installed.

I would have expected no warning, and no shell config modified, since there was no `uv` binary installed on the device and `$HOME/.local/bin` is already on `PATH`.

## Cause

`install.sh:1298` sets the install dir without resolving the path:

```shell
_install_dir="$XDG_DATA_HOME/../bin"
```

`check_for_shadowed_bins (install.sh:1434)` then compares a resolved path against that raw string.

```shell
_shadow="$(command -v "$_bin_name")"        # /Users/me/.local/bin/uv
if [ -n "$_shadow" ] && [ "$_shadow" != "$_install_dir/$_bin_name" ]; then
    # /Users/me/.local/share/../bin/uv  →  never equal
```

The same string is used for the already-on-`PATH` check at `install.sh:1401`.

```shell
case :$PATH: in *:$_install_dir:*) NO_MODIFY_PATH=1 ;;
```

`PATH` contains `/Users/me/.local/bin`, not `/Users/me/.local/share/../bin`, so this never matches and `shotgun_install_dir_to_path` (`install.sh:1409`) runs against `.profile` `.bashrc` `.bash_profile` `.bash_login`

Reinstalling with `UV_INSTALL_DIR="$HOME/.local/bin"`, even after rm -rfing the binaries still warns, because the rc line added by the first run is now prepending `$HOME/.local/share/../bin` to PATH in every shell. `command -v uv` resolves through the unnormalized entry and the comparison fails again. The only fix is manually removing the line the installer added, which is non-trivial to track down.

## Suggested fix

Normalize once, at the point the default is chosen with something like

```shell
_install_dir="$(cd "$XDG_DATA_HOME/.." 2>/dev/null && pwd)/bin"
```

This would make the shadowing check and the $PATH$ check agree, and the `NO_MODIFY_PATH=1` branch at line 1401 then correctly suppresses all six rc edits on systems where the directory is already on `PATH`.

### Separately, and lower priority

creating `~/.config/fish/` on a machine with no fish binary seems worth gating on `command -v fish`, and writing to `.bashrc`, `.bash_profile`, and `.bash_login` unconditionally is more invasive in my opinion than the situation calls for. I'd personally rather be told which line to add than have it added for me. That said, the path resolution bug is the actionable part here, and fixing it means the rc files mostly stop being touched at all.

### Platform

macOS 27.0 (build 26A428, Darwin 27.0.0, arm64)

### Version

uv 0.12.17 (635500036 2026-09-18 aarch64-apple-darwin)

### Python version

Python 3.14.7

Title: test fixture test/packages/fake-uv/src is a committed symlink that breaks on an unprivileged Windows checkout
Text:
test fixture test/packages/fake-uv/src is a committed symlink that breaks on an unprivileged Windows checkout

## Summary

`test/packages/fake-uv/src` is committed as a symlink (git mode `120000`) pointing to `../../../python/`. It is the only symlink in the repository.

On Windows, a user without elevation or Developer Mode has `core.symlinks=false`, so `git checkout` writes that entry out as a **regular text file containing the target path** (`../../../python/`) rather than as a link.

The `fake-uv` package is then malformed: its `src` is a one-line text file instead of a source tree. `crates/uv/tests/python/python_module.rs` installs `fake-uv` as `uv==0.1.0` in roughly 14 cases, so those tests fail locally for such a contributor.

## Why CI does not catch it

The workflows under `.github/workflows/` run Windows heavily (`ci.yml`, `build-release-binaries.yml`, and others), but GitHub's Windows runners can create symlinks, so the fixture materialises correctly there.

The breakage is therefore invisible in CI and shows up only in an unprivileged Windows contributor's local checkout — where it is usually read as a misconfigured machine rather than a repository issue, and never reported.

## Reproduce

On Windows, non-elevated, Developer Mode off (`git config core.symlinks` returns `false`):

```
git clone https://github.com/astral-sh/uv
type test\packages\fake-uv\src
```

Prints `../../../python/` — a text file, not a directory.

## Possible fixes

Listing options rather than assuming one; the fix is a fixture or Rust change and the approach is yours to pick.

- Materialise the fixture link at test setup instead of committing it: create the symlink in Rust, and skip or fall back to a copy if creation fails on Windows.
- Replace the committed symlink with the real files, or generate it in a small build step.
- At minimum, document the requirement (Developer Mode, or `git config --global core.symlinks true`) in `CONTRIBUTING.md`, so contributors are not left guessing.

Happy to put up a PR for whichever direction you prefer.

## Environment

```
Windows 11 (10.0.26200), non-elevated, Developer Mode off, git core.symlinks=false
uv at HEAD (test/packages/fake-uv/src confirmed still mode 120000, target ../../../python/)
```

Title: uv version modifies pyproject.toml on disk even when lock_and_sync fails (e.g., under --locked)
Text:
uv version modifies pyproject.toml on disk even when lock_and_sync fails (e.g., under --locked)

### Summary

When updating or bumping a version with `uv version` (e.g., `uv version --bump minor --locked`, or in CI environments where `UV_LOCKED=1` is set), `pyproject.toml` is written to disk before `lock_and_sync` executes.

If `lock_and_sync` fails—such as when `--locked` detects that `uv.lock` needs an update—the command aborts with an error, but `pyproject.toml` remains modified on disk.

This violates the expectation that `--locked` leaves project state untouched when lock validation fails, and leaves `pyproject.toml` desynchronized from `uv.lock`.

### Steps to Reproduce

```bash
# 1. Create a clean project with a lockfile
mkdir uv-version-repro && cd uv-version-repro
uv init --name demo
uv lock

# 2. Run uv version with --locked
uv version --bump minor --locked

# 3. Check git status
git status -s
```

### Expected Behavior

Because `--locked` was provided and the version change requires updating `uv.lock`, the command should abort without leaving changes on disk. `pyproject.toml` should remain at `0.1.0`.

### Actual Behavior

The command errors with:
```text
error: The lockfile at `uv.lock` needs to be updated, but `--locked` was provided. To update the lockfile, run `uv lock`.
```
However, `git status` shows `pyproject.toml` was already modified:
```diff
--- a/pyproject.toml
+++ b/pyproject.toml
@@ -3,3 +3,3 @@
 name = "demo"
-version = "0.1.0"
+version = "0.2.0"
```

### Root Cause

In `crates/uv/src/commands/project/version.rs`, line 334 calls `update_project` before `lock_and_sync`. Inside `update_project` (line 452), `fs_err::write(pyproject_path, &content)` writes the new `pyproject.toml` to disk before `LockOperation::execute` runs with `LockMode::Locked`.

When `LockOperation` returns an error at line 647, the command exits without reverting the file on disk. In contrast, `crates/uv/src/commands/project/add.rs` performs the lock check against the in-memory representation first and only writes to disk once `LockOperation` succeeds.

### Platform

Title: Test helper function `git_version_info_expected` doesn’t compile with custom profile: `PROFILE` is unset
Text:
Test helper function `git_version_info_expected` doesn’t compile with custom profile: `PROFILE` is unset

### Summary

Downstream in Fedora, we build Rust with a custom profile called `rpm`, which inherits from `release`. For practical technical reasons, we build tests the same way.

We find that the test helper function `git_version_info_expected`, used by the test `self_version_json`, now fails to compile because

https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/blob/a1b84bcbda122236faae8fa5fdcbe16cfb76cde2/crates/uv/tests/it/version.rs#L2162

accesses the `PROFILE` environment variable at compile time, but it is not set.

```
error: environment variable `PROFILE` not defined at compile time
    --> crates/uv/tests/it/version.rs:2158:8
     |
2158 |     if env!("PROFILE") != "release" && option_env!("UV_INTERNAL__BUILD_GIT_INFO") != Some("1") {
     |        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
     |
     = help: `PROFILE` may not be available for the current Cargo target
     = help: Cargo sets build script variables at run time. Use `std::env::var("PROFILE")` instead
```

Looking at https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-build-scripts, I see:

> `PROFILE` — `release` for release builds, `debug` for other builds. This is determined based on if the profile inherits from the `dev` or `release` profile. Using this environment variable is not recommended. Using other environment variables like `OPT_LEVEL` provide a more correct view of the actual settings being used.

but I also note that this documentation section is entitled “environment variables Cargo sets for build scripts,” and that this is not a build script. The section “environment variables Cargo sets for cargo test” promises only to set `CARGO_BIN_EXE_<name>`, so there appear to be no documented guarantees about `PROFILE` here.

I thought of suggesting something like this,

```diff
From 076a0a55e41e217ef9b6c2b25a7c09d426e51f06 Mon Sep 17 00:00:00 2001
From: "Benjamin A. Beasley" <code@musicinmybrain.net>
Date: Sun, 20 Sep 2026 17:14:18 +0100
Subject: [PATCH] In test `git_version_info_expected`, support `PROFILE` unset

Allow this test to build in situations where the `PROFILE` environment
variable is not set, e.g. downstream in Fedora using the custom `rpm`
profile.
---
 crates/uv/tests/it/version.rs | 4 +++-
 1 file changed, 3 insertions(+), 1 deletion(-)

diff --git a/crates/uv/tests/it/version.rs b/crates/uv/tests/it/version.rs
index e5b3ec7bd..70977f753 100644
--- a/crates/uv/tests/it/version.rs
+++ b/crates/uv/tests/it/version.rs
@@ -2155,7 +2155,9 @@ fn version_get_fallback_unmanaged_short() -> Result<()> {
 
 /// Whether this build should include Git metadata in its version output.
 fn git_version_info_expected() -> bool {
-    if env!("PROFILE") != "release" && option_env!("UV_INTERNAL__BUILD_GIT_INFO") != Some("1") {
+    if option_env!("PROFILE") != Some("release")
+        && option_env!("UV_INTERNAL__BUILD_GIT_INFO") != Some("1")
+    {
         return false;
     }
 
-- 
2.55.0

```

and that would make the test work in practice, but it’s not necessarily logically correct: `option_env!("PROFILE") != Some("release")` evaluates false even though our profile inherits from `release`.

For now, I’m just going to carry a patch that unconditionally returns `false` here, but I would be happy in principle to offer a PR that meant I didn’t have to do that forever. I’m not sure that the premise of checking `PROFILE` here is really valid, but I’m not quite sure what to suggest instead.

### Platform

Fedora Rawhide, x86_64

### Version

uv 0.12.7 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu)

### Python version

Python 3.15.0rc2
Reply: cc @charliermarsh

Title: uv pip install -r pylock.toml ignores `default-groups` entries not also listed in `dependency-groups`
Text:
uv pip install -r pylock.toml ignores `default-groups` entries not also listed in `dependency-groups`

> **Revised 2026-09-23.** The original framing of this issue was too broad — it said uv ignores `default-groups` outright, which is not true. uv honors it in one lock shape and not another, and the distinction is the actual bug. Rewritten below; see the comments for what changed and why.

### Summary

uv seeds `dependency_groups` from a lock's top-level `default-groups` **only when the same group name also appears in `dependency-groups`**. A `default-groups` entry that is absent from `dependency-groups` is silently dropped, and every package gated on it is skipped — exit code 0, no warning.

That is a problem because PEP 751 specifically tells lockers *not* to list those names in `dependency-groups`:

> The groups listed by this key SHOULD NOT be listed in `dependency-groups` as the groups are not meant to be directly exposed to users by name but instead via an installer's UI.

and tells installers to seed from them:

> Gather the extras and dependency groups to install and set `extras` and `dependency_groups` for marker evaluation, respectively.
> - `extras` SHOULD be set to the empty set by default.
> - **`dependency_groups` SHOULD be the set created from `default-groups` by default.**

So uv honors `default-groups` only in the shape the PEP tells lockers to avoid, and ignores it in the shape the PEP prescribes for synthetic groups. `pip` seeds unconditionally.

### Minimal reproducible example

One base file, one dependency-free wheel. Only the group-declaring keys change between variants.

```toml
lock-version = "1.0"
default-groups = ["mygroup"]
created-by = "hand-written"

[[packages]]
name = "mypy-extensions"
version = "1.1.0"
marker = "\"mygroup\" in dependency_groups"
requires-python = ">=3.8"

[[packages.wheels]]
name = "mypy_extensions-1.1.0-py3-none-any.whl"
url = "https://files.pythonhosted.org/packages/79/7b/2c79738432f5c924bef5071f933bcc9efd0473bac3b4aa584a6f7c1c8df8/mypy_extensions-1.1.0-py3-none-any.whl"

[packages.wheels.hashes]
sha256 = "1be4cccdb0f2482337c4743e60421de3a356cd97508abadd57d47403e94f5505"
```

```console
$ uv pip install --dry-run -r pylock.toml
warning: The `--pylock` option is experimental and may change without warning. Pass `--preview-features pylock` to disable this warning.
Checked in 0.02ms
Would make no changes
```

Substituting only the top-of-file keys, with no `--group` passed:

| # | `dependency-groups` | `default-groups` | pip 26.2.1 | uv |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | *absent* | `["mygroup"]` | **installs** | **nothing** |
| 2 | `["othergroup"]` | `["mygroup"]` | **installs** | **nothing** |
| 3 | `["mygroup"]` | `["mygroup"]` | installs | installs |
| 4 | `["mygroup"]` | *absent* | nothing | nothing |

Rows 1 and 2 are the bug: pip installs `mypy-extensions`, uv reports `Would make no changes`. Row 2 isolates it to name membership rather than the mere presence of the key. Row 3 is why this can go unnoticed. Row 4 is the control — with no default, neither installer selects the group, which is correct.

Identical results on **uv 0.9.17, 0.12.17 and 0.12.18**, so this is long-standing rather than a recent regression.

### Expected

Rows 1 and 2 install `mypy-extensions`. `default-groups` should seed `dependency_groups` regardless of whether the name also appears in `dependency-groups` — under the current behaviour a locker has to violate the PEP's "SHOULD NOT" to obtain the PEP's documented default, which makes the two pieces of guidance impossible to satisfy together.

### Notes

- **No workaround for rows 1 and 2.** `--group mygroup` does not help; it appears to select only names listed in `dependency-groups`, so it is also a no-op on those files. An undeclared name is accepted silently too — `--group totallybogus` exits 0 with no warning.
- **Silent.** No warning that packages were skipped, and `-v` output contains nothing mentioning the group or the marker.
- **Real-world consequence.** pipx hit this. `pipx manifest lock` generated group-scoped locks its own `pipx manifest sync` could not install ([pypa/pipx#2049](https://github.com/pypa/pipx/issues/2049)). The fix, [pypa/pipx#2052](https://github.com/pypa/pipx/pull/2052), was to have its locker emit the group in **both** keys — row 3 — because that is the shape uv accepts. It works, but it means a downstream tool is now emitting the shape PEP 751 says it should not, specifically to satisfy uv. That PR is also where the over-broad wording of my original report was caught.
- Lockers do produce rows 1 and 2 naturally: `nab lock --project-default-group <name>` emits row 1.

I appreciate `--pylock` is experimental and that these are SHOULD-level requirements, so this may be a known gap or a deliberate reading of `dependency-groups` as the authoritative set of group names. Flagging it because uv and pip diverge on identical input, uv's side fails silently, and the affected shape is the one the PEP recommends.

### Platform

Linux 6.18.33.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2 x86_64 GNU/Linux (Ubuntu 26.04 on WSL2)

### Version

uv 0.12.18 (also reproduced on 0.12.17 and 0.9.17)

### Python version

Python 3.14.5 (pip 26.2.1 for the comparison)

Title: Race condition in SIGPIPE causes network errors to kill uv run
Text:
Race condition in SIGPIPE causes network errors to kill uv run

### Summary

Hi,

I noticed that in some of our CI jobs, the command `uv run --frozen -m modulename` exits with code 141 (128+13 = `SIGPIPE`). This happens under high IO load.

After a long AI-powered investigation I tracked that to a behavior in `uv` regarding SIGPIPE handling in the network code.

Namely:
- an HTTP/2 connection to a repository gets closed due to timeout;
- `uv` gets a `SIGPIPE` (and a `writev` sees `EPIPE`);
- `uv` forwards it to its child (through code added in #13017 I believe);
- if it's early enough in `python` startup code, the signal is not yet ignored;
- `python` dies because of `SIGPIPE`;
- `uv` exits with code 141.

I'm attaching a (AI-generated) repro case based on docker. Tested on 0.12.8. [uv-sigpipe-repro.sh](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32554046/uv-sigpipe-repro.sh)

Not sure what the correct fix is for this, but happy to provide more info if needed.

Thanks!

### Platform

Linux amd64

### Version

0.12.8

### Python version

3.13.5
Reply:
I think for cases like these, we could just stop forking and `exec` python. We must fork e.g. `--isolated` but shouldn't need to for this case.

Not sure how much work that would be.

We could also not forward `SIGPIPE`. It would mean that `kill -PIPE <uv PID>` wouldn't get forwarded, but that should be fine given that `uv run ... | foo` would still work correctly (the writing child would get `SIGPIPE`).

One thing is for sure, trying to correlate `SIGPIPE` with `EPIPE` is a fool's errand.

Another idea that crossed my mind was to exec a holding process which just handles cleanup and then spawn the child from there... But that seems hard to get right.

If no virtual environment exists, uv sync automatically creates the project's virtual environment (typically .venv) and then installs/synchronizes all dependencies specified in pyproject.toml and the lockfile into it.

The command `uv venv` supports the `--relocatable` flag and `UV_VENV_RELOCATABLE` envvar to make the virtual environment relocatable: https://docs.astral.sh/uv/reference/cli/#uv-venv--relocatable

Case 2: A virtual environment exists:

Title: `uv lock` scales exponentially with the size of a single `[tool.uv] conflicts` group
Text:
`uv lock` scales exponentially with the size of a single `[tool.uv] conflicts` group

### Summary

`uv lock` time grows exponentially with the number of extras declared mutually-exclusive in one `[tool.uv] conflicts` group — but only when the project also has a dependency shared across those forks with a large release history (e.g. `transformers`). It roughly doubles every 5-10 extras (24s at N=50 → 110s at N=65), and past a threshold (~70 in the minimal repro below) it no longer completes within any reasonable time.


### Minimal reproduction

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# repro.sh - for each N, generates a pyproject.toml with N empty extras all
# declared mutually exclusive in one [tool.uv] conflicts group, plus one real
# dependency (transformers, chosen for its large release history), and times
# `uv lock`. Prints the full table from this report.
set -euo pipefail
TIMEOUT_S="${TIMEOUT_S:-120}"

gen_pyproject() {
  local n="$1" workdir="$2"
  {
    echo '[project]'
    echo 'name = "repro"'
    echo 'version = "0.0.1"'
    echo 'requires-python = ">=3.10,<3.15"'
    echo 'dependencies = ["transformers>=4.40.0,<6.0.0"]'
    echo
    echo '[project.optional-dependencies]'
    for ((i = 0; i < n; i++)); do echo "e${i} = []"; done
    echo
    echo '[tool.uv]'
    printf 'conflicts = [\n    ['
    for ((i = 0; i < n; i++)); do
      printf '{ extra = "e%d" }' "$i"
      [ "$i" -lt $((n - 1)) ] && printf ', '
    done
    printf '],\n]\n'
  } > "$workdir/pyproject.toml"
}

echo "uv: $(uv --version)"
echo

for n in 5 10 20 30 40 50 55 60 65 70 80 90; do
  workdir="$(mktemp -d -t uv-conflicts-repro-XXXXXX)"
  gen_pyproject "$n" "$workdir"
  start=$(date +%s.%N)
  if timeout "$TIMEOUT_S" uv lock --project "$workdir" > /dev/null 2>&1; then
    outcome="resolved"
  else
    [ $? -eq 124 ] && outcome="TIMEOUT(${TIMEOUT_S}s)" || outcome="error"
  fi
  end=$(date +%s.%N)
  elapsed=$(awk "BEGIN { printf \"%.1f\", $end - $start }")
  printf 'n=%-4s  %-16s  %6ss\n' "$n" "$outcome" "$elapsed"
  rm -rf "$workdir"
done
```

```bash
chmod +x repro.sh
./repro.sh
```

### Timings

| N extras in the group | time |
|---|---|
| 5 | 0.0s |
| 10 | 0.0s |
| 20 | 0.2s |
| 30 | 1.2s |
| 40 | 6.5s |
| 50 | 23.4s |
| 55 | 41.0s |
| 60 | 70.7s |
| 65 | 109.9s |
| 70 | doesn't finish within 120s |
| 80 | doesn't finish within 120s |
| 90 | doesn't finish within 120s |

Grouping shape: splitting the same total extras into many small *disjoint* `conflicts` groups performs identically to one big group — it's the total distinct extra count across `conflicts`, not group size or group count, that predicts the time.

### Context

Found while investigating `uv lock` runs that took multiple hours on [embeddings-benchmark/mteb](https://github.com/embeddings-benchmark/mteb) — one run [wasn't finished after 12 hours](https://github.com/embeddings-benchmark/mteb/issues/5482) and had to be killed. mteb declares ~44 extras mutually exclusive in one group alongside `transformers`/`torch`/`sentence-transformers` as base deps (their real threshold was ~40, lower than this single-dependency repro's ~65 — consistent with multiple large-history deps compounding).

### Related issues

- **#21399**: same *kind* of fix, but scoped to workspaces with many member projects — doesn't cover a single project's own `conflicts` group.
- **#18317**: lock file size scaling with `conflicts`.
- **#17990**: asks for conflicting groups to resolve as independent targets instead of one universal resolution — would likely fix this too.
- **https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/16779**: Similar problem


### Platform

\macOS 27.0 arm64

### Version

uv 0.12.17

### Python version

_No response_
Reply: Yeah, I think this is roughly the same as https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/18317 though?

Title: uv sync leaves an environment with missing NCCL library unchanged
Text:

installation output, exact uv/Python versions, or a reproducer of the file
loss. We cannot establish whether installation, a corrupt cache, or a later
operation removed the files. The observed behavior is that a subsequent
sync accepted the incomplete environment. Is there a supported way to
detect missing installed files without forcing a reinstall?

  after remove/add on macOS, but also a missing RECORD; our RECORD existed.
- https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/19683 was closed after a clean cache

Title: Direct URL requirements with a `sig` query parameter are reinstalled on every run: `direct_url.json` stores the redacted URL (regression in 0.12.8)
Text:
Direct URL requirements with a `sig` query parameter are reinstalled on every run: `direct_url.json` stores the redacted URL (regression in 0.12.8)

### Summary

Since 0.12.8, a direct URL requirement whose query string contains `sig=` (e.g. an Azure Storage SAS URL) is reinstalled on every `uv pip install`, and `uv pip install --dry-run` never reports "Would make no changes" for it.

The `sig` value is redacted not only for display but also in the `direct_url.json` written at install time (`sig=****`). The next install compares the requirement's real URL against the stored, redacted one, sees a different URL, and reinstalls. Other query parameters are also re-encoded in the stored URL (`st=2026-09-15T16:34:14Z` is stored as `st=2026-09-15T16%3A34%3A14Z`).

Bisected: 0.12.7 is fine, 0.12.8 is the first bad release, 0.12.18 still has it. 0.12.8 includes "Redact Azure shared access signature (`sig`) query parameters from displayed URLs" (#21360), which looks like the cause.

Minimal reproduction (any host works; PyPI ignores the extra query parameter):

```console
$ uv venv -q
$ echo 'six @ https://files.pythonhosted.org/packages/b7/ce/149a00dd41f10bc29e5921b496af8b574d8413afcd5e30dfa0ed46c2cc5e/six-1.17.0-py2.py3-none-any.whl?sig=abc' > req.txt
$ uv pip install -q -r req.txt
$ cat .venv/lib/python*/site-packages/six-1.17.0.dist-info/direct_url.json
{"url":"https://files.pythonhosted.org/packages/b7/ce/149a00dd41f10bc29e5921b496af8b574d8413afcd5e30dfa0ed46c2cc5e/six-1.17.0-py2.py3-none-any.whl?sig=****","archive_info":{}}
$ uv pip install -r req.txt
Resolved 1 package in 0.80ms
Uninstalled 1 package in 0.27ms
Installed 1 package in 1ms
 - six==1.17.0 (from https://files.pythonhosted.org/packages/b7/ce/149a00dd41f10bc29e5921b496af8b574d8413afcd5e30dfa0ed46c2cc5e/six-1.17.0-py2.py3-none-any.whl?sig=****)
 + six==1.17.0 (from https://files.pythonhosted.org/packages/b7/ce/149a00dd41f10bc29e5921b496af8b574d8413afcd5e30dfa0ed46c2cc5e/six-1.17.0-py2.py3-none-any.whl?sig=****)
```

Every further `uv pip install -r req.txt` repeats the uninstall/install. With uv 0.12.7, `direct_url.json` keeps `sig=abc` and the second run prints `Would make no changes` / installs nothing.

Expected: redaction applies to displayed and logged URLs only; `direct_url.json` records the URL as requested (as pip does), so an installed direct URL requirement is recognized as satisfied.

| uv | `sig` in `direct_url.json` | second `uv pip install --dry-run` |
|---|---|---|
| 0.12.5, 0.12.7 | `abc` | Would make no changes |
| 0.12.8, 0.12.15, 0.12.16, 0.12.17, 0.12.18 | `****` | Would uninstall 1 package / Would install 1 package |

### Platform

Linux 7.0.0-1014-azure x86_64 GNU/Linux (Ubuntu)

### Version

uv 0.12.17 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu); also reproduced with 0.12.8 and 0.12.18

### Python version

Python 3.13 (also 3.11, 3.12)

Title: uv sync accesses unavailable files even when told not to
Text:
uv sync accesses unavailable files even when told not to

### Summary

If a dependency is in an optional group, and comes from a path, and the dependency is available when the lock file is generated.  Then even if the optional group is NOT selected at time of `uv sync --locked` then it still tries to access the inaccessible file.  The problem can show up with path packages with different operating systems, but can be also seen on a single operating system where some machines have access to the path and some do not.

         And because your project requires bugreport:lab, we can conclude that your project's requirements are

```

Putting a `[[tool.uv.dependency-metadata]]` section in the `pyproject.toml` also doesnt work, but gives a different error - it complains that it needs a hash value (but putting a hash value into the metadata is invalid).

Is this a bug? If not, how is this scenario supposed to be handled?  Thank you.
