Title: uv tool install --force --reinstall mutates the tool environment in place: concurrent readers observe missing files for tens of seconds while the install exits 0
Text:
uv tool install --force --reinstall mutates the tool environment in place: concurrent readers observe missing files for tens of seconds while the install exits 0

### Summary

### Summary

`uv tool install --force --reinstall <tool>` replaces the tool environment *in place*. A concurrent reader of that environment, such as the running tool itself, or any process importing from its site-packages, observes missing modules and files for the duration of the replacement, while the reinstall exits 0, implying success.

I measured the window with a 10 Hz observer loop: **59 missing samples across ~43 seconds** during a single reinstall of a tool with a few hundred files.

This is the reader-side sibling of #12751 (writer-vs-writer on concurrent `uv sync`). In this bug, for comparison, there there is only one writer, unserialized against readers.

### Repro

Terminal A (observer, 10 Hz):

```bash
while true; do
  ~/.local/share/uv/tools/<tool>/bin/python -c "import <package>" 2>/dev/null \
    || echo "MISSING $(date +%H:%M:%S.%N)"
  sleep 0.1
done
```

Terminal B:

```bash
uv tool install --force --reinstall <tool>
```

Observed: 59 `MISSING` lines spread across ~43 s of the reinstall. Interleaving two reinstalls of the same tool makes the window worse and both still exit 0.

### Expected

Either:

- the replacement is serialized/atomic: build the new environment in a sibling directory and swap (rename or symlink flip), so a reader never observes a partially populated environment; or
- the window is documented as expected behavior, so callers know to route unattended reinstalls through a build-then-flip mechanism. (And maybe then add an example of this mechanism.)

### Workaround

I now install tools into an immutable per-version directory and flip a symlink pointer myself; the race becomes impossible. The cost is duplicated disk per version and manual reaping.

### Platform

macOS 15.7.3 arm64

### Version

uv 0.12.6 (7938ca5d5 2026-08-25)

### Python version

Python 3.13.15
Reply:
If we ever delete the old environment, it won't necessarily matter that it was swapped atomically using symlinks, because the old process can still hold references to directories in the old environment and can still use those references to attempt to open files which would now be missing.

I don't necessarily think there's an expectation for the tool you're updating to work at every moment during an update...

This is something we may consider but I'm marking this as a feature request rather than a bug for now.

Looking around in uv, #21000 with uv 0.12.4 seems to have introduced the current sorting of resolution markers, and I believe the Renovate image is recent enough to use that version of uv. Title: Wheel variant preview implementation tracker
Text:
Wheel variant preview implementation tracker

I'm using this issue to keep track of the wheel variants PRs for the implementation of PEP 825 and following PRs in preview. This issue will be updated as new parts are added.

**Try it out**

```
uv pip install --preview <name> --index-url <url>
```

Only the pip interface is currently supported.

## Ready for review

No PRs are currently ready for review.

## Implementation

The overall flow goes like this, say for an initial and a subsequent `uv sync`:
* There's wheels with variant labels we need to recognize. A difference to before is that we don't know yet which are compatible, we'll only know that later after we ran the providers.
* Whenever there are variant wheels, we need their variant metadata. Each variant wheel contains `*.dist-info/variant.json`. When using an index, we should fetch its `{name}-{version}-variants.json` instead, so we need to support different wheel sources individually.
* The variants json gives us a list of providers. We need to support various kinds of providers and get variant properties from them
* All the important providers are vendored, so we need to implement those
* We match the variant properties against the wheels, order the wheels and pick the best one
* We need to compare against an installed wheel: Unlike with regular wheels, we want one variant wheel to replace an existing variant wheel with a different label, e.g. to switch from CPU to GPU
* We also need to lock variant wheels and the lock and hash the variants.json
* When installing from a lockfile, we need to collect the variants.json and run all the providers (in parallel) before we select the wheel to use. we must be secure about the hash checking.

We need to break https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/12203 into pieces. The prototype currently builds on #22758.

Title: `lock-without-metadata`: `uv lock --check` re-resolves when a conflicting group has `pkg` and `pkg[extra]`
Text:
`lock-without-metadata`: `uv lock --check` re-resolves when a conflicting group has `pkg` and `pkg[extra]`

### Summary

With `lock-without-metadata`, `uv lock --check` always re-resolves when a group in `conflicts` lists a package with and without extras. Offline with an empty cache, it fails.

**Edit:** #21951 partially fixed this, see below follow up comment. 

Turning the feature off, or dropping the conflict or either entry, avoids it.

#### Why a project ends up like this

We lock two Airflow versions in one `uv.lock`, one conflicting group each, to test upgrades beside the current version. Each version's group includes a shared group with `apache-airflow`, then adds its pin with extras, e.g. `apache-airflow[celery]==3.3.2`. So one group has both `apache-airflow` and `apache-airflow[celery]`.

### Reproduction

Run `docker build . --progress plain --no-cache` on:

```dockerfile
FROM --platform=linux/amd64 ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.12.19-python3.12-trixie-slim

COPY <<EOF /mre/pyproject.toml
[project]
name = "mre"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = []

[dependency-groups]
a = ["requests", "requests[socks]"]
b = []

[tool.uv]
preview-features = ["lock-without-metadata"]
conflicts = [[{ group = "a" }, { group = "b" }]]
EOF

WORKDIR /mre
RUN uv lock
RUN uv cache clean
RUN uv lock --check --offline -v
```

The last step fails:

```
DEBUG Resolving despite existing lockfile due to mismatched resolved dependencies for: `mre==0.1.0`
  Requested: [Dependency { ... name: PackageName("requests") ... extra: {} ... }, Dependency { ... name: PackageName("requests") ... extra: {ExtraName("socks")} ... }]

...
error: No solution found when resolving dependencies for split (included: mre[group:a]; excluded: mre[group:b])
```

Without `preview-features` it passes: `Existing uv.lock satisfies workspace requirements`.

Title: `uv audit` reports "no known vulnerabilities" (exit 0) when the OSV querybatch response has fewer results than queries
Text:
`uv audit` reports "no known vulnerabilities" (exit 0) when the OSV querybatch response has fewer results than queries

### Summary

When `/v1/querybatch` answers `200` with fewer `results` than the queries it was sent, `uv audit` pairs queries with results by position and silently drops the unmatched queries. The packages whose results are missing are never checked, but the command prints `Found no known vulnerabilities …` and exits `0`. A truncated or empty `200` body — from an intermediary proxy, a captive portal that happens to return JSON, or a service-side bug — therefore turns into a green audit.

### Reproduction (uv 0.12.21)

`pyproject.toml`:

```toml
[project]
name = "repro"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = ["python-multipart==0.0.6"]
```

`fake_osv.py`, an OSV stand-in that answers `200` with `N` fewer results than queries:

```python
import json, sys
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer

class H(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def log_message(self, *a): pass
    def do_POST(self):
        n = len(json.loads(self.rfile.read(int(self.headers["Content-Length"])))["queries"])
        body = json.dumps({"results": [{}] * max(n - int(sys.argv[2]), 0)}).encode()
        self.send_response(200); self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(body))); self.end_headers(); self.wfile.write(body)

HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", int(sys.argv[1])), H).serve_forever()
```

```console
$ uv lock
$ uv audit --frozen --preview-features audit-command                     # real OSV
  ...
  Advisory information: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-40347
$ echo $?
1

$ python3 fake_osv.py 18777 1 &                                          # one result short
$ uv audit --frozen --preview-features audit-command --service-url http://127.0.0.1:18777
Found no known vulnerabilities and no adverse project statuses in 1 package
$ echo $?
0

$ python3 fake_osv.py 18778 999 &                                        # {"results": []}
$ uv audit --frozen --preview-features audit-command --service-url http://127.0.0.1:18778
Found no known vulnerabilities and no adverse project statuses in 1 package
$ echo $?
0
```

Also reproduced on 0.12.9 and 0.12.19.

### Expected

A response whose `results` length differs from the number of queries in the batch is an error (exit `2`, like other service failures), not a clean result.

### Where

`crates/uv-audit/src/service/osv.rs`, `query_identifiers`, on `main`:

```rust
pending_batch.iter().zip(batch_response.results.iter())
```

`zip` stops at the shorter side. A length check before it (`batch_response.results.len() == pending_batch.len()`, otherwise an error) would close this. OSV's API documents one result per query, in order.

### Why it matters

`uv audit` is typically used as a CI gate or a scheduled check, where a false "clean" is the one failure nobody looks at. We found this while hardening a nightly audit job and currently guard against it with a known-vulnerable canary lock that must come back vulnerable before the real locks are trusted.

Title: Support per-project environment constraints for workspace dependency resolution
Text:
Support per-project environment constraints for workspace dependency resolution

### Problem Statement

Python's packaging spec doesn't define a way to specify that a project is compatible only with a particular operating system. Developers can use the `project.classifiers` field to define compatible operating systems, but that is informational-only, not a firm requirement for installers to abide by.

As a result, uv errors if you have a workspace with the following members:

```toml
[project]
name = "a"
classifiers = [ "Operating System :: Microsoft :: Windows" ]
dependencies = [ "numpy==1" ]
```

```toml
[project]
name = "b"
classifiers = [ "Operating System :: POSIX :: Linux" ]
dependencies = [ "numpy==2" ]
```

The user never intends to install these two members at the same time, but since uv doesn't know that, `uv sync --all-packages` errors. The most robust solution to this issue is to explicitly pin an environment for each dependency, for example:

```toml
[project]
name = "a"
classifiers = [ "Operating System :: Microsoft :: Windows" ]
dependencies = [ "numpy==1; platform_system=='Windows'" ]
```

```toml
[project]
name = "b"
classifiers = [ "Operating System :: POSIX :: Linux" ]
dependencies = [ "numpy==2; platform_system=='Linux'" ]
```

There are a couple issues with this approach:
* It's redundant. The compatible platform is already listed in the classifier.
* It's excessively verbose. If you have hundreds of dependencies, it's gross to need to add "platform_system=='Windows'" to all of them.
* It's not strict. uv will still attempt to install the member, even if it skips installing all of its dependencies.

### Proposed Solution

Add a `supported-environments` setting to uv. Developers can specify supported environments in each member's pyproject.toml.

Example:

```toml
[project]
name = "a"
classifiers = [ "Operating System :: Microsoft :: Windows" ]
dependencies = [ "numpy==1" ]

[tool.uv]
supported-environments = [ "platform_system=='Windows'" ]
```

```toml
[project]
name = "b"
classifiers = [ "Operating System :: POSIX :: Linux" ]
dependencies = [ "numpy==2" ]

[tool.uv]
supported-environments = [ "platform_system=='Linux'" ]
```

The available environment markers and semantics are the exact same ones uv currently respects for dependencies: https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/blob/c4e9150bc11eb29ae8f366430332b9592b9f9044/crates/uv-pep508/src/marker/environment.rs#L18-L30.

Misc. notes:
* if `supported-environments` is not specified, uv behaves the same way it currently does
* running `uv sync --package` on a project with an incompatible environment gives a helpful error message
* running `uv sync --all-packages` syncs all projects with compatible environments

### Alternatives I Considered

* Going off of `classifiers` directly.
    * `classifiers` doesn't actually have a firm definition. It also feels directionally incorrect to have two distinct ways of defining environments. It would be nice if we could reuse the exact same environment markers and semantics as dependencies.
* Reusing the existing `tool.uv.environments` field in members' pyproject.tomls.
    * These usages seem related but distinct, so I suggest a distinct field `supported-environments`.

Title: uv aborts (SIGABRT) when stderr is a non-blocking stream that returns EAGAIN
Text:
uv aborts (SIGABRT) when stderr is a non-blocking stream that returns EAGAIN

### Summary

uv aborts with SIGABRT when its stderr is a **non-blocking** stream whose buffer is momentarily full. `eprint!` in `crates/uv/src/printer.rs:131` panics on `EAGAIN` ("failed printing to stderr: Resource temporarily unavailable (os error 11)"), and the panic message itself cannot be written, so callers only see `Aborted (core dumped)` / exit 134 partway through the output.

This happens in practice when uv runs under a Node.js or Bun parent. Their child "pipe" stdio is a Unix socketpair, and they set `O_NONBLOCK` on stdio they share with children. When the reader falls briefly behind, uv's per-package lines (one `write` each) fill the socket buffer and the next write returns `EAGAIN`. We hit it intermittently in a `uv sync --locked` run inside a Git worktree hook launched from a Bun script. Other tools in the same chain (Bun, Go programs) retry the write and keep going.

Minimal reproduction (Linux; any packages will do, more output makes it more reliable):

```python
import socket, subprocess, tempfile, time

def run(nonblocking: bool) -> None:
    venv = tempfile.mkdtemp()
    subprocess.run(["uv", "venv", "-q", venv], check=True)
    parent, child = socket.socketpair()  # what Node/Bun use for a child's "pipe" stdio
    child.setblocking(not nonblocking)   # Node/Bun set O_NONBLOCK on stdio they share
    proc = subprocess.Popen(
        ["uv", "pip", "install", "--python", venv, "fastapi", "httpx", "boto3", "sqlalchemy", "rich", "pytest"],
        stdout=child, stderr=child, stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL,
    )
    child.close()
    time.sleep(3)  # a reader that falls behind
    out = b""
    while chunk := parent.recv(65536):
        out += chunk
    print(f"nonblocking={nonblocking} returncode={proc.wait()} bytes={len(out)}")

run(False)
run(True)
```

Output with uv 0.12.21 and 0.12.23:

```
nonblocking=False returncode=0 bytes=754
nonblocking=True returncode=-6 bytes=615
```

`strace -f -e trace=write,tgkill` on the failing run:

```
write(2, "s3transfer", 10)      = 10
write(2, "==", 2)               = -1 EAGAIN (Resource temporarily unavailable)
write(2, "\nthread 'main2' (1948927) panicked at crates/uv/src/printer.rs:131:17:\nfailed printing to stderr: Resource temporarily unavailable (os error 11)\n", 145) = -1 EAGAIN (Resource temporarily unavailable)
tgkill(1948926, 1948927, SIGABRT) = 0
+++ killed by SIGABRT (core dumped) +++
```

Expected: uv completes the install (retrying the write on `EAGAIN`, or at worst dropping output), rather than aborting mid-install. `--quiet` avoids it, which is our workaround.

### Platform

Linux 6.8.0-139-generic x86_64 (Ubuntu 24.04)

### Version

uv 0.12.23 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu); also 0.12.21

### Python version

Python 3.14.7
Reply:
Can you share an example of spawning uv through one of those runtimes that demonstrates the problem?

For context (per responses in #22195): this is arguably a bug in any parent process that forces its children to inherit `O_NONBLOCK`, since most tools expect to be run with blocking I/O, particularly for things like stdout and stderr.

I know this is the default for a lot of JS runtimes since they're fundamentally asynchronous, but it would be helpful to see the exact code so that we can understand whether there's an idiomatic caller-side solution here.

Title: uv_build: optionally respect .gitignore / VCS ignore rules
Text:
uv_build: optionally respect .gitignore / VCS ignore rules

### Summary

`uv_build` currently includes files from the configured package/module tree regardless of whether they are ignored by Git. Its default exclusions appear to be limited to `__pycache__`, `*.pyc`, and `*.pyo`, plus explicit `source-exclude` / `wheel-exclude` rules.

This is surprising compared with backends such as Hatchling and Poetry, and can be a packaging/security footgun when developers keep local, generated, scratch, or sensitive files inside a package directory and rely on `.gitignore` to keep them out of the repository.

### Example

Given:

```text
src/
└── avite/
    └── generate/
        ├── __init__.py
        ├── main.py
        ├── debug_dump.json
        └── local_notes.md
```

and:

```gitignore
src/avite/generate/debug_dump.json
src/avite/generate/local_notes.md
```

with:

```toml
[build-system]
requires = ["uv_build"]
build-backend = "uv_build"
```

the ignored files are still eligible for inclusion in the wheel unless they are separately listed in `source-exclude` or `wheel-exclude`.

### Request

Could `uv_build` support an opt-in setting to respect VCS ignore rules when selecting files, for example:

```toml
[tool.uv.build-backend]
respect-vcs-ignore = true
```

This could remain opt-in if the current deterministic, VCS-independent behavior is intentional.

An alternative that would preserve current build semantics would be an opt-in warning when a Git-ignored file is about to be included in an sdist or wheel, e.g.:

```toml
[tool.uv.build-backend]
warn-vcs-ignored-files = true
```

### Rationale

I understand the reasons for decoupling packaging from Git state: generated files may intentionally be ignored but still need to be packaged, and build behavior should ideally be reproducible outside a Git checkout.

However, the current behavior also creates a non-obvious risk: many developers treat `.gitignore` as a practical boundary for files that should not leave the working tree. An opt-in VCS-aware mode, or at least a warning mode, would catch accidental publication without changing the default behavior.

Related design context: #8779 discusses how other backends handle VCS ignore rules.

Title: Allow index override when using uv sync --frozen
Text:
Allow index override when using uv sync --frozen

### Summary

When using `uv sync --frozen`, I want to be able to override the location from which packages are installed (defined  in URLs in my frozen uv.lock file) using the `UV_INDEX` environment variable or the `--index` command line argument. This is particularly useful in air-gapped networks or on networks where pypi.org/pythonhosted.org are unreachable. I think this behavior should also apply to `uv run --frozen <cmd>` when the auto-syncing of packages occurs. In my case, not being able to override the indexes is forcing me to manually manage my venv in my air-gapped network, which half defeats the purpose of using uv. 

I have a repository that is mirrored to an air-gapped network. My uv.lock file is built and committed to my project repo on an internet facing machine before being mirrored. The python dependencies for building/running the project are mirrored to a GitLab python registry that in no way matches the paths within my lock file (pypi.org/pythonhosted.org). Rebuilding my lock file on the air-gapped network is not feasible because not all dependencies for all groups and all python versions are mirrored on the air-gapped network, just the versions for the version of python I'm using.

Design details:
- In order for packages from overridden indexes to be synced, they need to match the name, version and hash from the uv.lock file
- Index overrides take precedence over the URL listed in the lock file. If they don't exist, fall back to the URL in the lock file
- The lock file will not be modified because the `--frozen` flag is in use in these cases


### Example

When a user is using a frozen uv.lock file in an air-gapped network or on a corporate network using a proxy PyPi registry, currently they must manually manage their virtual environment because `uv sync --frozen` will refuse to accept index overrides. With the requested changes, a user could set up some environment variables (UV_INDEX and optionally UV_INDEX_MYINDEX_USERNAME and UV_INDEX_MYINDEX_PASSWORD) and then `uv sync --frozen` and `uv run --frozen <cmd>` would behave and sync dependencies as if the user were on the internet. The user would no longer have to manually manage the virtual environment.

```
export UV_INDEX=myindex=https://mygitlab.org/api/v4/projects/4/packages/pypi
export UV_INDEX_MYINDEX_USERNAME=<gitlab-username>
export UV_INDEX_MYINDEX_PASSWORD=<gitlab-personal-access-token>

uv sync --frozen
```
In this example, uv would try to sync dependencies listed in the uv.lock file from `https://mygitlab.org/api/v4/projects/4/packages/pypi` first and then fall back to the URL listed in the uv.lock file.


### Example Code Changes
Here are some example code changes: https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/compare/main...rxanp:uv:rxanp/allow-index-override-on-sync

https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/19625
https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/16996

Title: Darwin release markers lose opaque-string semantics during evaluation and simplification
Text:
Darwin release markers lose opaque-string semantics during evaluation and simplification

## Summary

Darwin `platform_release` markers have two inconsistent behaviors for non-version release strings accepted by the public `MarkerEnvironment` API. Reproduction-only draft PR #22258 contains two small failing tests; it does not include a proposed production fix.

1. With `platform_release = "not-a-version"`, `platform_release == '24'` evaluates false, but `marker.negate()` also evaluates false. This violates the public logical-negation contract.
2. With `platform_release = "3-invalid"`, `platform_release >= '9' or platform_release < '24'` evaluates true. Numeric range simplification makes the union universal before runtime evaluation. Under lexical fallback both comparisons are false (`3-invalid` sorts between `24` and `9`); the current specification's opaque strict-ordering rules also make both false.

These are synthetic API inputs, not evidence of failure on an ordinary macOS release string. No end-to-end installation impact is claimed.

## Reproduction

Check out the test branch from #22258 (commit `946e286a63dc6972e45bc2f43a80301439f2d7b7`) and run:

```sh
cargo +1.99.0 test -p uv-pep508 --test darwin_release_fallback
```

Observed output:

```text
running 2 tests
test darwin_unparseable_release_negation ... FAILED
test invalid_darwin_release_is_not_a_numeric_tautology ... FAILED

assertion failed: marker.negate().evaluate(&env, &[])
assertion failed: !marker.evaluate(&env, &[])

test result: FAILED. 0 passed; 2 failed; 0 ignored
```

Expected: the equality's logical negation is true, and the second expression is false for the supplied opaque release string.

## Analysis / repair boundary

The `VersionString` evaluator returns false on an unparseable environment value, including for a complemented node. Separately, lowering to numeric ranges can discard the opaque-string behavior before evaluation. Changing only the parse-error return does not address the second test.

A complete repair needs to account for both numeric and opaque values during simplification and preserve the result through printing/serialization. Existing lexical fallback and the current specification's string-ordering rules imply different generalized designs; the tests above agree under both. This report leaves that broader contract choice open.

Related: #21766 introduced Darwin release inference. The [marker comparison specification](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/dependency-specifiers/#marker-comparisons) describes Version/String fallback. This report concerns the two concrete API inconsistencies above.

## Platform

Tests run on macOS / Darwin arm64. The supplied marker environment explicitly selects Darwin; Python is not invoked.

## Version

uv source base `eaa0fb829a581ef50fd75c53b5ca964bc73d31c6`; Rust 1.99.0. The PR adds tests only.

Assisted-by: GPT-6.1 Sol and Codex.

Title: Feature Request: Support environment markers / conditions for `include-group` in Dependency Groups
Text:
Feature Request: Support environment markers / conditions for `include-group` in Dependency Groups

### Summary

### **Problem Statement / Background**

Currently, PEP 735 dependency groups allow including other groups using `{ include-group = "group-name" }`. However, unlike standard dependency specifications (e.g., `package; python_version <= '3.13'`), there is no way to attach **environment markers** (such as `python_version` or `platform_system`) to an `include-group` entry.

This creates a limitation when composing larger optional dependency groups (like `all` or `dev`) that include platform-specific or Python-version-restricted optional dependencies.

---

### **Use Case**

Consider a project configured as follows:

```toml
[dependency-groups]
libtorrent = [
    "libtorrent~=2.1",
]

all = [
    { include-group = "libtorrent" },
    # other optional groups...
]

```

* `libtorrent` does not support **Python 3.14+**.
* If a user explicitly requests to install the `libtorrent` group (`uv sync --only-group libtorrent`) on Python 3.14, it **should fail** as expected.
* However, if a user requests to install the `all` group (`uv sync --group all`) on Python 3.14, we want `uv` to **silently skip** the `libtorrent` group instead of failing resolution due to the incompatible Python version restriction.

Without marker support on `include-group`, it is impossible to conditionally inherit dependency groups based on Python versions or operating systems.

---

### **Proposed Solution / Feature Request**

Allow environment markers to be specified on `{ include-group = ... }` declarations (or support inline marker syntax), similar to how markers work for standard package dependencies.

**Proposed Syntax Options:**

1. **Inline string marker syntax:**
```toml
[dependency-groups]
all = [
    { include-group = "libtorrent; python_version <= '3.13'" },
]

```


2. **Or structured table fields (if preferred for TOML consistency):**
```toml
[dependency-groups]
all = [
    { include-group = "libtorrent", marker = "python_version <= '3.13'" },
]

```
Reply: Unfortunately this would need to go through the Python standards process as-proposed, since that's a standardized field. But it's plausible we could support this with uv-specific metadata.

- Include reqsign's credential-loading warnings in uv's `-v` output.

Title: uv aborts when a hardlink fallback warning cannot be written to stderr (EDQUOT)
Text:
uv aborts when a hardlink fallback warning cannot be written to stderr (EDQUOT)

### Summary

uv aborted while synchronizing dependencies when stderr was redirected to a file on a quota-exhausted filesystem.

The underlying storage failure was caused by my execution environment. I’m reporting the subsequent `SIGABRT` to ask whether uv should exit with a controlled error when writing a diagnostic fails.

The original sequence was:

```bash
uv sync --frozen --group dev --python 3.12 --quiet;
uv run --frozen --group dev pytest ... \
  > /tmp/tests.log 2>&1
```

Both the virtual environment and the log were located on `/tmp`, a tmpfs with a per-user quota. The first command failed to copy a dependency with `Disk quota exceeded`. Because I used `;`, the second command still ran and attempted synchronization again.

The core dump places the panic in `uv_fs::link::atomic_hardlink_overwrite`, at the hardlink fallback warning. Inspection of the saved error identifies a failed stderr write with `EDQUOT`.

#### Reproduction

I reduced this to a synthetic wheel containing one Python module:

1. Put the uv cache and installation target on different filesystems.
2. Create the module’s destination file beforehand to exercise atomic replacement.
3. Install with `--link-mode=hardlink`.
4. Inject `EDQUOT` into stderr writes containing the warning.

Without injection, uv prints the hardlink warning, copies the file, and succeeds. With injection:

```text
thread 'main2' panicked at crates/uv-fs/src/link.rs:812:9:
failed printing to stderr: Disk quota exceeded (os error 122)
```

The subprocess exits with `-6` (`SIGABRT`).

This reproduces with Fedora’s 0.12.19 package, Astral’s official 0.12.19 binary, and Astral’s official 0.12.23 binary.

The injected error reproduces the crash mechanism; the original incident involved an actual filesystem quota failure.

#### Expected behavior / policy question

Would a controlled nonzero exit be preferable to a panic and core dump when diagnostic output fails with a permanent error such as `EDQUOT`?

I’m not proposing retries or assuming installation should continue after storage exhaustion. I’m also aware of #22170 and the discussion in #22195 about unsupported nonblocking stdio. This case involves a regular redirected log file and a permanent quota error rather than `EAGAIN`.

If this behavior is considered worth changing, I’d be interested in contributing a focused regression test and discussing the appropriate error-handling policy before implementing it.

### Platform

Fedora Linux 44, x86_64

### Version

uv 0.12.19 (Fedora: 0.12.19-1.fc44); also reproduced on official uv 0.12.23 - both x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu

### Python version

Python 3.12.14
Reply:
If I understand correctly, this happens because you've (1) redirected `stderr` to a file, and (2) the disk that the redirection is on runs out of quota, so you hit `EDQUOT`. Is that right?

If that's correct, then I'm not really sure what uv can do here: the failure in question happens on a call to `warn_user_once!`, which is more or less just a wrapper around `eprintln!`:

https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/blob/17cdcc31b2ace1be03af2f850fb49edd699491be/crates/uv-warnings/src/lib.rs#L121

`eprintln!` in turn is infallible at the type level because stderr writes aren't really expected to fail. I guess we could bind `io::stderr()` instead and write through that, but we almost certainly won't be able to guarantee that every stdout/stderr write that uv performs is checked (and more generally doing so is problematic, since plenty of stdout/stderr writes _should_ fail hard).

If I understand the report correctly, this is all downstream of using `;` instead of `&&` to chain commands. I think we'd recommend you do that when you need to guarantee that interdependent operations chain correctly (or fail consistently).

Title: `uv run --with` packages invisible to project entrypoints when the venv path forces the /bin/sh shebang wrapper
Text:
`uv run --with` packages invisible to project entrypoints when the venv path forces the /bin/sh shebang wrapper

### Summary

`uv run --with <req> <entrypoint>` stops seeing the `--with` packages when the project venv's path is long. A >127-byte shebang is enough.

- In that case `format_shebang` (`crates/uv-install-wheel/src/wheel.rs`) writes the launcher as an absolute `/bin/sh` wrapper (`#!/bin/sh` / `'''exec' '/abs/.venv/bin/python' "$0" "$@"`).
- `copy_entrypoint` (`crates/uv-project-commands/src/run.rs`) only recognises the *relocatable* `/bin/sh` form and a bare `#!<python>` line, so it skips this form. The trace shows: `Skipping copy of entrypoint .venv/bin/pytest: does not start with expected shebang`.
- The base launcher then runs the base interpreter, and the ephemeral `--with` environment is invisible to it.

The same project at a short path works. The bug shows up only at long paths, e.g. deep git worktrees or CI workspaces.

### Reproduction

```bash
d="$TMPDIR/$(python3 -c 'print("a"*200)')/proj"   # any path giving a >127-byte shebang
mkdir -p "$d" && cd "$d"
uv init -q --bare --name repro
uv add -q pytest
printf 'def test_x():\n    import six\n' > test_x.py
head -1 .venv/bin/pytest                    # -> #!/bin/sh
uv run --with six pytest -q test_x.py       # -> ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'six'
uv run --with six python -m pytest -q test_x.py   # -> 1 passed (workaround)
```

Run the same steps under a short directory (shebang ≤127 bytes) and `uv run --with six pytest` passes.

### Expected

`copy_entrypoint` should also accept the absolute `/bin/sh` wrapper that uv itself writes for long paths, and rewrite it to point at the ephemeral interpreter.

### Platform / version

- macOS aarch64 (Darwin 27.0.0); uv 0.11.32 and 0.12.17 (same behaviour).
- I read the code on `main` @ c0110fc, and `copy_entrypoint` still matches only the two forms above.

Title: Separate runtime workspace ownership from cache cleanup
Text:
Separate runtime workspace ownership from cache cleanup

### Summary

The cache holds both reusable artifacts and files that live processes need. A cache lock held by uv cannot protect those files after uv dies.

A local PEP 517 reproduction demonstrates this on macOS: kill only uv, then run plain `uv cache clean`. The backend remains alive, but its environment disappears and its next write fails with `ENOENT`. The removal loop merged in #22171 permits the same failure through prune. Another reproduction needs no signal: one parallel build fails, and uv removes another live backend's environment.

A possible architecture fix:

1. Put uv-owned execution workspaces outside `UV_CACHE_DIR`. This includes build sources, temporary environments, and reusable executable environments. Cache clean and prune remove reusable artifacts.
2. Give the child and its workspace one owner, with explicit async shutdown. Cancellation goes through that owner. It keeps the workspace through exit and output collection.
3. Make those workspaces independent of cache paths. Copy or clone package files, or hardlink immutable files. Avoid runtime dependency symlinks into the evictable cache. Create environments at their final path and reuse them there.

Completed build outputs enter the cache after the build completes. Old execution entries need conservative retention during migration.

Unknown process lifetime means keep the workspace. A dead parent, an unlocked lease, or direct-child exit cannot prove that every descendant stopped. Automatic recovery after crashes remains a separate problem. The tradeoff is retained workspaces after uncertain exits.

### Example

After parent-only `SIGKILL`, cache cleanup leaves the backend's workspace and imports usable. An error in another parallel build also preserves them. A detached descendant with closed output pipes retains its workspace.

The recorded reproductions cover macOS 26.6.2 arm64 with Python 3.14.7. Cache clean fails this requirement on uv 0.12.23. The prune reproduction used PR CI revision `013216c409a2ce74821f25d9d84ce0747a0301ba`. The proposed architecture has no implementation or Linux/Windows runtime validation yet.

Related to #22167, #18962, and #20116.

Codex helped prepare the reproductions and this proposal.

Title: `uv build --all-packages` deadlocks with a cold cache: wheel-lock waiters exhaust the tokio blocking pool
Text:
`uv build --all-packages` deadlocks with a cold cache: wheel-lock waiters exhaust the tokio blocking pool

### Summary

`uv build --all-packages` on a large workspace (54 members, all `hatchling` + `hatch-vcs`) intermittently hangs forever when the cache is cold (`UV_NO_CACHE=1`, or a fresh `UV_CACHE_DIR`). uv never spawns a build backend, and the 5-minute `UV_LOCK_TIMEOUT` default does not fire. In CI the hang lasts until the 6h job timeout.

### Observations (uv 0.12.23, x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu)

- All 54 `[pkg] Building source distribution...` lines print, then nothing. The `uv` process has **0 child processes**.
- `-v` logs 530 `INFO Waiting to acquire exclusive lock for .../wheels-v6/pypi/<build-req>/<version>-py3-none-any.lock` lines within the same second. They cover the ~10 shared build requirements (hatchling, hatch-vcs, setuptools-scm, vcs-versioning, packaging, pathspec, pluggy, trove-classifiers, setuptools, tomlkit), ~53 waiters each.
- The process sits at **514 threads**, with ~541 open `.lock` fds and 11 flocks held by the same pid (`/proc/locks`). These numbers don't change for more than 6 minutes, and no lock-timeout error is ever printed.

### Likely mechanism

`LockedFile::lock_file` (`crates/uv-fs/src/locked_file.rs`) waits for a contended lock with `tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || mode.lock(&file))`, which is a blocking `flock` on the blocking pool (default cap 512). `lock_wheel` (`crates/uv-distribution/src/distribution_database.rs`) holds the wheel-cache lock across download and extraction, and extraction also runs on the blocking pool. Once the waiters (54 builds × ~10 shared build requirements ≈ 540) occupy all 512 blocking threads, the lock holders' extraction work is queued behind them and never runs, so the locks are never released.

The `tokio::time::timeout(*LOCK_TIMEOUT, …)` around the waiter also doesn't seem to rescue this. A waiter that times out still leaves its blocking thread parked in `flock`, and the holders (which have no timeout) keep the overall build pending.

### Reproduction sketch

1. A workspace with ~50+ members, each with `[build-system] requires = ["hatchling", "hatch-vcs"]`.
2. `UV_NO_CACHE=1 uv build --all-packages --out-dir dist/`

The hang is timing-dependent: a few percent of runs on a 4-vCPU CI runner, and nearly every run on a heavily loaded 4-core host.

### Workaround

Building members in separate processes with bounded parallelism (`uv workspace list --paths | xargs -P4 -I{} uv build {} --out-dir dist/`, sharing one cache) avoids the hang.

### Suggestions

- Wait for contended locks without parking a blocking-pool thread per waiter, for example by polling `try_lock` with backoff, or by deduplicating in-process waiters on the same path with an async mutex before taking the flock.
- And/or bound concurrent build-environment setup so that waiters can't exceed the blocking pool.

Title: Feature request: `uv auth` supports pluggable token provider for short-lived tokens
Text:
Feature request: `uv auth` supports pluggable token provider for short-lived tokens

## Summary

Currently `uv auth` supports only static credentials. Modern infrastructure frequently supports authentication routines to be handled using the short-living tokens. This also is specifically useful if later the `Bearer` auth scheme will be implemented. Dynamic credentials can be injected with `keyring`, but this hardly can be called reliable.

This feature request proposes an approach to introduce the support for external token vending app different from `keyring`. The motivation, analysis and example of the implementation spec are provided below.

If the approach is supported I will be glad to attempt contributing this.

## Detailed Proposal

The pluggable credential providers is not new and there are similar issues and requests already touching the scope. See e.g. (#19025, #7660), but this requests attempts to address some concerns on security side mentioned in the discussions. There are also existing workarounds that allow to enable this "sideways".

The further proposal text is structured as follows: I start with the use cases, then proposal and finally with the alternatives review. But there's no design decision yet that either promise the implementation or block it.

### Use cases

In enterprise environments and specifically with cloud services the access might be managed with a short-lived tokens. Users usually posess the tool/script/routine that obtains or refreshes required tokens. In majority of cases tokens are passed in `Bearer` scheme by adding it to HTTP headers. But if the identity provider is in place it's usually not difficult to tweak the ingress to validate the tokens in the HTTP basic schema.

### Proposal Specification

Add the following functionality with no strong opinion on exact naming of the flags/options

- `uv auth login --token-provider "{command}" {service}` allows to store the `{command}` decomposed into the call + arguments array.
- During the authentication loop `uv` performs a call for the provided command and streams the output as HTTP basic with `__token__` username by default.
- **Optional implementation details**. 
    - `--username` is still allowed and overrides `__token__`.
    - Feature flag to turn on/off the functionality (if needed, alike `native-auth`)
- **Caching**. AFAIK current `uv` authentication workflow doesn't support probes for staleness, so if the token is cached and expired - auth will fail. The exact approach to caching might be a design discussion, baseline - no caching or few seconds caching, or more advanced with configurable lifetime. I have no strong preference, but believe it's not a blocker.
- **Security**. The vending call is done with user impersonation and execute arbitrary code without sandbox. So few points:
    - **Prohibited as part of code**. No way to specify the `token-provider` as part of any configuration provided with code. The approach does not support anything but explicit local setup using `uv auth login` call. Handling such settings as part of `pyproject.toml/uv.toml` should be prohibited by design decision.
    - **Truncate output**. Output of the vending command is truncated by some (maybe configurable) max length.
    - **Prevent leaks to logs**. Vending call response is not logged.
    - **Protect config store**. If the vending call is stored as plain text in the credentials store - there's a risk that a third-party code will mutate the settings after `uv auth` calls. So storing in native store might be a better option, but require JSON support.
    - **No dynamic context**. Vending command is bound to service URL suffix, but user is responsible to path fixed service context as part of vending call definition if needed.
    - **Not a string**. Stored as command + arg list.

 ### Existing alternatives

1. **Wrappers/shims**. In this approach the actual `uv` command call is wrapped by adding a manual `UV_INDEX_{NAME}_PASSWORD` setup. E.g.

    ```sh
    UV_INDEX_EXAMPLE_PASSWORD=$(token-provider-cli -t service_name ...) path/to/uv
    ```    

    To wrap users either use `alias` approach or create a shell script that calls `uv`. This approach suffers from few problems regarding scaling:

    - Using identically named script like `uv` that calls `uv` is not considered a good practice. It requires `PATH` modification and also binds the exact path to `uv` (to avoid cycles).
    - Using differently named scripts breaks agentic coding experience as they are well trained to use `uv`.
    - Using aliases doesn't work in non-interactive sessions.
    - Suffers in enterprises as exact approach is OS-dependent.

2.  **Keyring**. There's a path to actually quickly generate a trivial `keyring` backend that will do the wrapping of the call to a token vendor. This is a closest alternative. But let's look at configuration efforts. E.g. assume the user is fine with having `keyring` as a global `uv tool`.

    ```sh
    # install keyring with custom backend
    uv tool install keyring --with {my_backend_path}

    # further configuration of keyring might be needed (priority of backends)
    ```

    This is what outlines the experience with this approach:
    - `keyring` is famous to have unstable behavior in Linux. Since keyring initializes all backends on every call - it may fail on system keyring backend even if it's not used.
    - `{my_backend_path}` will either have to be a GIT direct link or a PyPI.org package. The reason is that we are avoiding the chicken-egg problem, we cannot install packages from private indexes yet. Publishing to PyPI.org is not always preferrable, having GIT link technically works, but requires the user to set up authentication for non-public GIT index.
    - Mess with priorities. Some users might use `keyring` somewhere else, so changing priorities globally is unwanted as they might want to have priority of system keyring higher. That will ensure that we lose time on the call to system keyring,

Title: Does a uv script access the Internet every time it runs?
Text:
Does a uv script access the Internet every time it runs?

### Question

When running a uv script with the shebang `#!/usr/bin/env -S uv run --script`, the log message `Resolving dependencies` appears briefly every time.

Does this mean that dependencies are resolved from the internet on every execution?

Also, is the same true when running commands defined in `[project.scripts]` instead of using `--script`?

### Platform

Ubuntu 26.04, Linux 7.0.0-38-generic x86_64 GNU/Linux

### Version

uv 0.12.21 (7af826859 2026-09-29 x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu)
Reply:
Can you share the contents of your script, particularly the PEP 723 metadata block?

The short answer is that running a Python script through `uv run --script` should not directly access the internet, _unless_ you've declared dependencies. If you've declared dependencies and they aren't already cached, then uv needs to access the internet to resolve them.

(Similarly, if your script's metadata requests a Python version that you don't already have, uv will download it. But that should only happen once per Python version, unless you're regularly updating your scripts to use new Python versions.)

If you want to fully force uv to stay off the network, you can pass `--offline`.

### Summary

Then, they upgrade to a new version of the direct dependency which removes that indirect dependency, or remove the direct dependency entirely. Doing so won't remove the `constraint-dependencies` entry. If nobody notices it, it is possible this `constraint-dependencies` entry may linger long after it has ceased to serve any purpose.

What if there was a setting like `require-use-dependencies = true`, which would trigger an error if an individual constraint in `constraint-dependencies` (or `build-constraint-dependencies` or `override-dependencies`) wasn't actually used? That would mean, when you removed the indirect dependency, `uv lock` would fail?

## Summary

The current SchemaStore `uv.json` schema is missing `malware-check` and `malware-check-url` under `[tool.uv.audit]`, although both settings are officially supported by uv, documented, and already included in the generated `uv.schema.json`.

Title: Bug: `uv tool upgrade` doesn't respect changes to the global `exclude-newer` setting
Text:
Bug: `uv tool upgrade` doesn't respect changes to the global `exclude-newer` setting

### Summary

When `exclude-newer` is configured globally in `~/.config/uv/uv.toml`, its value is persisted in the installed tools' `uv-receipt.toml` and `uv.lock` files.

Removing or disabling the global setting does not clear the previously stored value. Consequently, `uv tool upgrade --all`, even with `--reinstall`, continues enforcing the old cooldown and prevents upgrades to newer package versions.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Add the following to `~/.config/uv/uv.toml`:

   ```toml
   exclude-newer = "3 days"
   ```

2. Install a tool:

   ```console
   $ uv tool install black@latest
   ```

3. Disable the global setting:

   ```toml
   exclude-newer = false
   ```

   The same issue occurs when you comment out the setting or remove it entirely.

4. Upgrade all installed tools:

   ```console
   $ uv tool upgrade --all
   $ uv tool upgrade --all --reinstall
   ```

5. Inspect the installed tool's `uv-receipt.toml` and `uv.lock`.

### Actual behavior

Both files retain the previous cooldown:

**`~/.local/share/uv/tools/black/uv-receipt.toml`**

```toml
[tool.options]
exclude-newer-span = "P3D"
```

**`~/.local/share/uv/tools/black/uv.lock`**

```toml
[options]
exclude-newer-span = "P3D"
```

The original `exclude-newer` timestamps also remain unchanged. Both upgrade commands still exclude packages published within the previous three days, even though the global setting is disabled.

### Expected behavior

`uv tool upgrade` should respect the current global `exclude-newer` configuration:

- When the global setting is removed or disabled, stop enforcing the previously inherited cooldown.
- Update `uv-receipt.toml` and `uv.lock` to remove obsolete `exclude-newer` and `exclude-newer-span` values.
- Allow upgrades to newer package versions without requiring manual modification of tool metadata.
- Preserve explicitly configured per-tool settings independently of changes to the global configuration.

### Platform

Darwin 27.0.0 arm64 Darwin

### Version

uv 0.13.0 (4ecd0eff2 2026-10-09 aarch64-apple-darwin)

### Python version

Python 3.15.0
Reply: I think this is working as intended. We treat the settings used to install a tool as part of its configuration, and `upgrade` intentionally retains the settings. I think you want `uv tool install black --upgrade --config-file /path/to/uv.toml` or similar (i.e., reinstall the tool rather than upgrading it) if you're looking to change the `exclude-newer` setting.

Title: pip compile selects backports-strenum with incompatible Requires-Python for Python 3.12
Text:
pip compile selects backports-strenum with incompatible Requires-Python for Python 3.12

`uv pip compile` selects `backports-strenum==1.3.1` for Python 3.12.6 although that release declares `Requires-Python: >=3.8.6,<3.11`. Installing the result succeeds, but `uv pip check` then reports the incompatibility.

Environment: macOS arm64, CPython 3.12.6, `uv 0.12.18 (01cb90c1a 2026-09-22 aarch64-apple-darwin)`.

Reproducer (requirements.txt contains only `ai-edge-litert==2.3.0`):

```sh
uv pip compile requirements.txt --python-version 3.12.6
```

The result contains:

```text
ai-edge-litert==2.3.0
backports-strenum==1.3.1
    # via ai-edge-litert
```

LiteRT's installed metadata requires `backports.strenum` without a marker. Both PyPI JSON and installed wheel metadata for 1.3.1 declare the Python upper bound. The error from `uv pip check` is:

```text
The package `backports-strenum` requires Python >=3.8.6, <3.11, but `3.12.6` is installed
```

Expected: select a compatible release (1.2.8 declares `>=3.8.6,<4.0.0`) or fail resolution. An explicit `backports.strenum<1.3` constraint selects 1.2.8 and restores a clean dependency check. This was reproduced using a dedicated uv cache during optional model-runtime provisioning.

Metadata references: https://pypi.org/pypi/backports.strenum/1.3.1/json and https://pypi.org/pypi/backports.strenum/1.2.8/json .
Reply: That behavior is generally intended -- see [our docs](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/pip/compatibility/#requires-python-upper-bounds) on `requires-python` upper bounds which links to more details. That `uv pip check` then errors feels like an inconsistency though.

Title: `uv pip compile -o /dev/null` replaces the /dev/null device with a regular file (atomic write over non-regular files)
Text:
`uv pip compile -o /dev/null` replaces the /dev/null device with a regular file (atomic write over non-regular files)

### Summary

When run as root, `uv pip compile requirements.in -o /dev/null` deletes the `/dev/null`
character device and puts a regular file holding the compiled requirements in its place.

The cause is how the output file is written. `OutputWriter::commit()`
(`crates/uv-command-support/src/lib.rs:123`) calls `uv_fs::write_atomic()`
(`crates/uv-fs/src/lib.rs:487`). That function creates a temp file in the target's parent
directory and renames it over the target. Nothing checks first whether the target is a
device, FIFO or socket. The only special case today is following symlinks.

`-o /dev/null` is a natural thing to type when you only want to know whether a resolution
succeeds. We hit this when an automated agent did exactly that inside a Docker container,
where `/dev` is a root-writable tmpfs:

- Nothing failed visibly at first.
- From then on, every program that daemonizes with glibc's `daemon()` broke, because it
  rejects a `/dev/null` that isn't char device 1,3. For example, every new tmux server died
  with `server exited unexpectedly`.
- Anything reading `/dev/null` got stale content instead of EOF.
- It took `mknod` or a container restart to recover.

**Minimal reproduction** (uses a scratch device node instead of the real `/dev/null`):

```console
# mkdir t && cd t
# printf 'six==1.16.0\n' > req.in
# mknod -m 666 null c 1 3
# stat -c '%F %t,%T %s' null
character special file 1,3 0
# uv pip compile req.in --no-deps -o null
# This file was autogenerated by uv via the following command:
#    uv pip compile req.in --no-deps -o null
six==1.16.0
    # via -r req.in
# stat -c '%F %s' null
regular file 144
```

The same command with `-o /dev/null`, run as root, does this to the real `/dev/null`.

**Expected:** writing to an existing non-regular file, such as `/dev/null`, `/dev/stdout` or
a FIFO, opens the file and writes to it, without the temp-file-and-rename. Alternatively,
uv refuses the path with an error. It should never replace the file. For `/dev/null` (and
`NUL` on Windows) uv could simply skip writing.

Other `write_atomic` callers that take a user-supplied path probably need the same check.

### Platform

Debian 13 (trixie) x86_64, Linux 6.1.0-53-amd64, running as root in a Docker container

### Version

uv 0.13.0 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu), installed with pip

### Python version

Python 3.12.15
Reply: Sorry about that, taking a look now.

Title: `uv tool uninstall` deletes the parent of the tools directory (including the user's `uv.toml`) when the last tool is removed
Text:
`uv tool uninstall` deletes the parent of the tools directory (including the user's `uv.toml`) when the last tool is removed

### Summary

When the last installed tool is uninstalled, `uv tool uninstall` removes the tools directory and then removes its parent directory if there are no other directories present. With the default Windows layout, this deletes the user-level config file: `uv tool dir` prints `%APPDATA%\uv\tools` (despite the [uv Storage docs](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/reference/storage/#tools) suggesting that the default tools location is `%APPDATA%\uv\data\tools`), whose parent `%APPDATA%\uv` is also where the documented user config (`%APPDATA%\uv\uv.toml`) lives.

### Steps to reproduce (Windows 11, PowerShell, default uv directory locations)

Before starting, check the folder contains no other subdirectories (e.g. a uv-managed `python/`), that no tools are installed, and create a test `uv.toml`:

```shell
"# test" | Set-Content "$env:APPDATA\uv\uv.toml"
Get-ChildItem "$env:APPDATA\uv"  # Should only contain files (e.g. uv.toml) - no subdirectories.
uv tool dir  # ...\AppData\Roaming\uv\tools
uv tool list  # No tools installed.
```

Install a tool:

```shell
uv tool install cowsay
Get-ChildItem "$env:APPDATA\uv"  # Should only contain tools/ and uv.toml if using non-uv-managed Python.
```

Uninstall the tool:

```shell
uv tool uninstall cowsay
Test-Path "$env:APPDATA\uv\uv.toml"  # False (expected True)
Test-Path "$env:APPDATA\uv"  # False (expected True)
```

#### Expected behaviour

Only the tool environment and its executables are removed. Files uv didn't create, such as the user's `uv.toml`, are left alone.

#### Actual behaviour

The parent of the tools directory is deleted along with every file in it, including `uv.toml`.

### Notes

- `uv tool install` doesn't delete anything, only `uv tool uninstall`.
- It only happens when the last tool is uninstalled. With another tool installed, nothing is cleaned up.
- Loose files in the parent don't protect it, only other subdirectories do (e.g. add a `test/` folder and `uv/` will be kept - the same logic applies to `python/` and `credentials/` subdirectories in `uv/`.
- `-v`, `-vv`, and `-vvv` output only shows the tool environment and executable being removed, with no message about the parent directory. For example, `-vvv` output shows:

```text
DEBUG Searching for user configuration in: ...\AppData\Roaming\uv\uv.toml
DEBUG Found user configuration in: ...\AppData\Roaming\uv\uv.toml
DEBUG uv 0.13.0 (4ecd0eff2 2026-10-09 x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
TRACE Checking lock for `AppData\Roaming\uv\tools` at `AppData\Roaming\uv\tools\.lock`
TRACE Acquired exclusive lock for `AppData\Roaming\uv\tools`
DEBUG Deleting environment for tool `cowsay` at `AppData\Roaming\uv\tools\cowsay`
DEBUG Removing executable: .local/bin/cowsay.exe
Uninstalled 1 executable: cowsay
TRACE Released lock at `...\AppData\Roaming\uv\tools\.lock`
```

### Possible cause

The "Clean up any empty directories" block at the end of `uninstall` in `crates/uv-tool-commands/src/uninstall.rs` seems to remove the tools root once all directories under it are temporary, then repeats the check on the root's parent:

```rust
// Clean up any empty directories.
if uv_fs::directories(installed_tools.root())?.all(|path| uv_fs::is_temporary(&path)) {
    fs_err::tokio::remove_dir_all(&installed_tools.root())
        .await
        .ignore_currently_being_deleted()?;
    if let Some(parent) = installed_tools.root().parent() {
        if uv_fs::directories(parent)?.all(|path| uv_fs::is_temporary(&path)) {
            fs_err::tokio::remove_dir_all(parent)
                .await
                .ignore_currently_being_deleted()?;
        }
    }
}
```

#### Possible fix

If I've read the above correctly, I suggest either making the tools directory `uv\data\tools` rather than `uv\tools` (as noted in the storage docs), or only remove the parent if it is actually empty (e.g. swap `remove_dir_all(parent)` with `remove_dir(parent)`).

### Platform

Windows 11 x86

### Version

uv 0.13.0 (4ecd0eff2 2026-10-09 x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)

### Python version

Python 3.12.5
Reply: Sorry about that, taking a look now.

Title: Bug: `uv tool upgrade --all` reports `Nothing to upgrade` despite outdated tools
Text:
Bug: `uv tool upgrade --all` reports `Nothing to upgrade` despite outdated tools

## Summary

On `uv` 0.13.0, `uv tool list --outdated` identifies newer package versions, but `uv tool upgrade --all` reports `Nothing to upgrade` without updating them.

This behavior was previously reported in #18522 and #19704, both closed as completed, but it still occurs.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Install a tool using `@latest`, without any version constraints such as `<` or `<=`:

   ```console
   $ uv tool install tombi@latest
   ```

2. Once a newer version becomes available, check for outdated tools:

   ```console
   $ uv tool list --outdated
   tombi v1.8.1 [latest: 1.8.4]

3. Attempt to upgrade all installed tools:

   ```console
   $ uv tool upgrade --all
   Nothing to upgrade
   ```

**Additional context:**

- The tool was installed using `uv tool install tombi@latest`, without any upper-bound version constraints.
- No `exclude-newer` setting is configured.
- The installed version remains outdated despite a newer version being available.

### Expected behavior

`uv tool upgrade --all` should upgrade outdated tools to the latest versions allowed by their installation constraints and effective configuration.

If an upgrade is prevented by a version constraint or another setting, `uv` should explain why rather than reporting `Nothing to upgrade`.

### Actual behavior

`uv tool list --outdated` identifies `tombi` 1.8.4 as available, but `uv tool upgrade --all` reports `Nothing to upgrade` and leaves version 1.8.1 installed, despite having no version constraints or `exclude-newer` configuration preventing the upgrade.

Title: 0.13.0: `uv build` rejects sdists whose group name is ≥32 characters ("invalid ustar gname field: missing NUL terminator")
Text:
0.13.0: `uv build` rejects sdists whose group name is ≥32 characters ("invalid ustar gname field: missing NUL terminator")

### Summary

Since 0.13.0 made the new tar backend the default, `uv build` fails to build a wheel from an sdist created by CPython's `tarfile` (and therefore setuptools) when the file group name is 32 characters or longer.

CPython's `tarfile` fills the full 32-byte ustar `gname` field with no NUL terminator in that case. For names longer than 32 characters, it also writes the full name in a pax `gname` record. uv 0.12.24, `UV_LEGACY_TAR_BACKEND=1`, GNU tar and Python's `tarfile` all accept these archives.

We hit this in Azure Pipelines container jobs. The agent maps the host build user and its (long, domain) group into the container, so every setuptools-backed `uv build` began failing after the runner picked up 0.13.0.

### Minimal reproduction

```python
# make_sdist.py
import io, sys, tarfile

n = int(sys.argv[1])  # group name length
files = {
    "demo-0.1.0/pyproject.toml": b'[project]\nname = "demo"\nversion = "0.1.0"\n[build-system]\nrequires = ["setuptools>=77"]\nbuild-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"\n',
    "demo-0.1.0/demo/__init__.py": b"",
    "demo-0.1.0/PKG-INFO": b"Metadata-Version: 2.1\nName: demo\nVersion: 0.1.0\n",
}
with tarfile.open("demo-0.1.0.tar.gz", "w:gz", format=tarfile.PAX_FORMAT) as t:
    for name, data in files.items():
        info = tarfile.TarInfo(name)
        info.size = len(data)
        info.gname = "g" * n
        t.addfile(info, io.BytesIO(data))
```

```console
$ python make_sdist.py 40
$ uvx uv@0.13.0 build --wheel demo-0.1.0.tar.gz
error: Failed to build `<tmp>/demo-0.1.0.tar.gz`
  cause: Invalid tar file
  cause: at byte 1024: invalid ustar gname field: missing NUL terminator
  cause: invalid ustar gname field: missing NUL terminator
```

### Results by group name length

| gname length | uv 0.13.0 | uv 0.13.0 + `UV_LEGACY_TAR_BACKEND=1` | uv 0.12.24 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 31 | ✅ builds | — | — |
| 32 | ❌ fails `at byte 0` | — | ✅ builds |
| 40 | ❌ fails `at byte 1024` (pax header precedes the entry) | ✅ builds | ✅ builds |

### Expected behavior

- A 32-byte `uname`/`gname` field with no NUL terminator should be accepted, as uv 0.12 did and as GNU tar and Python's `tarfile` do. CPython writes this form itself.
- When a pax `gname` record is present, it overrides the ustar field. The truncated ustar value shouldn't cause a hard failure at all.

Possibly related 0.13.0 tar-backend regression: #22492 (a different failure: hard-link members).

### Workaround

`UV_LEGACY_TAR_BACKEND=1`, or `uv build --wheel` from the source tree, which skips building an sdist.

### Platform

Windows 11 x86_64 (also reproduced in CI on Linux x86_64, Azure Pipelines container job)

### Version

uv 0.13.0 (4ecd0eff2 2026-10-09)

### Python version

Python 3.13.12
Reply: \cc @woodruffw

Title: Error with venv activation command for ksh on OpenBSD
Text:
Error with venv activation command for ksh on OpenBSD

On OpenBSD OS, `ksh` is the default shell (see https://man.openbsd.org/ksh).

With the latest version of `uv` (built from Git sources with Rust v1.98.1), creation of a virtual env. with `uv venv` command:
```sh
openbsd-dev$ echo $KSH_VERSION
@(#)PD KSH v5.2.14 99/07/13.2
openbsd-dev$ uv -V
uv 0.13.0 (x86_64-unknown-openbsd)

openbsd-dev$ uv venv
Using CPython 3.14.8 interpreter at: /usr/local/bin/python
Creating virtual environment at: .venv
Activate with: source .venv/bin/activate
```

There is an **error when trying to activate venv** with the described command:
```sh
openbsd-dev$ source .venv/bin/activate
ksh: source: not found
```

Indeed, on OpenBSD with ksh shell, **`source` command does not exist**. To activate virtual env, the correct command is `. .venv/bin/activate`.

To fix this issue (output of venv activate command with ksh), I propose to modify this function (new case for `Shell::Ksh`) in `crates/uv/src/commands/venv.rs`:
https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/blob/a79aac95dc8f1d79e4396fdcb262d22c520cc1f6/crates/uv/src/commands/venv.rs#L389-L394

---

NB: I'm the **official maintainer of OpenBSD port for `uv`**, see https://github.com/openbsd/ports/blob/master/devel/uv/Makefile

Title: Installers PATH shim named `env` shadows coreutils env, silently swallowing every `env` invocation (exit 0, command never runs)
Text:
Installers PATH shim named `env` shadows coreutils env, silently swallowing every `env` invocation (exit 0, command never runs)

The `~/.tmp/opencode/uvbin` path in that report is only the `--install-prefix` the reporter happened to choose when installing uv. OpenCode is not involved in generating the shim: its own installer writes only `export PATH=$INSTALL_DIR:\$PATH`, and `cleanShellConfig()` in its uninstaller only strips `.opencode/bin` PATH entries.

## Summary

`uv self update` / the standalone installer, when `modify_path` is enabled, creates a script named `env` inside the install prefix and sources it from the user's shell rc files. When that install prefix is on `PATH` (which is what `modify_path` arranges), the script shadows the system `env` binary and **silently swallows every `env` invocation**, because it only mutates `PATH` and never executes `"$@"`.

## Where this is created

All line numbers refer to the generated installer script, `https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh`.

**1. The path is computed — line 1257.** The filename is hardcoded:

```bash
_env_script_path="$_force_install_dir/env"
```

With `--install-prefix ~/.tmp/opencode/uvbin` this resolves to `~/.tmp/opencode/uvbin/env`. Sibling branches at 1265 and 1273 cover the other install layouts; 1289, 1301 and 1313 are the `XDG_BIN_HOME`, `XDG_DATA_HOME` and `~/.local/bin` fallbacks.

**2. The fish twin is derived — line 1326:**

```bash
_fish_env_script_path="${_env_script_path}.fish"
```

**3. The file is written — called at line 1539, defined at line 1614** (`write_env_script_fish` is called at 1541, defined at 1633):

```bash
write_env_script_sh "$_install_dir_expr" "$_env_script_path"
```

```bash
write_env_script_sh() {
    ensure cat <<EOF > "$_env_script_path"
#!/bin/sh
# add binaries to PATH if they aren't added yet
# affix colons on either side of \$PATH to simplify matching
case ":\${PATH}:" in
    *:"$_install_dir_expr":*)
        ;;
    *)
        # Prepending path in case a system-installed binary needs to be overridden
        export PATH="$_install_dir_expr:\$PATH"
        ;;
esac
EOF
}
```

The script is never given the executable bit and never contains an `exec`. It is built purely to be sourced.

**4. The rc line is added — line 1409, written at line 1532:**

```bash
add_install_dir_to_path "$_install_dir_expr" "$_env_script_path" "$_env_script_path_expr" \
  ".profile .bashrc .bash_profile .bash_login" "sh"
```

```bash
local _robust_line=". \"$_env_script_path_expr\""
```

That is the `. "$HOME/.tmp/opencode/uvbin/env"` line that ends up in `~/.bashrc` and `~/.profile`.

## Why this collides

`_env_script_path` **is the install directory itself**, and step 4 puts that directory on `PATH`. So the installer writes a source-only script to a path that is simultaneously on `PATH` under the name `env` — reachable as the coreutils binary, where the missing `exec` turns every invocation into a silent no-op.

The comment at lines 1490-1494 shows the indirection was a deliberate choice, so it could be added to many rc files and run repeatedly without problems, and stay compatible with rustup's own layout. The gap is that this solves idempotency for *sourcing* without accounting for the file also being reachable as an *executable*.

## The script as generated

For reference, this is the file written on the affected machine, byte for byte:

```sh
#!/bin/sh
# add binaries to PATH if they aren't added yet
# affix colons on either side of $PATH to simplify matching
case ":${PATH}:" in
    *:"/home/USER/.tmp/opencode/uvbin":*)
        ;;
    *)
        # Prepending path in case a system-installed binary needs to be overridden
        export PATH="/home/USER/.tmp/opencode/uvbin:$PATH"
        ;;
esac
```

Confirmed against `~/.config/uv/uv-receipt.json` on that machine:

```json
{"binaries":["uv","uvx"],"install_layout":"flat",
 "install_prefix":"/home/USER/.tmp/opencode/uvbin",
 "modify_path":true,"provider":{"source":"cargo-dist","version":"0.32.0"},
 "source":{"app_name":"uv","owner":"astral-sh"},"version":"0.13.0"}
```

## Impact

Any program on the system that resolves `env` through `PATH` gets the shim instead:

```console
$ env FOO=bar /bin/echo HELLO
$ echo $?
0
```

The command never runs, nothing is printed, and the exit status is 0. Because the exit status is 0, the caller cannot detect the failure.

This affects unrelated tooling, not just uv. Anything that builds a command through `env` is affected, which is a common pattern for:

- sanitizing an environment before exec'ing another program (`env -u VAR cmd`)
- cluster/job wrappers that construct a remote command with `env -u ...`
- build and test harnesses that rely on `env`'s exit status to detect failure

A concrete hit I came across: a job wrapper ran its remote command as `srun --pty env -u TMUX -u TMUX_TMPDIR tmux new-session -A`. The step exited 0, the command was never launched, and the wrapper reported success while doing nothing.

## Reproduction

```bash
# install with a prefix that is on PATH and modify_path enabled
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

# the shim shadows the real env
command -v env

# it swallows the command and still reports success
env FOO=bar /bin/echo HELLO; echo "exit=$?"
# -> (no output)
# -> exit=0

# the real binary is unaffected
/usr/bin/env FOO=bar /bin/echo HELLO; echo "exit=$?"
# -> HELLO
# -> exit=0
```

## Suggested fix

Preserve the sourcing behaviour while making execution behave correctly. Keying the check on `$0` rather than `$#` is important: the script is *sourced*, and when sourced, `$#` is the **caller's** argument count, so an unguarded `exec "$@"` would replace a sourcing script that has its own arguments and prevent it from ever finishing.

```sh
#!/bin/sh
# add binaries to PATH if they aren't added yet
# affix colons on either side of $PATH to simplify matching
case ":${PATH}:" in
    *:"/path/to/uvbin":*)
        ;;
    *)
        # Prepending path in case a system-installed binary need

Title: license-file globs find non-license files and complain about encoding
Text:
license-file globs find non-license files and complain about encoding

### Summary

I discovered this issue while experimenting with switching pip over to use `uv-build`, as part of research for a blog post. Pip is a pure Python project, but it does make heavy use of vendoring, and thus transitively includes some "data" files (in particular, precompiled stub executables used by `packaging` on Windows). It also keeps vendor licenses with the vendored code in the source tree.

Minimal "narrative" reproducer:

```
$ tree
.
├── dist
├── LICENSE.txt
├── pyproject.toml
└── src
    └── zzz
        ├── __init__.py
        └── _vendor
            ├── LICENSE.txt
            └── thing.bin

5 directories, 5 files
$
$ cat pyproject.toml 
[project]
version = "0.1.0"
name = "zzz"
description = "zzz"
license = "MIT"
license-files = [
  "LICENSE.txt",
  "src/zzz/_vendor/**/LICENSE.txt",
]
[build-system]
requires = ["uv_build>=0.13.1,<0.14"]
build-backend = "uv_build"
$
$ xxd src/zzz/_vendor/thing.bin 
00000000: ff                                       .
$
$ uv build --wheel
Building wheel...
Error: Invalid project metadata

Caused by:
    License file `src/zzz/_vendor/thing.bin` must be UTF-8 encoded
  × Failed to build `/path/to/zzz`
  ├─▶ The build backend returned an error
  ╰─▶ Call to `uv_build.build_wheel` failed (exit status: 1)

hint: Build failures usually indicate a problem with the package or the build environment
```
Here, we imagine that `thing.bin` is a binary data resource used by the code at runtime. `uv-build` seems to treat it as if it were a license file, suggesting that the glob in `license-files` is not being correctly processed — it should only match the vendored license file. (It would of course be catastrophic to try to force UTF-8 encoding onto such a file.)

It's perhaps expected that `thing.bin` wouldn't end up in the wheel built by uv-build by default, but adding a `[tool.uv.build-backend]` table with a `data` key doesn't solve the problem. (And would also not be workable in general; many real-world projects don't leverage `importlib.resources` and expect to find their data at paths relative to the source code, so redirecting them to the wheel's `.data` directory would also be disruptive.) 

Removing `**` from the glob *does* suppress the error; but then `thing.bin` remains in the wheel in its current location and so does the vendor license (in addition to being added to the `.dist-info/licenses`).

Even without specifically using data files, the error *is also triggered by cached bytecode, even though* it's inside a `__pycache__` folder which would normally be ignored. This produces very confusing errors for anyone who wants to have licenses side-by-side with vendored code in the source tree, unless bytecode caches are cleared before building.

### Platform

Linux Mint 22.3 (Linux 6.8.0-146-generic x86_64 GNU/Linux)

### Version

uv 0.11.25 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu)

### Python version

Python 3.12.3
